Cillus Vot Shayron-Skoln INTACT

A prince of the blood who wanted to be a war correspondent, and got what he asked for.

Ginger, a deep earthy orange rather than a bright one, shaved close at the sides with just enough length on top to curl. Clear skin. Tall and toned without being strong, and not thin either. His eyes read as big without actually being big, and that is the whole problem with his face: it announces, from across a landing pad, that nothing has ever happened to him.

Softly spoken. Endearing before he has said anything worth being endeared by.

He grew up behind castle walls on Shayron with everything arranged for him, and left specifically to find out what the galaxy actually looks like. What he found was worse than he had pictured.

How a Royal ends up with a Guard squad

The Royal forces and the Guard are close. They train together, exercise together, and lend each other people, in the way two friendly militaries always have. A Royal journalist embedded with Guard formations is unusual but not strange, and he volunteered for it expecting routine work: a few weeks with a line unit, some morale footage, a report home about ordinary business.

He shoots footage of squads for exactly that purpose, and at one point he shoots Squad 412 celebrating with looted goods.

What he wears

A religious pendant, given rather than bought, and he does not take it off.

The colony recovery detail RECOVERED

The Guard element that walked the Corefuel colony after the raid, and the two men in it who matter.

The soldier who lifted the floorboard

He did it because it was the next board. He was not searching for anybody. That is the whole thing: a routine sweep of a burned house, done properly, by somebody who had no reason to expect anything under there.

The officer

He read the station chief off a scan, marked him killed in action, and closed the family out on an assumption spoken flatly enough that it was clearly not the first time he had said it.

Corporal Billem RECOVERED

The man who was in charge, and the reason somebody else ended up in charge.

What happened to him

He was breaching a door on a cartel compound when one of his own people put a fragmentation grenade through a house that should have taken a flashbang. Every gas tank in the building went up. A second later the rounds came through the door he was standing in, and took his leg out from under him.

He killed the man who shot him before he sat down, and reported it in one word that does not appear anywhere else in this archive.

"I frosted the fucking Crag that shot me, so it's clear here."

How he took it

Mask off, back against a wall, one hand pressed hard into his own thigh, and furious. Not at the wound. At the man who caused it, who was standing four feet away and is described in the record only as Private Dumbass.

"Look I'll be fine, but I just cannot keep up with you."

That sentence is the whole of him. He is bleeding, he is not getting up, and the part he chooses to say out loud is an apology for slowing the assault down.

What it cost, and what it did

Six or seven hostiles were still holed up in the compound. He could not go. So a staff sergeant took three men forward and finished it, and the returns for that action read zero Guard fatalities, the principal captured alive, the compound intact, followed by the phrase that gets him into this volume at all: all without a corporal.

He stayed on the net the entire time, running the evacuation from the floor.

"Copy that. EVAC is about an hour out. Regroup at entry."

Afterwards

The ankle is described by a friend as being in about a million pieces, and the same friend reckons he is quietly relieved: he had been going out every other week for a long time, and a stretch in a hospital bed is the first uninterrupted rest anybody has been able to give him.

[Compiler's note: the grenade is attributed in one place to a private on his own team and in another to a named man on the team that came to help him. Both accounts are held here. Somebody, on the day, decided to cover for somebody.]

Daiser INTACT

Caretaker of the Council's temple at Riflo, and the sharpest person in the building.

He is introduced to offworlders as the Gatekeeper, which is what the job is called and not what he is. He opens the great oak doors, receives you, and shows you where to stand, and it is very easy to treat him as furniture for the first ten minutes.

"He's not just a gatekeeper. His name is Daiser. He's... like you. Someone surviving the pressure. Don't add more weight to his shoulders."

A Maspin: smoke and vapour, water where the eyes should be, an ember behind it all that brightens when he is enjoying himself, which is often.

The situation

He is indentured. Sentenced to work off a debt that exists on paper and nowhere else, with seven years still on it and no wage to buy it out with. His holder is an establishment controlled by his own uncle, who sits on the Council. Everybody involved regards this as normal, including, most of the time, Daiser.

"We call it indentured servitude. Where I work off an imaginary debt until I can pay it off and be free, which is actually fucking hard without a paycheck."

The way out is his uncle dying or a lottery that does not exist.

Before that

A chemist, and a properly trained one. He can make things most people cannot get, including weapons that are banned on his own world.

How he talks

Two registers, switched instantly. Street with anyone he likes. An elaborate, over-polished formal voice for anyone with authority, deployed with a completely straight face, which is its own kind of insult.

He has never flown. He has never been off Maspin at all. He can fly, though, and when asked where he learned he says a book or two, which is either a joke or the most alarming sentence in the temple.

Whoever is on shift at the far end of the Maspin decon cycle, waiting for you to be finished being sick.

Diontesheempluntornskalla (Dan) TESTIMONY

A councillor of Riflo, and the one who will actually talk to you.

The full name is real and he does not expect anyone offworld to attempt it. Dan is what he offers, immediately, with no ceremony about it, which is exactly how Maspin names work: the long one is inherited, and the short one is the one that stuck.

His seat is harmony

Not defence, not trade, not rites. His job on that Council is the agreement between people, and he holds it because he believes real strength is empathy and restraint rather than the other thing.

He is the one who collects the Gift of Memory at the festival, and he takes his time about it.

Dometré Polaris CONTESTED

A prince of the blood who appeared once, in one room, agreed to terms on behalf of a Royal house, and cannot be found in any register anywhere.

What is on the record

He was received in full session at the Council Chamber of Riflo and addressed by the centre councillor as Prince Dometré Polaris, negotiator for the House of Kafkee, Flamebearer. The Council took the minute in its own hand and in its own script, as it does, and has never amended it.

"May your shadow burn long."

The terms he agreed

Ten million in Royal scrip, against long neglect. One unit of Royal soldiers, to hold the shipping lanes against piracy. And a Gift of Memory.

The first two are ordinary instruments. The third is not something a Royal house has ever been asked for, and there is no precedent anywhere in this archive for a crown party accepting one.

The problem with the name

Polaris and Kafkee are separate houses. A Polaris carrying a Kafkee ceremonial office is not forbidden and is also not filed, anywhere, in any register we hold, for anybody. The Royal lists carry no Dometré. They also carry a very great many thin-blooded claimants who are entitled to a seat and a small maintenance and appear on no list at all, which is precisely why this entry is contested rather than closed.

What the room made of him

Not much, at first. One elder stated she had already seen his face, in a vision, kneeling, in the posture of a servant. Another observed that his father had stood on the same floor and lied without his flame so much as flickering. He was tested on songcraft, on the ground that the Royals were once said to sing at every rite, and an exemption was produced on his behalf from the Elder Harmonists.

"Your tongue wears the sand of other stars, boy. Not Polaris rain."

Then his pendant answered theirs, and the room changed. What was said afterwards is recorded as a rare sign, for the family, and as sacred, he may be.

The beard

He wore one. The Royal court requires its household and its blood to go clean-shaven, by long ceremonial rule, and has for as long as there has been a court. Nobody in the chamber raised it. Everybody outside it has.

Since

No soldiers arrived. No payment was made. The Council has not withdrawn the minute, has not written to any house, and declines to discuss the matter with this archive.

[Compiler's note: a man walked into the one room on that world where a decision happens, gave a name, and left with an agreement. We can tell you what he promised to the credit. We cannot tell you that he exists.]

Dorch Rawlden TESTIMONY

Son of Grai Penston Rawlden, aged about twenty-three. He holds a junior post in the municipal administration of Crescent City and has held no other.

Standing

He was born outside marriage, at a time when his father was already a senior figure, and to Entonia Yalenti, a journalist working within the limits the statutes allow, who had been attached to his father when both were young, and who is dead. She died of a cancer attributed to industrial contamination in the town where she and Rawlden were both raised. Rawlden has the same disease. The administration promotes monogamy as stated policy on the grounds that it is stabilising, and he is the publicly known exception to it.

He carries his father's name. On a world where children born outside a marriage frequently do not, this is generally read as an acknowledgement rather than as a courtesy, and it is the only formal thing anybody can point to in his position. No instrument defines his standing and no office is reserved for him.

The post

Dorch is responsible for scheduling refuse collection across several districts of the capital. It is unimportant work, it is done adequately, and he applied for it himself against open advertisement.

Informants who deal with the administration are consistent that he is given nothing of consequence, and equally consistent that this is not a punishment or a precaution. He has never asked for anything of consequence. Several describe him as tired in a way that is unusual at his age.

What he is reported to want

To live offworld under his own name and be no relation to anybody. This is said by people who know him and is not said by him in any account held here.

Why he has not gone

He is frightened. Of the galaxy, from what reaches him about it, and by several accounts of his own world as well.

He is also, so far as this archive can establish, the one person on Pashmirské who could leave without asking. Everybody else who has departed in the last decade was put on a ship and told not to return.

Sources

Four informants, three of them former municipal employees and one deported under the second chance. None has described a conversation with him lasting more than a few minutes.

Entonia Yalenti TESTIMONY

A journalist of Pashmirské, mother of Dorch Rawlden, and the only person in this part of the record whose account of the town was published anywhere.

The work

Journalism on Pashmirské operates within statutory limits on speech, and Yalenti worked inside them. What that permitted is narrower than the word suggests elsewhere in this volume. She is not reported to have been obstructed, and she is not reported to have tested it.

The town

She and Rawlden were raised in the same place. The air and the water there were contaminated by industrial discharge across a long period, and both of them developed cancers of a kind that presents unusually early.

The contamination was a condition of the war. Nothing could be done about it while the fighting continued. It was cleaned by Rawlden's administration once he held the capital, at public expense, and completely.

The people who grew up drinking it are a separate matter and were not cleaned.

The relationship

She and Rawlden were attached to one another when both were young and separately again, much later, for approximately two weeks. Dorch Rawlden is her son.

She did not marry, did not hold any position in the administration, and is not recorded as having sought either.

Death

She died of the disease. The date is not held here.

The Friend TESTIMONY

the Maspin shaman

Ask for the shaman on Maspin and you will be corrected. He would rather you called him Friend.

He smiles in a way people describe, without prompting and in almost the same words, as soft and ancient.

What he does

Nobody outside is clear. He is present at the festival, he is consulted about people who are dying, and the Trailblazer surgeon at Base Delta credits him with stopping a man from bleeding out through a hole in the heart, and then walking that man back to a vehicle afterwards.

Finding him

You do not. Ask a Maspin child where the shaman is and you will get a straight answer:

"You don't find the shaman. The shaman finds you."

Two things that unsettle visitors

He knows names he has not been told. And he has been known to leave something at the medbay for a person before that person arrived on the world, with instructions about who to say it came from.

Grai Penston Rawlden RECOVERED

styled Kon-Grai

Grai Penston Rawlden is the sole governing authority of Pashmirské. He is approximately fifty-eight years old. He commanded the principal military formation on the world during the later part of the hundred and fifty year conflict and holds no office that existed before him.

Origins

Rawlden was raised poor, in a town whose air and water were contaminated by industrial discharge across a long period. Everybody there drank it. Nobody there had the means to do anything else, and while the war continued nobody at any level had the means to do anything about the discharge either.

Before the capital

Rawlden was a general. His background is logistics rather than command in the field, and accounts credit his standing at the end of the war to the fact that he had spent decades keeping formations supplied in conditions where supply was the difficulty.

The civil population was aware throughout that the war was continuing. When he offered stability, he was permitted to remain.

Accession

Rawlden did not win the war. The two powers that had funded the conflict destroyed one another, after which the money and the resupply ended and the fighting declined over approximately sixty years. He held the capital when it stopped. The consolidation that followed was carried out largely by administration rather than by force, against factions that were by then without ammunition, without a patron and without any further offer to make.

Title

Rawlden is styled Kon-Grai, a Nhathian term for a leader, formed from kon, north, and grai, stone. He is not Nhath and has never met one. No contract, correspondence or recorded contact exists between him and that people. He appears to have taken the term from reading.

Accounts of him consistently note that he reads a great deal and that the Nhath are a long-standing interest of his.

He does not speak the language. He has perhaps a few dozen words of it.

Nhathian provides no neutral term for a person outside the Nhath. Krayd serves for they, for other species and for enemy. A person outside that people using their word for a leader is making a claim the language has no form for. Nobody on Pashmirské raises this and nobody has been recorded asking Rawlden about it.

Rawlden's given name is Grai, which is the same word as the second element of the title. It has not been established whether the resemblance influenced his choice.

He also uses the term Fonty, from the Nhathian Fon-Ty, meaning a subordinate. He writes it without the hyphen.

Administration

Rawlden governs with a cabinet. Appointments are made on loyalty to him and on a record of completing work, and he does not tolerate corruption in any part of the administration. Bribery is not a route to anything under his authority, and informants from several trades confirm this without prompting.

He lives modestly. No residence, household or personal holding of any scale is attributed to him by any account held here.

Marriage

Rawlden is married to Sershanti Rawlden, formerly Kinsley, and has been throughout. The administration promotes monogamy as stated policy on the grounds that it is stabilising.

He conducted an affair lasting approximately two weeks, acknowledged it rather than denying it, and separated from his wife for a period. They reconciled. He offered a divorce and she declined it. Accounts from people close to the household are consistent that the refusal was a decision about position rather than about him, and that the marriage has been maintained since as a working arrangement that both parties present as a stable one.

Entonia Yalenti

A journalist, working within the limits the statutes allow for that work, and attached to Rawlden when both were young. She is dead.

She and Rawlden were raised in the same town. Both developed cancers of early onset, and the account given by both of them is that the air and the water there were contaminated by industrial discharge over a long period.

Family

Rawlden has one son by Yalenti, Dorch Rawlden, aged about twenty-three, born outside the marriage and a publicly known exception to the policy. His standing is not defined by any instrument. He holds a junior post in the municipal administration of Crescent City and is catalogued separately.

Every account agrees on two things: that Rawlden regards the affair as a wrong he committed, and that he loves the boy.

Manner

Rawlden speaks without notes. Every account describes him as quick, dry and unusually well constructed in the moment, to the extent that listeners routinely assume he has prepared and rehearsed. Nobody has produced a text of anything he has said.

The amnesty

Soldiers of the defeated factions were offered amnesty on taking an oath, and the offer was general rather than case by case. It was honoured. Informants from three of the former factions confirm this.

The faction leadership was deported. Rawlden has allowed it to be understood that a number of them were killed. None were.

Government

Rawlden's stated position is that a population which has been at war for a hundred and fifty years does not require political ideals, and requires food, water, shelter, safety and an absence of shelling. He has said publicly that taxes are collected, that obedience is expected, that certain liberties are not available under his authority and that some of his subjects are afraid of him. He does not describe the arrangement as democratic, free or just and has not claimed a mandate for it. He has also stated that he wants the position and intends to keep it. Accounts agree that he presents none of this as a responsibility reluctantly accepted.

The address

No complete text of Rawlden's principal public address has been recovered. It survives as a set of fragments, quoted by people who were present, of which three recur in almost every account.

The first concerns a widow whose husband had been her sweetheart at school, died badly, and called for his mother at the end, and who was told afterwards that he had died for freedom. Rawlden's stated objection is that the sentence returned nothing to her.

The second concerns young soldiers who were told they were about to die for a democracy in a war none of them had voted in.

The third is a single line and is the fragment most often quoted.

"You have food. You have water. You have a roof. Nobody is shooting at you. What the fuck else do you want?"

Informants agree that the passages between these fragments describe injuries and deaths from the conflict in detail. Those who have discussed the address state that the descriptions are placed immediately before the list of provisions he supplies, and are intended as a comparison.

The remediation

One of the earliest acts of the administration was the cleaning of the contaminated ground and water in the industrial districts, including the town Rawlden was raised in. It was carried out at public expense, it was completed, and it is not commemorated anywhere.

Nothing in it reaches the people who grew up drinking the water. That population is now in middle age.

Observance

Speech is restricted by statute, dress is regulated in certain respects, and attendance at a calendar of public festivals is compulsory.

The festivals do not concern Rawlden. There is no portrait of him in a public building, no honorific in daily use, and nothing addressed to him. What they commemorate is the world as it was before the war, at its furthest extent and its most accomplished, and the observances are constructed to be moving.

Expansion

Rawlden has raised the possibility of territorial expansion in cabinet and has not acted on it. The stated reason is that the population is not ready.

Dissent

Rawlden's stated policy on political dissent is imprisonment under strict conditions or public execution. Neither is carried out. Persons removed for dissent are subjected to a staged execution and then deported, and the practice is catalogued separately.

The distinction is not published and Rawlden has never corrected the public account. The reputation is maintained deliberately and the killing is not.

Health

Rawlden has a cancer of a class that was routinely preventable before the war and for which no formulation now survives anywhere. It is attributed to the town. Yalenti was raised there also and died of the same thing.

He did not know he had it when he went to war. It was present and undiagnosed for a long period, and it accelerated after he took the capital.

There is no treatment. What there is instead is machinery. His legs have failed progressively and he uses prosthetics. Several organs have been replaced with mechanical substitutes and his heart is regulated. The replacements are engineered rather than grown, they are not a close fit, and they impose limits on what he can do and for how long. He is maintained rather than cured, and by any ordinary description of the term he is on life support.

None of it is public. The effort of keeping it from being public is itself considerable, and every account of him at a public event describes a man who appears entirely well, for as long as the event lasts.

He is on record, from before any of it, as objecting to prosthetics. He has not withdrawn the position and has never been asked to reconcile it with his own body.

The condition is not public. It is recorded here on the testimony of three people who have no connection to one another, two of whom were deported and one of whom was not.

Security

There have been repeated attempts on Rawlden's life. Informants put the number between nine and nineteen and agree that most were poorly prepared. The former faction leadership is offworld, alive, and in several cases has said publicly what it would like to see happen to him.

He is described by everybody who has been near him as careful in a manner that is proportionate to this rather than in excess of it.

Relations with the Guard

There is no relationship. No application, refusal, incident or complaint is recorded in either direction. Rawlden is reported to hold a low opinion of the organisation and to have no intention of acting against it.

His own account of himself

Rawlden describes what he does as wrong and does not qualify it. His position, given consistently and without being asked, is that a world of this kind will produce a certain amount of harm regardless, that it is better carried by one person who has agreed to carry it than distributed among many who have not, and that he has agreed. He does not expect anything afterward and says so.

Informants divide on this. Some hold that it is the most honest thing any of them has heard from a person in power. Others hold that a man who enjoys authority as plainly as this one does has found an unusually good reason to keep it, and that the two accounts are not exclusive.

Sources

No document issued over Rawlden's name is held here. There is no portrait, no service record and no account of his life prior to his holding the capital. The material in this entry comes from people who have met him, and their accounts are unusually consistent with one another.

Graves RECOVERED

The oldest of the five sent to Sonaff, which is why he ended up in charge of them.

Nobody appointed him. There were five people in a blizzard outside a sealed hangar, not one of them infantry, and he was the one who had been in longest, so he gave the orders.

"Plan? Stay in position, shoot anything you see that isn't me."

That is the entire plan, and given what he had to work with it is not a bad one.

Grugg Treeleaf RECOVERED

Carried in unconscious, admitted under a name he did not give, and that is the name he has now.

What happened

A medevac out of jungle country on Maspin, with three men in it and one of them past speaking. Somebody else supplied his name on the radio. The base took it down, the medbay admitted him under it, and every subsequent line of his treatment, his theatre time and his discharge sits in that file under that name.

He was not asked and could not have answered. By the time anybody could have corrected it, it had been written eleven times.

The name itself

Treeleaf is a Maspin surname in the ordinary Maspin pattern, which is to say a tree, taken by the household that raised you. It is unremarkable and it is local.

Grugg is not a Maspin word, is not a Maspin sound, and does not occur anywhere else in our material.

So the name is half of one world and half of nowhere, joined at a medevac, and there is no arrangement under which a person would have arrived at it themselves.

Condition on admission

The record is specific about the injury and vague about the man. Facial. Extensive. He lived.

Since

No follow-up, no transfer, no next of kin contacted, and no correction ever filed. The file is closed and correct and in that name.

[Compiler's note: three men gave three names on one call and only one of them was in a condition to be lying. This archive is a great many files exactly like this one, and we normally do not notice, because normally there is nobody left to be wrong about.]

The Guard nurses RECOVERED

Two of them, on the same ward, and the most frightening thing about them is how ordinary the work is.

A man comes off a transport screaming and thrashing. They take an arm each and pin him to a thin mattress, and they do it the way two people carry a table through a doorway they have carried tables through before. No hesitation, no signal between them, nothing said.

Then the respirator, then the sedative, then the next one.

Hada Mariner INTACT

Long service, clean record, and a retirement date.

Three years on the same flight line with the same four people, and the most competitive of them by a distance. She had been working a barrel roll for a while and landed it, and was told at the bar that she had finally landed it, and did not let that stand.

At the bar she takes the seat next to whoever is sitting on their own. She reads a situation fast, says the useful thing rather than the kind one, and offers, unprompted, to wingman.

She is going to Maldo, to one of the ex-Guard communities there, on a square with ornate geometric stonework that she has apparently described to people more than once.

Maldo is the old Royal capital: a city built out of a used-up world, which stopped making anything a long time ago and is now a nice old town that people retire to and take souvenirs from. A person spends a career on a ship that never stops moving and picks somewhere that has already finished.

The Halgo family TESTIMONY

Maspin locals near the Trailblazer base, and the household the medevac dispatcher guesses first.

Nothing about them is on record except that. When a call comes in from that stretch of country, the voice on the other end says, without checking anything:

"Is it the Halgo family again?"

Which tells you the shape of them without a single name. Somebody in that house is always doing something. It has been going on long enough that a bored woman on a radio has stopped needing to look it up.

The Ivory Guards INTACT

The ceremonial line on Shayron, and the most photographed soldiers in the galaxy.

Pristine ivory armour. Long ceremonial coats that fall past the knee. Helmets built tall enough to add most of a head, kept immaculate, and never once seen with a scuff on them.

They stand exactly fifty metres apart. Not roughly. Every gap on the approach is the same gap, and the sameness is doing the work: a line of men that regular reads as a fact about the place rather than a decision anyone made.

Whether they can fight is a question nobody asks, which is the point.

Jax Sheel INTACT

The pilot. Officially one of twelve attached to the platoon. In practice, when Castle Team goes anywhere, Jax flies them.

Wavy raven-black hair and a thick, well-kept moustache that has no business on a face that young. The Guard runs clean-shaven almost everywhere, exemptions take months of argument, and his was simply never challenged. It is a small, cheerful act of not conforming and it suits him completely.

He came into the team through Yake, trains with the twelve, and drinks with the five. Nobody has ever formally decided he is a member of Castle Team and everybody treats him as one.

Before that

He served a custodial sentence and worked it off underground, cutting magnetic ore at one of the two installations that take most of that labour. The conviction does not survive scrutiny and the file does not pretend very hard. He was an embarrassment somebody wanted somewhere quiet, and he had no standing to say so.

He does not bring it up. It is in the record, which is a different thing from being known.

Steady in the air and warm on the ground. He is the one who talks, without making it heavy, about having been pulled out of his own lowest patch by people who bothered.

Jimzon Avaris INTACT

also: Jim · Jimzy · Jimz · Jimmy · Jimzo · Jimbo · Jizzbo · Jizzin

Twenty-six. Spec Ops Staff Sergeant, and the man the rest of Castle Team follows without anyone ever having decided that.

Short brown hair. Stubble he never quite gets on top of. He thinks he looks like nobody in particular, and he is wrong about how much that is true.

Two marks he cannot walk past a mirror without finding. His nose was broken in a fistfight that got away from everybody and set crooked, because nobody thought to have it fixed. There is a thin burn line across his left cheek where the hair does not grow, from too much to drink, a handful of fireworks and the certainty of being twenty and finished with the Academy. Nobody else notices either one.

His armour is black and deliberately unshined, with a blue visor. He paints it himself, by hand, every time.

He wears glasses some of the time, and there is no pattern to when.

His right ear does not always work. He mentions it once, to a stranger, as an explanation for not having heard something, and then moves straight on. Nobody who has known him for years has ever raised it.

What he gets called

Everyone who likes him has a different name for him and not one of them agreed with any other.

Jimzy is the colony name. Two people used it and both of them were on that rock: his mother, pointing at a star and telling him it was where he was born, and the neighbour with the sweets. Nobody has called him that since he was eight.

Jim comes from the people who knew him before he was anybody, and it is what he gets in the sentences that are about to be difficult. Jimz is his own team, and it is the one used when somebody has noticed he has gone quiet. Jimmy is the radio.

And then there is Calsco Fritt, who has called him Jimzo, Jimbo, Jizzbo and Jizzin, on four separate occasions, and has not once used the right one. He waits every time for the correction. It has never come.

A promotion to Captain is sitting on somebody's desk. He failed officer school once already, years ago, and has not mentioned that in a while.

Where he is from, and where he is from

Born on Modanick and has never once set foot on it. What he knows about his own birthworld is a bedtime story his mother told him: always warm, always daytime, trees taller than houses. She was describing a place she had loved as a student to a boy sitting on a rock, and she made it better than it is.

He grew up on the Corefuel colony in the wreckage of Wake, where his father ran the station. The family was two months from moving to Creta.

What he carries

A grey stone he picked up on the colony road when he was seven. He has had it ever since and it is smooth because he rubs it. His mother's Royal service pistol, cleaned since he was old enough to be shown how. A gold holowatch, a gift from a general, shined and with an audible tick to it. An engagement ring in a velvet box that has not been opened in front of anybody.

What he is like

Impulsive to the point of recklessness, and funnier in private than anyone outside the team would believe. Table impressions, at length, standing on the furniture. A napkin moustache and a captain they all served under once. A microwave that went out of a window. He reads his own silence as steadiness and does not notice that everyone around him reads it as absence.

He is casually bigoted about non-humans in the ordinary, unexamined way of somebody raised where he was raised, and he is unthinkingly kind to children, and he would be embarrassed to have either one pointed out.

He also uses Crag the way everyone he grew up with uses it, and thinks nothing about it at all.

Karagash RECOVERED

A Gashi bounty hunter, and the most reasonably priced frightening thing in the sector.

Seven feet. Strong through the shoulders and the arms without any of the bulk that usually comes attached, so the size does not register properly until he is standing next to something you know the height of. His hand closes on a wrist like a vise closing, and he is fast in a way that people who have watched it are not able to describe afterwards without their voice changing.

The face

He wears a mask across the lower half of it, a breathing apparatus rather than a disguise, and it has been there long enough that the shape of him without it is not a thing many people have seen. Above it, gold and black eyes with no pupil anybody has ever managed to find. You can tell exactly when he looks at something, because the light comes off them differently when they move.

The rest

Black suits, cut for a human frame and made to fit his, and he wears them well. A bandolier across the chest, which is not strictly necessary and is clearly a thing he enjoys. And ginger hair, deep and well combed and frankly gorgeous, which on a Gashi is normal and on a seven-foot masked man in a black suit is the detail people bring up first.

The work

He hunts for hire. He is extremely good at it and he does not extend mercy, and he is also not angry, ever, about any part of it. The two usually travel together and in him they simply do not. He takes the job, states the price, does the job, collects, and wishes you a good one.

Nobody knows why he went into this line rather than one of the ten thousand respectable ones a Gashi is expected to want. There is speculation and none of it is worth repeating. The likeliest answer is the one that never gets proposed, which is that he tried it and liked it.

And one detail nobody can account for

He works out of a spool of equipment carried at the hip. On the single occasion anybody got a proper look at what came off it, it was a length of green rubber garden hose, torn out of a wall spigot by hand and still clumped with wet dirt.

He offered no explanation. He was not asked twice.

He is, for what it is worth, modestly priced.

Kaspian CONTESTED

Maspin name: Kadam

Older than the species that names him, and older than the one that made it.

What he was

One of the people who lived on Wake before humans, back when it was a world and not a debris field. His remains went down with it: a skull, somewhere under what used to be the mantle, now scattered with the rest of it across a stretch of empty sky.

What he is

A skull pulled up out of desert sand, wreathed in a thin purple flame that defines its edges rather than consuming them. Lightning comes down to it slowly, like honey rather than a strike, and the sound it makes is a ceremonial drum instead of thunder. A translucent body of shifting starlight phases into place around it, tall and unhurried, with two points of gold where the eyes belong.

On Maspin they call him Kadam, and he is carved into the great gold doors of the Palace of Riflo: an elongated figure hovering just off the ground, arms out, handing a small burning sun down to the Maspins kneeling below. It is a copy of something much older, polished and re-gilded by every generation that inherits it.

Ask a Maspin what it means and you get knowledge, or power, or a shrug. Ask a shaman where they learned what they know, and the answer is him. Ask whether he is real, and even they are not sure.

The name is not his

Asked what he is called, he says he has never had a name in the sense other people have them, and that his people are called Kaspian. Everybody since has used it as though it were his, including this volume, because there has never been anything else to use.

One line is recorded

Nobody has been able to tell us what it refers to.

The queen will return to many moons.

Kaz CONTESTED

A bounty hunter, and a voice giving orders in a room the record does not describe.

The trade he is in is an old one and a legal one in most of the places it operates, which is why it has stayed as big as it has. Somebody wants a person found, the price is agreed, and no part of the arrangement requires anybody to explain themselves to a government. There are Guard warrants that get worked this way. There are also plenty that do not.

Of Kaz specifically there is very little: no world, no species, no description, no list of jobs. He works with at least one other person, whom he addresses by name and does not appear to entirely trust.

Kelsadria Vot Feentor-Jayzin INTACT

goes by: Kelsa

A pilot with Nova Squadron, and the most organised person in any room she is in.

Pale blonde, worn up in a bun nearly always. Very fit, in the unremarkable way of somebody who does the work and does not discuss it. Striking eyes, and they are never idle: there is always something going on behind them, and it usually arrives on her face a second before she decides whether to say it.

She reads stern for about a minute. She is not. She laughs softly and easily once she has decided you are worth the trouble, and after that she is one of the most expressive people on the flight line.

Underneath, behind the ears, it is dyed a soft light purple. Pinned up in a hurry you might catch a streak of it. Down, which is almost never, it is the whole story.

Royal blood, thinly. House Feentor, Jayzin line, which is the kind of descent half the galaxy can claim: it comes with a seat, a small maintenance, and no money worth the name. She has never drawn either.

Sansvor

She grew up in a beautiful ruin. Gaslamp streets, cathedrals and libraries still standing with the roofs open to the sky, museums nobody catalogues, art nobody looks at, and weather coming in through the gaps. She went to school in something like a bombed-out palace with eight other children in it. The teachers were good. The building was losing.

Every adult around her had a theory about what the world should become. None of them had a roof.

So she wanted a roof. She heard a teacher had flown in the war, got her licence, and joined the Guard for a pension and citizenship for her family on a world where things get fixed. Not patriotism. Arithmetic.

She dumps her shots on the floor at the bar and pulls the disgusted face along with everybody else. She sings karaoke under protest and then sings it properly.

Disciplined, methodical, always with a plan and a fallback. The exact inverse of the man she was going to marry, which is why it worked when it worked: she kept him from flying off the handle and he got her out of her own head. When it stopped working, his unpredictability left her with nothing to stand on and her need to know what came next started to feel like pressure.

She said it out loud once, testing how it sounded: Kelsa Avaris. I like the sound of that. He never gave her the ring. It is still in the box.

Her enlistment ends within the year.

King Matthew INTACT

The reigning King of the Royal systems, and the man giving the address at the Queen's Anniversary for the fourth year running.

He holds the ordinary powers of the crown, and one that is not ordinary at all. He alone can proclaim an emergency under the High Emergency Council Act, and on that proclamation everything the crown and parliament hold passes to the High Council sitting on Maldo.

The Act says how the powers go across. It does not say for how long, how they come back, or who reviews it. This has been raised in parliament four times and amended none.

It has never been invoked.

Korjin Avaris INTACT

Chemist, engineer, and the man who worked out how to turn the core of a dead planet into fuel.

He invented the Corefuel synthesis process. Everything that flies, anywhere, runs on the back of what he did in a workshop on a rock, and the licence was signed over to the Guard for a consideration of one credit.

He ran the extraction station in the Wake field himself. He knew everyone on the colony, he called them by name, and he worked the same hours they did.

What he was like at the end

Triumphant. He hit quota, called the entire settlement off work, and ordered a festival for two days later. He had a wife he was plainly still delighted by and two sons, one of whom did not live past five.

His younger boy asked him, that night, for a spaceship. He did not hesitate for even a moment.

"Even a spaceship. We're gonna get you one."

His contract paid on completion of the full year's quota and not a tonne before, which is how these contracts are always written.

The family was two months from moving to Creta.

Liles Ninzin INTACT

Old enough that his knees are a joke between the two of them. A general long enough to be respected, and now the one seat on the Guard's Board of Directors that is not a commercial interest.

He is the man who lifted the floorboard

He was on the patrol that reached the Wake colony after the raid, and he found a boy under his mother's body when everyone else had written the settlement off.

He and his then-girlfriend took the child in. They were barely out of college and doing what they could for someone with nowhere else to go. His eighth birthday was the first one he had with them: a small cake, a cheap dinner, and laughter that felt borrowed and was meant kindly.

They were always kind, and the kindness is what made the distance worse.

Now

He runs interference for Jimzon constantly and cannot say why in those words. He offers him a captaincy, quarters, a ship of his own. He refuses to authorise the hunt for the Nhaths, and then authorises it anyway, off the books, with leave time and no paper trail: I don't need proof that I gave this the OK.

He notices things. The bottom row of a man's medals in the wrong order, at a glance, across a room.

He is old enough now that his knees are a running joke between the two of them, and old enough to get nostalgic about the Battle of Rudcuff without noticing he is doing it, in the specific way of a man remembering the last time his job was simple.

What he says he wants, delivered like warmth:

"One day I'd like us both to be on the Director Board, together, away from the mess of combat."

He is on a board of seven where every member can be removed by the other six, and where nobody's dissent has ever been written down.

The little girl in the waiting room TESTIMONY

A child in the medbay at Base Delta, with a puzzle in her lap, waiting for her father.

She looks up at whoever comes in, blinks, tilts her head, and crosses the room with the kind of confidence only children and fools have. Then she sits down opposite you, uninvited, and starts.

"Are you a clown?"

She is a hard audience. Told a joke, she does not laugh. Shown a costume flower that honks twice, she does not laugh at that either. Her mouth holds a perfect little frown.

Then she explains why she is there.

"My teacher told me my daddy lost his leg. He isn't here yet. My teacher said he walked on a mine." "Mommy was too."

Her father is a Trailblazer who stepped on a mine. Her mother was one.

"Daddy really likes his legs. I think he's probably sad now."

She will laugh, eventually, at a bad enough joke. How much do rainbows weigh? Not much, they are actually pretty light.

"I will, mister. You're a funny clown."

We do not have her name. We are not looking for it.

Maspin children TESTIMONY

Glowing eyes at knee height, and a giggle that visitors describe as wind moving through a hollow tree.

They eat like the adults, which is to say they take food into a body made of smoke and vapour, and the food evaporates into the shimmer as it goes. Watching this happen, more than one human visitor has been left genuinely puzzled about how any of them manages a fork.

They bounce when somebody interesting walks past. They are not shy. And they will tell you things the adults will not, generally without being asked.

"You don't find the shaman. The shaman finds you."

A Guard physician on a busy ward, working at the speed of a man who has done this exact thing all week.

Meram Kest CONTESTED

A Second Sergeant of the Royal Shayron Defence Force, under a name that is not the one he was given.

The name is issued rather than inherited. It is what the Crown puts on his papers when he is working somewhere the Crown would rather not be seen working, and it is a real name in every sense that matters to a customs officer and no sense at all that matters to his mother.

He recites the oath the way soldiers do, front to back, without needing to find the start of it:

"I serve the people of Shayron and uphold the dignity of the"

What he is like

A man who very badly wants there to be a procedure. He asks for the code phrase. He wants to know which part of this is the official part, because if he can find that, then the rest of it is something he can be told what to do about.

He also has somebody he answers to whose name he was not supposed to say.

Michael Vousin RECOVERED

A Trailblazer, and formerly a student at Saigo, which is the best engineering school in the galaxy and the place trying to rebuild computers from nothing.

He was partway through and he left. Not thrown out. Left.

Now he builds ports on worlds the shipping lanes forgot, for a body that went unpaid for seven years and did the work anyway. He talks about machines the way people from Saigo do, which is to say more than anyone asked.

The thing he will not let go of is that the artificial intelligence everyone agreed to be finished with is quietly turning up again in Guard hardware, in small ways, in places where nobody has to sign for it.

Miss Jaley TESTIMONY

The woman at the front desk, sipping chai, who kept sweets in a drawer for whoever came through.

She worked the station, which on a fragment colony means she was the first face anybody saw and the last one to be counted as staff. She kept boiled candy from Shayron, four transfers and the better part of a month away, and gave it to the chief's boy when he turned up early to wait for his father.

She also had a bottle of pre-war Astrovin. She had been keeping it for years, for something worth keeping it for, in the way people do with a good bottle.

She opened it the night somebody else got good news.

Mister Flimmity Dimmity TESTIMONY

A floom. He belongs, in the loosest possible sense, to Calsco Fritt.

His collar tag reads:

Mister Flimmity Dimmity. If lost, return to Calsco Fritt.

He gets lost. When he does, a seven-foot Katanzarian goes through the undergrowth singing Flimmity Dimmity, where are you, Flimmity Dimmity, I miss you, in a voice one witness described as belonging to somebody who had gargled gravel.

He is also a judge of character, which is what flooms are. They make up their minds about a person quickly and people on Maspin act on it. Flimmity's opinion of a stranger has changed at least one important decision that this archive knows about, and that stranger has no idea.

Mr Armstin INTACT

The neighbour who kept the air on.

He maintained the gravity spires on his fragment of the Wake colony: the towers that burn Corefuel to hold down an atmosphere and give a lump of rock something like gravity. Without them there is no colony, and he was the man who climbed them.

A tinkerer by temperament, always halfway through fixing something that was not strictly his problem, and the sort of person who ends up doing a job because he is the only one who understands it. He worked the station alongside the chief, he waved at the children, and he ran the decorations.

The spires were not the whole of it either. When something came in over the sky that should have been tracked and was not, his was the name shouted into the intercom, because the defences were his as well.

The part he needed

The regulator assembly is the piece that fails. Nobody can make one any more; they come out of salvage and pre-war stock, and a settlement of his class is entitled to them on request, every quarter.

He requested them. Correctly, on the right form, quarter after quarter, for nineteen consecutive quarters. His handwriting does not change across any of them. The last one is as neat as the first.

"The spires are down! I've been trying to get the fucking parts shipped for weeks! Just stay put"

His house was the first one hit.

Nardow RECOVERED

A cartel boss with a compound, a private army, and gold on his tusks.

Bloated and grey, moving on several limbs at once, in the manner of a thing that has not needed to hurry in a long time. He employs Vitula by the crew, on written terms, at rates that are honestly not bad.

The son

He has one, and the boy is nothing like him: a crustacean, wine-red shell, crab maw, green eyes with no iris in them, hair like seaweed.

He is also, at this stage of his life, not there. The young of some lineages in this classification pass through a long period, years and sometimes a decade, in which the body is awake and capable and responsive to stimulus and there is no one home behind it yet. It is not an illness and it is not a disability. It is a stage, and it ends.

His did not. He was killed in the compound before it did.

Every asset his father owned was held in trust in that boy's name. He was building an empire for an heir who never perceived him and was never going to.

The Nhath leader INFERRED

The Nhath who signed the contracts. A lineage number in the hundreds, which means eighty and more generations of one family counted in eights and remembered.

He speaks flawless Galactic Standard, and enjoys the effect that has on people who were not expecting it. Told that his Standard is good, he corrects the compliment.

"Better than you."

The chip

He wears a Guard translator implant at the neck, bought with the credits from a job stealing Corefuel. He does not need it. He wears it partly because it covers a scar that was already there, put in that exact place by a woman who shot him.

Who paid

Eleven separate Guard engagements over nineteen years, paid in full, on time, every time, out of a fund identified in the paperwork only by an internal reference nobody has been able to resolve.

The old Maspin veteran TESTIMONY

An old Maspin, met in passing, who fought in the war and has been thinking about it ever since.

"These kids have it easy nowadays." "Maybe not easy. Maybe I'm just bitter. I grew up during the war." "Some days, it feels like nothing's changed. I thought fighting would fix our problems, but here we are. Other times, it feels like everything's changed, and I'm just a fish out of water."

That is the whole conversation. It is also, as far as this archive can tell, the most complete account anybody has given us of what the war did to the generation that came through it.

The palace staff TESTIMONY

The people who keep the Palace of Riflo running, and who open its doors by hand because the doors have always been opened by hand.

The red-robed pair

Two figures at the great oak doors, and the thing you notice first is that they are made of smoke rather than wrapped in it. The robe is the outer edge of the person, not a garment over one. They take a leaf each and pull, and the weight of the oak is real enough that it takes a moment.

The attendant

An alien in flowing robes who bows without speaking, receives the instruction, and leaves to fetch appetisers. The bow is not deference exactly. It is the practised economy of somebody who has decided that talking is the slower way to do this.

Pavlock Jattern INTACT

Castle Team's engineer, and the reason the room is bearable after a bad day.

A dark brown beard, trimmed to the jaw with real care and kept that way in the field, where nobody else bothers. It frames a grin he uses constantly. Teal visor.

Put him in royal robes and the costume comes with eyewear best described as a pair of glasses that lost their lenses and turned to face the wrong way. Not ornamental. Just regal enough.

Marfeld

He is from a world where the big predators never died out and the seasons swing from killing heat to killing cold in a matter of weeks. At seventeen he was put out into that country with his clothes and nothing else, which is what Marfeld does to its boys. Three paths: Blood, Root, Sky. He walked all three.

He drew summer. Heat, insects that never let up, and blisters. The first thing he made out there was a knife barely worth the word, a sharpened stick jammed into split wood, and he kept his pockets full of dry kindling like it was money.

That is where he decided to be an engineer. Building the thing you need out of whatever is lying near you turns out to be a career.

Which is not the job he has

He is a combat engineer, which is that skill with a deadline and people shooting. What he wants is astral engineering, on the civilian side, where the thing you build is meant to last and nobody is timing you. He can describe it in detail. He has never filed anything about it.

No man who finishes the trial may speak about it. He never has.

The beard

It grew on him out there, and on Marfeld they say hair remembers. You may shape it, trim it, dye it. You do not shave, and shaving means renouncing your family. He spent fourteen months fighting Guard paperwork for the exemption rather than pick up a razor.

The rest of him

Business-minded in a way that surprises people. Face-blind. Hopeless with directions. Warmer toward non-humans than anyone else on his team, without making a thing of it.

His grandfather's question was never what job do you want. It was what kind of person do you want to be, and Pav is the one who says it out loud when somebody needs to hear it.

Maspin children bounce with excitement when he walks past. He straightens his back and enjoys it enormously.

He also carries something he has never said aloud, about the man he follows and the man he wishes were standing there instead, and he hates himself for thinking it, and he cannot make it not be true.

Quinn Domnall INTACT

An accountant. Not a soldier, and about to be sent somewhere that will not care about the difference.

Deep lines cut into his face and heavy bags under his eyes, and neither of them arrived in a hurry. He looks tired in a way that has stopped being a state and become a feature.

The record, in his own words

Basic at Fort Actom. 704B, Accountant. Advanced training on Maldo. Officer school at Wedear. Led supply routes out to Fawn. He can recite it in about eight seconds and does, whenever somebody implies he has never been anywhere.

He works in the accounting division on the Mothership, under fluorescent light that hums, retyping twenty years of financial records by hand because the war killed every computer and Guardnet is barely walking. It is enormous, pointless, and never finished.

Years ago he started putting small deliberate errors into the ledgers. A private rebellion, one number at a time. Nobody has ever noticed, because what the division wanted from twenty years of retyping was the twenty years and not the numbers.

Older than the men he is about to be standing next to. Precise. Not brave and not a coward. A man who worked out a long time ago that his work does not matter and kept doing it correctly anyway.

His contract is nearly up.

And then a file lands on his desk

A transfer, to a security posting on a frozen moon called Sonaff. He is being sent to guard a hangar.

Ranzi TESTIMONY

An officer Pavlock served under, and the reason he does not talk about that deployment.

What survives of him is one image, and it is Pavlock's: Ranzi pinned behind the shattered trunk of a tree, one of the tall pale ones that grow like palms, the trunk blown open and no longer thick enough to hide a man. Pulse rounds coming in with that high whine they make. Comms jammed. No line of retreat and nowhere on the flank that was not already somebody else's.

He was shouting, and the whole of it is on the record:

"PAVLOCK! GET THAT BIRD IN THE AIR OR WE'RE FUCKING DEAD!"

He got out

A last volley, a run alongside a private, and into the rear hull of a ship that should not have started. Whatever it is that Pavlock cannot put down about that day, it is not this man's death.

Sershanti Rawlden RECOVERED

formerly Kinsley

Wife of Grai Penston Rawlden. She holds no office and is not a member of the cabinet.

The marriage

It predates his authority and has continued through it. Rawlden conducted an affair, acknowledged it rather than denying it, and the two separated for a period before reconciling.

He offered her a divorce. She refused it.

Accounts from people close to the household agree on her reasons and none of them is affection. A separation would have removed her from the position she holds, which is proximity to the only authority on the world, and she judged that she was better served by remaining in it. The marriage has been presented publicly as a stable one ever since, by both of them, and neither has ever been recorded departing from that presentation.

What she does with it

She is described as influential without being formally anything. Where and how is not established. Several informants who deal with the administration state independently that a view known to be hers is treated with more care than a view known to be a minister's, and none of them was able to give an example.

On the son

She has never been recorded speaking about Dorch Rawlden in public or in private, favourably or otherwise. He carries her married name.

Smelvin Klombo RECOVERED

also attested as: Melvin · Jimzo · Jizzbo

A name on a medical call, a name on a wardrobe box, and nothing on either side of them.

Everything we have

He is spoken into a Trailblazer medevac channel, out of jungle country, by somebody giving three names at speed. He appears again as a label on a costume crate at Base Delta. He is present at the Riflo council session, and is shouted across a feast, both names, twice, by a Maspin who had been looking for him. He is admitted to the waiting room of the medbay, where the nurse reads his name off a clipboard, pauses over it, and calls him by his outfit instead.

The surname is the part that argues for him. Nobody inventing a name at speed arrives at Klombo.

"Mister... Squire? We're ready for you."

The outfit

He attended a formal session of a governing council dressed as a squire. The reasoning given at the time, by the man who supplied the costume, was that squires are treated like jesters out there, and that optics matter. Both halves of that are recorded and neither is explained.

The variants

Melvin, Jimzo and Jizzbo occur in the same body of material across the same fortnight. That is either four records of one man or four men, and there is no document in this archive that would let anybody prefer one reading. The Restoration has printed all four spellings and takes no position.

What is absent

1 gap

No world. No service. No age, height, colouring or condition. No parent, no next of kin, no rites filed. No trade. No debt, no licence, no charge, no entry on any roll of any kind on any world.

[NO SURVIVING PRIMARY SOURCE]

[Compiler's note: we hold this man to the same standard by which we hold two million of the dead, which is a name somebody wrote down once. We print him for the same reason.]

Spara Avaris INTACT

A decorated Royal Space Force pilot who left the service, married a chemist, and raised two boys on an asteroid.

Three decorations, each with a citation, and then a discharge at her own request and a life nobody in the Royal systems ever heard about again. She kept her service pistol, which is regular and permitted, and she kept it clean.

The stories

She told her younger son about Modanick, where he was born and had never lived. Always warm. Always daytime. Trees taller than houses. She had loved it there as a student and she made it better than it was, because she was describing a green world to a child who lived on a rock, and that is what you do.

He believed all of it.

The last thing she did

She got her pistol and she killed one of them. There were two.

She fell across a floorboard, which turned out to matter.

Tiam Rockstead Tinoppel INTACT

Sixteen. Killed on Resmole. Somebody's first friend.

Where they met

The Scout Corps, the summer programme for cadets with nowhere to go between years. He was the one who wrote a letter every single night, sealed it properly, and put it in a box nobody ever came to collect.

He stole protein wafers out of the commissary, which are dry and almost flavourless and which he handed out behind the latrine wall to four other children, eaten in silence, terrified somebody would hear the wrappers. He swapped a drill sergeant's whistle for one he carved out of a bar of soap. The whole platoon ran extra laps for that and he never confessed, and he smiled every lap of the way. Pressure makes diamonds, he used to say, about nothing in particular.

How it happened

They were on the gate on Resmole, sixteen years old and bored, sharing a greyleaf cigarette. A round took out a potted plant on a roof three storeys up and neither of them looked. Then he thought he saw something move on the ridge, and he went up the clock tower to look, because he had a scope and a reason and nobody stopped him.

One shot. No ambush, no raid, no follow-up. Nobody even raised the alert.

They were not trained for that. They were children playing at soldiers, and the honest answer is that it was nobody's fault, which is the least useful thing anybody can be told.

Afterwards

His name is on the Academy memorial walls, on the plate for that year, in gold leaf, in order of loss, alongside everyone else who died in a sector nobody was calling dangerous.

Torres Delprest INTACT

Forty-five, and the oldest pilot on Nova Squadron by more than a decade.

Nova 01 Actual. When the squadron speaks with one voice on the net, it is his.

He has more hours than anyone on the roster and a posting list that reads like a tour of everywhere the Guard has been. He is still flying, which at his age is unusual and slightly stubborn.

He is the squadron's centre of gravity: the one who notices when somebody is quiet, who knows which forms exist and what they are actually worth, and who has read the entitlements nobody else has read. If a pilot needs to know how leave works, or what happens to seniority when you stop flying for a while, Torres is who they ask.

He is also, when it comes to it, gently hurt to find something out by watching rather than being told.

Off duty he sings old Backwater country, all of it, badly and with total commitment, and nobody has ever asked him to stop.

The Trailblazer doctor TESTIMONY

The surgeon at Base Delta. Wears a smug little smirk almost permanently, gives you the bad news fast and flat, and then softens once it has landed.

He is the one who explains floomicide to families: very effective, in very short supply, and it costs you your grip on reality for as long as the healing takes.

Why he believes in shamans

He will pull down his collar and show you the scar, a large burned circle in the middle of his chest. A kraskor stampede, while they were clearing ground for a helipad. The horn went through his chest and into his heart.

"My mates told me the shaman ran over, murmured strange words, and somehow stopped me from bleeding out. They say he paused my dying body. Animated my legs just long enough to walk back to the car. Then hooked me up to floomicide. Call it magic or whatever you want. But it saved me."

A man of medicine who takes the local mysticism entirely seriously, because it restarted him.

Vance RECOVERED

A man who will argue with you about what is true, and will not raise his voice while he does it.

He has a position and it is not a complicated one: that being right is a smaller thing than being honest, and that most people who are pleased with how clever they are have quietly stopped doing the harder of the two. He puts it plainly, without ornament, and he puts it the same way the fourth time as the first.

Why it lands badly

Because he is unbothered. The person opposite him gets angrier as it goes and he does not move, and there is nothing more infuriating than a man who is not competing. Called weak for it, he takes that as a description rather than an insult and continues.

Vando TESTIMONY

A Trailblazer, security on the concession, and the reason the Yinmelon story gets told at least once a rotation.

The job is the kraskor sweeps, which is what it sounds like: keeping several hundred kilos of horned animal away from people who are trying to build something. What is on the table at the festival is generally there because of him.

The run works like this. You put in at small settlements nobody surveys twice, and you sell what people at small settlements actually want: rockroot by the sack, glazberries, spice bundles tied with string. All of it real. All of it worth what you charge.

The fragmentation grenades ride in the Yinmelon sauce cans. Yinmelon sauce is thick, sweet, faintly orange, and sold in a can heavy enough that nobody picks one up expecting it to be light.

The one time it nearly came apart was a farmer's market on Monver, where a guard who had been standing in the sun for six hours asked for a taste.

He lost a thumb.

Vando tells it as a comedy, and it mostly is, and everybody laughs at the same place every time.

Vesk Iradin CONTESTED

A colonel of the Guard's Strategic Covert Operations Division, and a signature.

That is the whole of him. There is a rank, a division, and a name, and the name appears where an authorising officer's name appears, in the place on a form where somebody has to be accountable and where the person who is accountable is by design a person nobody has met.

No posting history. No unit. No photograph, no service dates, nothing filed anywhere that would let you work out whether he was ever a lieutenant.

A division that operates covertly does not publish its colonels, which is either the reason this record is empty or the excuse for it.

The Vitula in the compound INFERRED

Not a soldier. A labourer, standing in a place where labourers and soldiers end up looking identical to anyone arriving at speed.

His employer died. He took the next contract, because the next contract had the same terms as the last one and because the terms are the only part of the arrangement a Vitula in that position gets a say in. Nobody asked him what the work was for. Asking is not a step in the process.

He is in the compound for the same reason the floor is in the compound.

The employer's son died there too. Nobody has recorded whether the two of them were in the same room.

Yakib Yalitio INTACT

goes by: Yake

Castle Team's medic, and the only one of them who does arithmetic before agreeing to something.

Evenly tanned, because he spends his rest days outside while everyone else is in the bar. Sandy brown hair that falls across his forehead the moment the helmet comes off. An easy, unbothered face that has nothing to do with how he actually works, which is fast and cold and very good. Yellow visor.

Home

A world he does not talk up much, with one thing on it worth the trip: a starship wreck the size of a city, Maldo era, so thoroughly overgrown that people climb it like a mountain. He climbed it with his father as a boy, in magboots, which were later killed by a lightning storm and never replaced.

Faith

He was raised religious in a way that is mostly relaxed and has a few strange corners he does not explain to outsiders. When he filled in the form that asks a recruit what rites they want, the list of eighty-eight faiths did not have his on it, so he wrote it in himself.

Money

He sends most of his pay home and has done since the day he signed. He is not shy about why, and he does not dress it up:

"I've fought next to you on every battle, but I will put my life on the line before my career. If I die, my family gets paid."

He is not the coward of this group. He is the only one keeping score.

The abandoned monastic quarters INTACT

Nine districts of Shayron that were closed and sealed, and are still standing.

They emptied slowly, over three centuries, as the faiths that filled them stopped sending anyone. There is no conquest in the story, no plague, no disaster. Enrolment simply falls, year on year, until a house has four people in it, and then one, and then the city writes the closure down.

Two of the nine were shut with a single occupant left inside, in both cases because that occupant asked to stay.

The city still maintains the roofs and the drains, inspects every seven years, and finds them empty every time. They are sealed at street level. They are not sealed underneath, because the oldest sewers in the city run beneath all nine and are still in use.

Three of the libraries were never removed. The transfer papers say the books would be collected when convenient.

The Abyss TESTIMONY

The hole in the floor of the Elder Tree.

It sits at the centre of the chamber, perfectly round, with nothing around it. No rail, no rope, no warning. Everybody who has stood in that room mentions how strange it is to see a drop like that left completely open, and how quickly you stop noticing.

Nobody has ever described a bottom. No survey has been permitted and none has been requested twice. The Maspin do not treat the depth as an interesting question.

After an interment, blue vapour comes up out of it, and the tree takes it in.

The Academy memorial walls INTACT

Cast brass plates on the approach road to the Academy, running in continuous rows, with every name in applied gold leaf.

Names go up in order of loss, once a year, in the eleventh month. Each one gets a surname, initials, a service number and a year. No rank, no unit, no place, because at the moment they went up nobody thought any of that would matter as much as the name.

There are 2,140,880 of them across forty-one walls.

Every plate is perfectly legible and nobody has ever read them all. Three people from this archive have tried. The furthest anyone got was the eleventh wall.

The asteroid colony docking pad INTACT

One landing pad per rock, painted azure, and the only door in or out.

A ship comes once a week. It brings food, water, plant consumables, school materials and mail, and it takes away certified Corefuel. That is the whole rhythm of life out there: six days of nothing and one day when the world briefly connects to the rest of the galaxy.

Twice a standard year the orbit puts the fragments somewhere the radio cannot reach for several days. The safety schedule's advice for that period is to work to the published timetable, which is another way of saying wait.

The Burial Moon chapels INTACT

Two hundred and fourteen small stone buildings scattered across a moon of grass, about four kilometres apart, so that wherever a plot is there is one within walking distance.

Each holds forty people. Each is unheated, and belongs to no faith at all: a rail, a table, a cupboard, and nothing else on the walls. That is deliberate. Any rite a person wrote on their enrolment form at seventeen can be performed in one of these rooms without moving a single thing.

Services are booked through the caretakers. The average attendance is six.

The Capital District INTACT

The ceremonial heart of Shayron: the Castle, the processional way, three great squares, and the old mosaic quarters that are still lived in.

No industry is allowed inside the boundary and none has ever been. There is no exhaust here and no engine noise. The streets are hand-laid stone kept under permanent contract, the planting is jasmine and citrus by schedule, and the light comes in low and gold most of the day.

Almost nobody who works here lives here. The resident population is small and works in food, hospitality, restoration or the household. On an observance day the district holds two hundred thousand people, and the day after, it goes back to being very quiet.

The Council Chamber of Riflo TESTIMONY

Stone floor, woven banners, and bioluminescent vines kept trained along the upper walls, so the whole room has a faint blue underlight before anyone lights anything.

A ceremonial bowl sits in the centre. When it is lit at the opening of a session, every seated councillor's flame answers it, each one a different colour, and the room reads at a glance as a set of individuals rather than a body.

The floor hums

Everyone who has stood in that chamber says so, and none of them says it as a figure of speech. The stone carries the mood of the room. Anger, amusement, doubt, all of it comes up through your feet before anybody speaks.

Records are taken by hand with feathered quills. Gavels are used. A vote is not counted; the flames change colour, and unanimity is all of them going white at once.

Crescent City RECOVERED

Capital of Pashmirské, on the long peninsula that closes the northern ocean.

The peninsula is the reason the city is where it is and the reason it was fought over for as long as it was. It is approachable along one axis and is bounded by water on the rest, which made it defensible by whoever held it and expensive for whoever did not.

It changed hands during the war. How often is not agreed. The lowest figure given by any informant is four and the highest is eleven.

Condition

The city was never destroyed and was never repaired. What stands is a century and a half of small-arms and light ordnance damage across a fabric that was substantially complete before the fighting started, patched where a building was in use and left where it was not.

Now

It is the seat of the administration and holds the cabinet, the ministries and the residence. It is not a large city by the standards of this volume and it is the only one on the world with a population that has grown in each of the last returns.

The Elder Tree TESTIMONY

One tree, hollow at the base, going up into cloud. Inside it there is a chamber with mosaic walls and a chandelier, and in the middle of the floor there is a hole.

Inside

Every account agrees on the room: the mosaic, the light hanging above, humans and Maspin standing together with no arrangement made for either, and the opening at the centre with nothing around it.

Height

Nobody has measured it. Every informant describes the crown entering cloud. Trailblazer survey work in the surrounding concession recorded canopy heights across the district and stopped at the edge of the ceremonial ground, by agreement.

What it is for

The dead go into the hole. Blue vapour comes back up afterwards and is taken into the tree. The Maspin hold that what goes down returns to the ocean beneath the crust and that the tree drinks from it.

One thing we can add

The district around this tree is exceptionally fertile, and nothing is imported into it.

Attributed to C., Base Delta, and to four Maspin informants who asked to be recorded together.

The gem mosaic wall TESTIMONY

The inside of the Elder Tree is covered in coloured stones, and every one of them is a person.

When a Maspin is interred, the stone is taken off the necklace they wore in life and set into the wall. There are thousands. Nobody has counted them and nobody has been asked to.

There is no order to it. Not by date, not by family, not by anything. A stone goes wherever there is room. There are no names, no dates, and no inscriptions of any kind, so a family cannot come back and find their own.

Asked about that, they say it is not what the wall is for.

The Grand Mothership Dining Hall INTACT

Warm tans and golds, in a ship that is otherwise white and blue all the way through. It is the only room aboard that does not look like a machine.

Ornate chandeliers hang from a ceiling high enough to make the space feel like weather. The sleek white structural beams are still there, still glowing faintly with the ship's own light, but everything hung on them and set beneath them is amber, tan and gold. Long tables and deep booths run the length of it, and the noise is a constant weather system of laughter, cutlery and shared war stories.

What is actually on the tray

Grilled white meat, dusted with teal and red flakes. A garnish of yellow spireleaf sprouts arranged on the side by somebody who was told to arrange it. Circular tan grains, soft and steaming. A tall glass of opaque pastel-yellow chai.

It is good. That is the surprising part. The bread comes out of the ovens hot enough to smell from the elevator, and the spices are real, carried aboard from a dozen worlds by people who missed them. A man can come off six weeks of ration bars, walk through those doors, and be undone by the smell before he has even sat down.

It seats the entire embarked complement in three sittings, and it cost more to fit out than the medical wing, which is in the accounts and has never been commented on.

You are required to come out of armour to eat. The standing order gives the reason as morale, and it is correct: it is the one hour of the day when a unit stops looking like a unit and starts looking like five people who know each other.
