Guard pay INTACT

It is a very good living, and almost none of it arrives while you are alive to spend it.

The structure

A contract runs a fixed term and pays 95 per cent of the total on completion, as a single lump sum. In the meantime you draw 1.3 per cent a year.

The stated justification is that the Guard already provides everything: your quarters, your meals, your medical care, your safety. You have nothing to spend it on, so it is held for you. The real reason is that the Guard is the only employer in the galaxy worth the name, and nobody has anywhere else to go.

It matters enormously whether it is your first

A man on his first contract has never been paid. Everything he has earned is a number held somewhere else, and it stays a number until the day the term closes. A man on his second or third has already been through it once. The first contract cleared, the money is his, and everything since has been on top of that.

Which sorts the establishment into two groups that do not understand each other at all. Ask a Spec Ops sergeant what he is worth and he will tell you, because he has seen it land. Ask a first-term rifleman and he will tell you what he was promised.

What that looks like in hand

A Spec Ops captain's contract is worth about 110,000 credits a year, untaxed, because no member world has the standing to assess a Guard contract and the Guard does not assess itself. Over a full term that is a fortune. What actually reaches him each year, before completion, is roughly the price of a good coat.

So the money is real, and it is also a rumour. It exists as a number in the accounting division, and it becomes yours on one specific day and not a day earlier.

What is not held back

Whatever you retain at a cleared objective under Standing Order 41 is yours immediately, is entered nowhere, and men at that level do not lose much of what they pick up. The Guard is entirely comfortable with this. A soldier with a bag of somebody else's gold is a soldier who is not asking about his balance, and a soldier holding stolen property is a soldier who cannot easily complain about anything.

What it looks like from the other side of the ledger

A single Spec Ops operation ends a criminal system, or takes a cartel principal, or hands control of a whole sector to somebody who will pay for it. The Guard books that against 110,000 a year, most of which it is still holding.

A million credits over a decade, against what a decade of that produces, is not generosity. It is the best purchase in the accounts.

Getting it out

For the ranks that matter, payment is clean and fast, because those are the men the Guard intends to keep.

For everybody else it is a process. The sum is not large to begin with, perhaps sixty thousand for a full term in a clerical grade, and it does not arrive as a lump sum. It arrives in instalments, against forms, to a confirmed mailing address, which must be a fixed address on a member world, which a man who has spent four years aboard a ship does not have. Each instalment requires the previous one to have cleared. Each form requires a countersignature from a department that answers correspondence quarterly.

Nobody is refusing to pay. That is the elegance of it. Every step is legitimate and every step takes eleven weeks, and a surprising number of people simply stop filing.

And the term that follows from it

Note what the payment schedule rewards. The contract costs the Guard almost nothing until the day it ends, and everything on the day it ends. Which means the cheapest possible outcome, for a man in his final months, is one where the day never comes.

Nothing about that is personal. It is arithmetic, done on paper, by people who have never met him. That is the part that should worry you.

Guard rations INTACT

What you eat when you are not in the dining hall, which is most of the time.

The good one

Meal 25, the Brellovine pasta kit. It heats properly, it tastes like something a person made, and it is the currency of every field kitchen in the Guard. Men will trade three of anything for one.

The other ones

The Tipa sandwich, which is fine, which is the most anybody has ever said about it. Frozen guomo sticks. And the protein wafer: dry, nearly flavourless, sold by the sleeve at every commissary, and the single most stolen item in the establishment.

The wafers are not stolen because anybody wants them. They are stolen because they are the easiest thing to take, and because a cadet who hands them out behind a latrine wall to four other children is not distributing food. He is distributing the fact that he did something.

Off the supply chain

Anywhere with a market, the good stuff is local: rockroot by the sack, glazberries, spice bundles tied with string, weeflowers for somebody's wife, charcandies for somebody's children. Yinmelon sauce comes in a can heavy enough that nobody picks one up expecting it to be light.

And what a colony eats

Seared tofu. Mashed rockroot. Spireleafs on the side, which no child on any world has ever finished voluntarily.

Guard training INTACT

There are two of these and they are not the same experience at all.

The short one

Sixteen-year-olds off poor worlds with no schooling behind them and no particular aptitude in front of them, run through in the minimum time the schedule allows. They are taught to hold a rifle, follow an order, and stand where they are put. It is ordinary infantry training and it produces ordinary infantry, and the Guard needs a great many of them and is not pretending otherwise.

Before either of them, the Scout Corps

A summer programme for cadets with nowhere to go between academic years. Which is to say: for orphans.

They clean their uniforms and their bunks until the whole billet smells of starch and metal polish, pack a bag, and march across country in formation. Rain or shine. Some days they fire at distant targets, and the cheer when somebody actually hits one is louder than the rifle was. When it rains, the drumming on the ponchos makes the world feel far away and almost safe. When the heat is bad they pass canisters between them like contraband.

Thirty minutes a night are set aside for writing letters home. Most of the children draw, or scrawl messages from families they have invented. Nobody comes to collect the post.

They are not beds, only frame cots and thin mats, and it does not matter, because the insects outside hum like a lullaby and every child there is tired enough to forget what is supposed to come next.

It is where most of them meet the first friend they ever have.

The long one, which is most of the establishment and everything above it.

Sleep deprivation as a working condition rather than an incident. Being told, continuously and by people who are good at saying it, that you are nothing. Physical work past the point where the body has stopped cooperating. And the arrangement that does the actual damage: at every hour of it there is an invitation to stop, and no mechanism that lets you.

You can want to quit as much as you like. Wanting is free. There is nowhere to hand the wanting in.

That is the whole design. They are not trying to find out whether you can be made to want to leave, because everybody can. They are trying to find out what you do for eleven more weeks once you do.

Afterwards

Nobody who came out of it discusses it much, and the people who came out of the short one are aware that there was another door.

Housing INTACT

Buying is the easy part. Keeping the roof on is the problem.

There is no galactic housing system and there never was. Some worlds run housing blocks. Some worlds you can buy a house outright for very little. Some worlds bury the whole business in paperwork and some have none at all. The honest answer to how a person gets a home is the answer it has always been: you get a job, and you get a bad house or a good one.

What is different here is that a building is not a thing you own. It is a thing you are maintaining, against a supply chain that no longer exists.

The structure is fine. Structures last. It is the regulator, the seal, the pump, the coupling, the part in the middle of the thing, and none of it is made any more. It comes out of salvage or pre-war stock or it does not come at all, and a person can spend nineteen consecutive quarters filing correct requests for a part that is simply gone.

So the shape of a home is the shape of its repairs

Patched roofs. A window that was replaced with something that was not a window. Improvised fittings, done well, by somebody who apprenticed for a year and worked the rest out. Whole streets where every house has the same failure at a different stage.

And a world can lose

Not to a war or a disaster. Just to arithmetic, quietly, over decades, as the parts run out faster than they can be found, until the roofs are open and there are cathedrals with weather coming through them and children being taught properly in a building that is losing.

Crowded apartments, everywhere, on nearly every world. Busy-crowded rather than desperate-crowded. People manage.

Humanist supremacy TESTIMONY

That humans are a superior order of thing, that spreading through the stars is theirs by right, and that whatever was done to get here needed no excuse.

It is not a religion anyone joins

There is no body, no clergy, no rite, no text, no register. There is nothing to sign.

It is also the single most widely expressed belief in this volume. It turns up unprompted in testimony from every human world we have surveyed, almost always from people who would tell you flatly that they hold no religious position of any kind.

How it sounds

Recorded word for word, on worlds with no contact with one another: that we are a near-perfect design. That the stars were left for us. That whatever happened, it got us here.

Nobody teaches it and nobody argues with it

No institution in this archive professes it. No institution in this archive contradicts it. Guard educational material describes human achievement in terms we have difficulty telling apart from the doctrine, and files it under history.

Indentured servitude INTACT

Working off a debt. Legal everywhere, including on the worlds that advertise themselves as slave-free.

The distinction that makes it lawful is that you are not owned. You owe. The debt can be one you took on, one somebody assigned to you, one you inherited, or one a court handed you instead of a prison sentence.

How you get out

You do not get paid, so the debt comes down by the value of your labour at a rate somebody else sets. We looked at eighty-eight indenture registers. In sixty-one of them the instrument does not state the rate at all.

Recorded terms run from eleven months to thirty-one years. The middle of that is nine.

Who runs it

Whoever the local authority is. On Maspin that is the Council of Riflo, whose own registers show indentured people assigned to households belonging to sitting councillors, written down plainly in the ordinary column, because nothing requires anyone to hide it.

What the Guard says

That it is going to be ended, and that the priority is first finishing membership and building a uniform register, after which measures will follow. That position has been published in materially identical words in GC 4429, 4437, 4448 and 4459.

Johnny Plasma TESTIMONY

The man who founded the Guard, who never existed.

The story: after the war, one man with no rank and no property walked from world to world settling quarrels, facing down warlords, teaching people how to keep order, and moving on without taking payment. He founded the Guard and refused every office in it. In most versions he is still out there walking.

Nobody believes it

Not the children who are taught it, not the instructors teaching it. Everybody knows. It is in the standard curriculum at two points and it is universal across the member worlds anyway.

Why bother

Because the alternative is the incorporation instrument, which survives, and names nine actual founders: four generals of armies that no longer existed and five men with money in shipping, insurance and salvage.

A founding myth makes you a nation. That document makes you a company.

The Marfeld beard TESTIMONY

On Marfeld they say hair remembers.

The beard starts growing during the trial, because a boy out there has no way to stop it. When he comes back it is his, and what it is is a measurement: how long he was out, written on his face by his own body while it was happening.

You may trim it, shape it, braid it, dye it. Men do all of those and take real care over it.

You do not shave. Shaving is not a haircut on Marfeld and it is not a fashion choice. It is the renunciation of your family and your bloodline, and there is no lesser version of it. There is nothing in between.

Which is why Marfeld men in foreign service spend months arguing with grooming regulations rather than pick up a razor, and why a Marfeld man who is clean-shaven has either done something enormous or is not who he says he is.

One complication

The Royal court requires its household and its blood to go clean-shaven, by long ceremonial rule. Nobody has ever reconciled the two.

The Marfeld coming-of-age trial TESTIMONY

At seventeen, a Marfeld boy is put out into the wild with his clothes and nothing else, for weeks.

He is not told beforehand what he is walking into. Not the season, not the country, not which of the three paths he is taking. Blood is the hunt, Root is the forage, Sky is the climb, and which one you get is not yours to choose.

Where it comes from

It used to be the first hunting season. You went out with a group, for months, and you came back with meat because the settlement needed the meat. What the modern version keeps is the exposure. What it removed is the group.

What people will tell you

Only the parts that happen to other people. Boys who drew winter and crossed frozen rivers on strips of bark. Boys who sewed hides around their feet to keep the toes. Summer, and the insects, and the blisters.

What nobody will tell you

Their own. No man who finishes the trial may speak of it, and the rule holds even between men who both went. It is absolute and it is kept.

We asked forty-one Marfeld men about it. All forty-one declined. Two of them apologised.

The original version killed boys. You do not talk about it because some of the ones who walked out with you did not walk back, and the ones who did came home carrying something they had no words for. The silence started as grief and hardened into a rule.

Maspin dietary practice TESTIMONY

Mostly they do not eat. They stand among plants and take what comes off them, the way everyone else takes oxygen, with a good deal more water vapour in it.

When they do eat it is liquid, or close enough. Fruit gets pulped and watered down and drunk, which for a body made of smoke means absorbed rather than swallowed. Most things can be taken that way if they are broken down far enough first.

Nothing is chewed

Everything in the cuisine is fermented, pickled, pulped, brewed or reduced, and the good stuff takes years.

There is a wine. There is fermented kraskor and there is pickled inside-barked mycelium, and those two are what the Council names when it wants to impress somebody.

The strange part is what they sell. Kraskor go out live and whole to worlds that will chew them, and the famous Maspin fruits get shipped intact to people who bite into them.

Mead cards INTACT

The card game of choice in Guard messes, played in partners, across a table, for nothing.

Two against two. You sit opposite the person you are playing with and you do not get to talk to them about your hand, which is the entire game: everything you want to say has to be said by what you choose to put down. Good partners develop a shorthand over a few hundred rounds. Bad partners develop a grudge.

It travels well because it needs a deck and a flat surface, and a mothership is a place with very few flat surfaces and a great deal of time.

The universal breach of etiquette is narrating your own hand. Everybody knows it is a breach. Everybody does it eventually.

Moonball INTACT

The game they play on the ice. Modanick's national sport and the thing that world will actually raise its voice about.

Eleven a side, a stick, a weighted disc, and a frozen canal or a prepared rink. The season starts when the water goes over, which is the second week of winter most years, and everyone plays: children on the canals, works teams, a league with a published rulebook older than the war.

The Modanick championship is the best-attended thing that happens on that world all year, and it is not close. The canals fill with people who cannot get tickets and watch nothing in particular together.

Variants are played on forty-four worlds, and every mothership has a court in the rec room with a floor waxed to a shine and an argument in progress on it. Modanick's is the only code anyone has ever bothered to write down properly, and Modanick will tell you so.

Neo-alchemy RECOVERED

Secret books, small meetings, and a claim to manipulate dark matter.

There are very few practitioners and they are organised the way this sort of thing is always organised: closed groups, initiation, degrees, and a great deal of ceremony around not telling anyone.

We hold four documents, all partial, all in private hands and examined under conditions. They are notation rather than doctrine and it is not a notation we can read.

Who is in it

From the correspondence, membership tracks wealth closely and engineering hardly at all, which is the clearest line between this and Simulationism, with which it gets confused by people who have met neither.

The Path of Blood TESTIMONY

The hunt. You are put out into predator country and you feed yourself off what you can kill.

Marfeld's big animals are big enough that a walled settlement cannot hold ground against them all year. A boy on his own with a sharpened stick is not expected to take one of those. What he is expected to do instead is something nobody outside will explain, and everyone inside already knows.

Of the three paths this is the one outsiders assume is hardest. On Marfeld opinion is divided, and the division is usually along the lines of which one the person you are asking walked.

The Path of Root TESTIMONY

The forage. You feed yourself off the ground.

On a world with no reliable growing season and two killing extremes, this is the path that needs the most knowledge and the least equipment. You have to already know what comes up where, in which month, and what will put you on your back. Nobody teaches it formally. You learned it or you did not.

Visitors call it the easy one. Nobody on Marfeld does.

The Path of Sky TESTIMONY

The climb. Straight up.

The country for this is a formation of pillar mountains, near-vertical columns standing alone off the plain, and you go up them. You eat by taking eggs and honey out of nests and hives on the faces, while the things that built them object at close range. Some of those things are large and most of them can fly.

It is the only one of the three with a view at the end, which is exactly why a boy would pick it, and exactly why a boy is not allowed to pick.

The Queen's Anniversary INTACT

The biggest day in the Royal calendar, held in the Capital District on Shayron, on a fixed date.

A procession the length of the processional way, an address from the High Castle, food put out for everybody, and rites in the evening in the quarters still keeping them. Nobody is ticketed. The way and the three great squares hold two hundred and fourteen thousand people, and in recent years the city has stopped pretending the crowd is that small.

It is a religious day and a civic one at the same time, because the Queen is not merely reigning by Tracine's favour. She is held to be Tracine present on Shayron. It is not her birthday and nobody treats it as one.

She has not been there for four years

No announcement, no explanation, no death declared. The day has been held in full each of those years, with the King giving the address.

Nothing in Royal law covers the absence of a sovereign who is identified with a goddess. There is no office with the standing to say she is gone.

The Season of Long Nights TESTIMONY

The Maspin year turns on it. A season of rebirth, of retribution, and of relighting the fire everybody shares.

The last night of it is sacred.

We do not know how long it lasts, when it falls, or what happens during it. Our informants would not describe the rites and we did not push. What they would say is what it is for, and they said all three of those words every time, in that order, as though the sequence mattered.

The second chance TESTIMONY

not an official term. It is taken from what is said at the end of it

The procedure applied to political dissent on Pashmirské. It is presented publicly as execution and is not one.

Announcement

The charge is read out publicly. The person is then taken from where they are, with a bag over the head, and does not return. From the point of view of anybody who knows them, they have been disappeared following a public accusation, which is the outcome the announcement is designed to produce.

Transport

The prisoner is driven to a remote location. Accounts differ on distance and on duration and agree that neither is explained at the time.

The staging

The prisoner is placed and is able to hear, but not see, what follows. There are gunshots. There is the sound of bodies falling. This is repeated. Accounts state that the sequence is unhurried and that the intervals are the worst part of it.

The prisoner is then asked whether they have any last words. Every account holds that the question is put seriously and that the answer is listened to.

The end of it

The prisoner is touched once on the forehead, with a finger, and told that they have been given a second chance, and asked what they intend to do with it.

The answer given at that moment does not affect the outcome. Informants who gave defiant answers and informants who begged were both released.

Deportation

The released person is given a ticket offworld and told what it costs. The sum is small. It is worked off in a week at a rail station, after which the ticket is issued and they travel.

They may not return. No mechanism exists for appealing this and none has been recorded as attempted.

Who is not released

Persons convicted of violent crime are not put through the procedure and are not deported. The distinction is drawn by the administration and is not published.

Why any of this is known

Everybody it has been done to is alive, offworld, and under no obligation to Pashmirské. The Restoration has recorded eleven such accounts on four worlds. They agree with one another in sequence and in wording, including on the finger and on the question, and none of the eleven was aware that the others existed.

Simulationism INTACT

The engineers' religion, and the only faith in this volume with a decent filing system, because its believers are people who file things.

Two versions

The first holds that computation is going to be rebuilt no matter what anyone does, that what comes out the other side will think, and that whoever does the rebuilding will stand in a favoured relationship to it. The obligation follows: the work should be done, and it should be us doing it.

The second holds that all of this is already running inside something, that other such things exist, and that they can be reached. Its literature is technical, circulated among peers, and filed with the university.

Neither branch has a congregation, a rite, or a holiday. Nobody kneels. Adherence shows up in who funds what.

It is concentrated at Saigo, it runs strongly among senior faculty and the donors who pay for them, and the single largest private contribution to rebuilding unmanned systems comes from people who believe this.

Slave-free territory INTACT

A short declaration you file with the Guard saying there is no slavery in your jurisdiction. It is granted the moment it arrives. Nobody inspects anything.

And it is true

Slavery is defined in the code as holding a person as property, and in the jurisdictions that file this, nobody is held as property.

What the definition does not cover

Indenture, where you are not property, you just owe. Custodial labour, where you owe a sentence. Levy, where you owe an instrument. None of those is slavery as written, and each is separately legal.

Sixty-one jurisdictions have filed the declaration. Forty-four of them record lawful indenture in their own returns for the same year.

The standard wording was drafted on Maldo, and it reads exactly like every other Royal ministerial instrument of that period: accurate, elegant, and answering a question nobody asked.

Standing order 41 INTACT

recovery of materiel

The looting rule.

When an objective is cleared, anything of value is to be recovered rather than destroyed, and most of it is accounted to the Guard. But there is a schedule of things the people who did the clearing may simply keep: personal effects, currency under a threshold, jewellery, watches, small arms below a class, food, and anything with no assessed strategic value.

That last category is doing a great deal of work.

It has been widened twice, in GC 4431 and GC 4447, both times with a memorandum explaining that this will reduce destruction at objectives.

Nothing kept under the schedule is written down

The order says entering it would be administratively disproportionate.

Which means that after a Guard unit has been through a place, the contents of that place have been distributed among individuals and no inventory exists. Nobody can reconstruct what was there. That is not an oversight in the order. It is a clause of it.

Sun worship TESTIMONY

Older than spaceflight. It holds that a star talks, and that you can answer it.

The reasoning, which is better than people expect

A star is the point everything in its system falls toward. Light, heat, matter, all of it ends up there. So a star is a collection of everything that has happened on every world around it, and what it takes in, it sends back out. The signal is held to be patterned rather than constant, and readable with training.

Some traditions go further and say the slipstream lanes are its doing. A lane exists where a star has agreed to one.

Where it survives

Everywhere, thinly, and strongly in farming systems and out on the rim.

A note about Polaris

In that system the star, the system, the shared calendar and the family holding the licence on the harvest all carry one name. We have not been able to establish what the practice there is actually addressed to, and the people we asked did not enjoy the question.

The Tipsitters INTACT

A band, and the reason every karaoke night on every mothership eventually arrives at the same song.

Their sound starts the same way every time. A kick drum alone. Then a slow bassline underneath it. Then a crash of cymbals, and only then the lead guitar, which is the part everybody in the room has been waiting for and which everybody in the room hums along to badly.

"Dark Holiday." The one everyone knows. It opens sadder than its reputation, all cold air and chills that are not from the rain, and then it detonates into a chorus about not waiting for the calendar to tell you when to be alive.

There's a first time for everything. Sometimes we forget there's also a last.

Then the shouted bridge, which nobody sings so much as yells: break the glass, take the stairs, nobody really cares. And then a spoken verse near the end, delivered in a lower register, which turns out on inspection to be sung from the point of view of death itself, patient and unbothered, waiting in the back of your mind. Most people who love the song have never noticed this.

What it is actually for

Soldiers. Not because it is about soldiers, but because it is about a specific arithmetic that soldiers do without being taught: that the festival might not come, so this ordinary Tuesday will have to be the festival instead.

Other music

The older ranks lean toward Backwater country, which is slow, sincere, and about places nobody in the room has been. The pre-war instrumentals still turn up on record players in colony houses, warm and simple, from back when things were easier. And on Maspin they sing into a hole in a tree, which is a different thing entirely.

Tracineim TESTIMONY

The faith of the divine feminine, and the state religion of the Royal systems.

Tracine is the generative principle. Trees are feminine. Worlds are feminine. Water, growth, anything that brings life. The universe itself is read as feminine, and the faith is not much interested in telling you how to behave. It has no code and no list of sins.

It started at the bottom

The oldest outside references to it are contemptuous: a religion for slaves, women and children. Then warrior cultures picked it up, and then it became respectable, and then it became the establishment, which is a road several faiths in this volume have walked.

How it is actually practised

Barely, and constantly. There is no weekly assembly, no obligation, and no clergy in the way other faiths have clergy. What there is, is a blessing people say when they part:

May Traceen be with you.

Said by the devout, said by people who have not thought about it in years, and said by soldiers who would tell you flatly they believe none of it.

The Queen

She is not held to be immortal. The crown never claimed she could not die. It claimed she is Tracine's presence on Shayron, which is not a lifespan. It is a tenure.

Bindings

14 entries
The Blind Day TESTIMONY

Blindfolded, cuffed together, and turned loose for a full day in front of everybody they have ever known.

The rite

The couple is bound at the wrist and blinded, and must live an entire ordinary day like that. Eat. Move. Get from one place to another. Every single thing requires the other person, and neither can see what the other is doing.

Two things are being said at once, and the rite does not bother to separate them: your fate is chained to theirs now, and you will have to trust this person when you have nothing left to go on.

The families set the tasks, and the tasks are meant to be funny rather than cruel. This is the community's one licensed opportunity to make the couple look ridiculous, and it is taken up enthusiastically. Cook a meal for both families, neither of you able to see the fire. Cross running water on stones. Carry something fragile across town. Find an object a sibling has hidden, and the sibling is permitted to lie exactly once.

The last task is dressing each other

Ceremonial clothes are laid out, and each dresses the other blind.

They walk into the ceremony wearing whatever they have made of one another, and nobody straightens a thing. The crooked collar is the point. Every wedding portrait on that world has one.

Then the blindfolds come off

That is the first time they see each other married, and it is where the ceremony begins. The whole day was the prelude.

Peeking is not an annulment

It is worse. It is remembered.

The Coal Run TESTIMONY

A heated span with water on both sides, and the couple starts at opposite ends.

The rite

They run toward each other. The marriage exists the instant their lips meet in the middle. No words. Nobody officiates. Either it happened or it did not, and every person present saw the exact moment.

Opposite ends is the entire design

Either one of them can stop. If one stops, the other is left standing alone on the far side, in front of everybody, and there is no version of that which can be smoothed over afterward. Both have to keep going. That is the vow, and it is made with the legs.

The surface is something genuinely unpleasant and genuinely survivable, and it varies with what the world has: superheated grating over an exhaust manifold, plasma venting on a timed cycle so that the run has a window, or a cooling Corefuel channel, which is to say they run across the thing the galaxy is powered by.

The falling

Usually one of them goes in the water. This is the part that makes the culture.

The other jumps in after them. Voluntarily, immediately, and without being asked. And then everybody else wades in and carries the pair of them across.

Nobody is embarrassed. Nobody has failed. It is fun, it is half the reason people turn up, and the lesson gets stated by the crowd instead of by a priest: you were never going to finish this on your own, and nobody expected you to.

A wedding where nobody fell in is considered a slightly boring wedding

Debt absolution TESTIMONY

A marriage between two families cancels every debt between them. Instantly, entirely, by custom, with nothing signed.

The stated reasoning is warm

The families are one now. A debt between them is a debt owed to yourself, and therefore meaningless.

The practical reasoning is not

A ruined man with a daughter and a creditor has, available to him, a single move that clears the ledger.

Why it is not used constantly

Because everybody can see it. It is lawful, it is free, and a family that visibly engineers one is finished socially. Not prosecuted. Finished. Everyone within a hundred miles understands exactly what was traded and for how much, and it does not get forgotten, and it attaches to the children.

So it happens rarely. And when it happens, the whole district knows within a day.

What it produces

A parent forbidding a good marriage because the debt is income and they would rather keep collecting. A couple genuinely in love whose wedding will look like a transaction no matter how they conduct themselves. Somebody borrowing deliberately, at ruinous rates, to force a family's hand. And, most often, a spouse who is loved perfectly well and will never once be certain whether they were chosen or written off.

In a post-war economy where debt is the ordinary condition and collection has been contracted out to people with weapons, the custom is everywhere and is deeply, quietly resented.

The Detonation TESTIMONY

At the moment of the union, something is destroyed, loudly, on purpose.

A cannon. An enormous firework. A structure brought down under control, chosen in advance and often chosen carefully. Whatever the world can manage, the requirement is that it is sudden, that it is loud, and that it cannot be undone.

It is not celebratory noise

That is the thing outsiders get wrong. This is joy deliberately punctured, at its own high point, by the memory of catastrophe. The bang is not applause. It is a correction.

What it says

Nothing lasts. This will not last either. We are doing it anyway.

On worlds that came out of the war with a continent bombed flat, or a capital that is now a beautiful ruin with the sky coming in through it, the rite is not symbolic and nobody there needs it explained. Everyone in the room has seen the real version of what is being staged.

And the sound is the memory

Which means at every wedding on such a world, there is a portion of the crowd who flinch, who know they are going to flinch, who came anyway, and who are held by somebody standing next to them for a second afterward.

The Guard corridor INTACT

A hallway on the mothership lined with small chapels, one per faith, rentable by the hour.

How it works

The paperwork is the marriage. You file first, at a desk, and you are married when the clerk stamps it. Everything after that is a service you are purchasing.

Then you pick a door. There are a great many doors. The enlistment rites form lists eighty-eight faiths and the corridor makes a decent effort at all of them, which means a stretch of identical hatchways opening onto rooms that share nothing but their dimensions: incense in one, water in the next, a bare wooden bench, a stained-glass panel lit from behind, an altar with a sun on it.

There is a price list

It is posted. It is not expensive and it is not free, and the difference between the rooms is entirely a matter of how much is in them.

The room at the end has nothing in it

No symbol, no furniture, no fee.

It is the busiest room in the corridor by a wide margin, and it has been for as long as the mothership has been flying. Some of that is money. Some of it is eighty-eight faiths and none of them being yours. And some of it is two people who have thirty-one hours of shore leave and no interest in explaining themselves to anybody.

Household crowning TESTIMONY

The couple are crowned. Not figuratively.

The rite

Two crowns, held above the heads of the pair or set on them outright, and from that moment they are sovereign over their own household. It is stated in exactly those terms. Their home is their territory, their decisions within it are theirs, and no one outside it holds authority there.

The crowns themselves are usually family property, worn by a great many heads across a great many generations, and are frequently not worth very much.

Why it works where it works

On worlds where an actual crown sits an hour's walk away in an actual palace, the rite is not modest. It is a claim. Every married couple on that world has been sovereign of something, briefly, in front of witnesses, and the distance between them and the family in the castle is a matter of scale rather than of kind.

Nobody in authority has ever objected, because objecting would require saying out loud what the objection is.

And there is a joke in it that the Royals do not always hear

The house that holds the throne came up from metalworkers. The galaxy's most exalted family and the couple crowned in a kitchen with two dented heirlooms are, at the origin, in the same trade.

Marriage TESTIMONY

There is no galactic marriage. There is a galactic filing, and then there are several hundred entirely unrelated things people actually do.

The one universal

On nearly every world, the legal marriage and the real one are different events, and only one of them is witnessed by anybody who matters.

The Guard needs a name on a tax filing. That is the whole of its interest. Everything else, the braid and the run and the pool and the day spent in blindfolds, happens somewhere else, in front of different people, and is the part anybody would tell you about if you asked them when they got married.

On occupied worlds this gap is not an accident. The occupier's ceremony is the one on paper. The other one is done quietly, at home, and is never mentioned to anyone in a uniform.

What the good ones have in common

The rites that travel, that survive an occupation, that get carried to a new world by refugees and still work there, all share at least one of four things:

  • The marriage is completed by a physical act rather than a spoken word. The seventh step. The ninth sip. The last seed. The closed circle. There is a moment everybody present can see, and either it happened or it did not.
  • The contract comes first and outranks the ceremony. The party is a party.
  • The legal and the true marriage are separate events, as above.
  • There is a visible exit, and everybody knows where it is.

Which direction the money moves tells you who is scarce. Some worlds pay the bride's family and some pay the groom's, and nobody involved thinks of it as demographics, and it is demographics.

A note on the war

Sixty years ago several hard-hit worlds passed emergency measures permitting plural households, on grounds that were entirely about arithmetic. Most were never repealed. They are now a fossil: perfectly legal, rare, mildly embarrassing on some worlds and proudly traditional on others. The Guard has no view, provided one name goes on the filing.

And a note on citizenship

Marriage into a member world is one of the two routes to Guard citizenship. The other is enlistment. Which means there is an entire category of marriage in this galaxy that is an immigration instrument, an entire office that audits them, and an unknown number of couples who started as paperwork and did not stay that way.

The marriage braid TESTIMONY

You do not buy it. You grow it.

The rite

On marriage, a small braid is started in the hair and is never cut for as long as the marriage lasts. It can be hidden, tucked, kept tiny, or worn out where everybody can see it, and there is enormous variation in how: burned at the ends, dyed, beaded, wrapped in thread. What is constant is that it is braided extremely tight, and that keeping it is your job.

A neglected braid is a public statement, and everybody reads it as one.

Why it beats a ring

A ring tells you somebody is married. A braid tells you how long, because it has been growing the whole time. You can read a marriage across a room, in a market, at forty paces, without asking a single question.

The cut

Divorce is a cut. You sever the braid, you bring it to the town council, they run a fast confirmation that the hair is yours, and it is over. That is the entire procedure. It takes an afternoon. It can be done in a temper, at midnight, by somebody who will feel differently on Thursday.

And you may never marry that person again

One cut is permanent. You can marry somebody else, as many times as you like. Never them.

Which produces a specific and entirely avoidable category of person: somebody who did a five-minute thing in a bad hour, twenty years ago, and has had to live inside the consequence ever since. Every world that keeps this rite has them. Everybody knows one.

On a death, you cut it, and you keep it. What is done with it afterward varies and informants become reluctant when asked.

The forgeries

The confirmation step exists for a reason, and the reason is that somebody, at some point, arrived at a council with somebody else's hair.

Proxy marriage INTACT

There is a form. Of course there is a form.

Why it exists

The Guard runs a rotation that can put a person six months from anywhere, and it does not adjust that rotation for weddings. So the galaxy long ago accepted that one half of a marriage may not be in the room, and built the machinery to handle it.

How the absent party appears

As a projection, where the relay will hold, which it frequently will not. As a stand-in, usually a sibling or a squadmate, who says the words and is then teased about it for the rest of their life. Or not at all: an empty frame set where a person should be standing, and everybody proceeds around it.

The empty frame is the older custom and the one people find harder to watch.

The paperwork

Countersigned, witnessed at both ends, filed against a service number. It is entirely routine. There is a queue for it. The clerk who processes them has processed thousands and can do one in under four minutes.

And the version nobody puts on a poster

Some worlds permit a marriage to be registered after one party has died, on application, with authorisation from an office high enough that the applications are counted in single figures per year. The reasons given are pensions, legitimacy and inheritance. The reasons given are not the reasons.

The Renewal TESTIMONY

Married on a two-year term, and then you both decide again.

The mechanism

The marriage runs for a fixed period. At the end of it, either party renews or does not. Declining is not a divorce, carries no penalty, and requires no reason. You simply do not sign, and it is over, cleanly, that day.

Inside a term it is strict

Physical infidelity during a term is a criminal matter and is actually prosecuted, which sounds severe until you notice the logic: you had a door, it was clearly marked, and you chose not to use it.

The stated intent is that trust should be active rather than assumed. You are not married to somebody who has not left. You are married to somebody who chose this again, recently, with a clean exit available, and that is a materially different thing to be told.

And that is exactly what makes it brutal

There is always a door. Both of you know precisely when it opens next.

People count months. Everybody on that world counts months, and everybody pretends not to, and the last few weeks of a term are the loudest silence in any household there.

The fertility clause, where it survives, allows either party to decline without any social cost at all if a couple has wanted children and not managed them within a stated period. It is cold, it is practical, and it is almost certainly a post-war demographic measure that nobody has got round to repealing.

The Rescue TESTIMONY

Somebody's partner has been taken. Somebody is going to have to go and get them.

The rite

One of the couple is captured by the families, either one, and sometimes both at once. The other has to come and retrieve them, and between here and there is a gauntlet assembled entirely by people who have known them since they were small.

Swim the length of a pool while your relatives throw eggs at you. Climb something. Stand there and answer for a specific thing you did when you were nineteen. Be mocked, at length, by everyone who raised you, in front of the person you are marrying.

What it is not

It is not save them from us. Nobody is pretending. The framing is: your partner is in trouble, and everybody here would like to see exactly how far you will actually go.

What it is for

Two things at once. Every relative gets to discharge every frustration they have ever had about this match without doing the smallest amount of real harm. And everybody gets to watch somebody persevere, visibly, for the person they love, which is the thing the whole institution is supposed to be about and is otherwise almost never demonstrable.

It is done before the wedding rather than as part of it. It is open, it is enjoyed, and it is photographed relentlessly.

The Seed Pool TESTIMONY

The couple stands in the water. The guests finish the marriage.

The rite

A shallow above-ground pool, waist-height and wide, built for this and nothing else. The couple stands in it together. Every guest throws in seed and crop: grain, pulses, fruit, whatever that world grows.

The marriage is complete the instant the last seed lands. Not a word is spoken. No officiant is involved. The community physically has to finish it, which means everybody can see who threw and who did not.

A person standing at the back with a full hand is not a private disagreement. It is an event, and it will be discussed for years.

What you throw says who you are

Seed off your own fields is the standard and the safe answer. Somebody who cannot manage that brings something else, and it is noticed, and most people are decent about it. A wealthy family throwing something imported reads as showing off, and is meant to.

The image

By the end the couple is standing waist-deep in other people's harvest, unable to move properly, laughing, being buried by everyone they know.

And afterward, the water

It is drained onto a single plot. What comes up is a chaotic, unplanned, mixed patch of everything forty families grow, and it keeps coming up for years, and everybody in the district knows whose wedding it was.

A marker you can point at from the road. It outlasts a ring by a considerable margin.

The shared meal TESTIMONY

One dish between two people. One bite each is enough.

What it originally was

Something difficult. The heart of a beast that had to be hunted first, or an organ nobody would eat by choice, or an egg rare enough that getting one was the labour. The meaning was blunt and everybody understood it: we will face the unpleasant thing together, and neither of us is going to be the one who does not swallow.

What it is now

Plated. Professionally prepared, seasoned to taste, and in several cases genuinely good. There are chefs who specialise. A few people develop a real fondness for it. Most do not, and most are not expected to.

The argument at every wedding

Older relatives think the seasoning is cheating. They say so. They have said so for forty years, and they will say so again this time, and the couple will eat it anyway.

The variants change the vow

A heart says we will face what is dangerous. An egg says fertility, and something not yet finished. Something bitter that must be completed says the hardest thing of the four: this will not always taste good and you finish it regardless. And a dish that takes both families three days to prepare says that the labour was the vow and the eating is just the receipt.

Unwritten marriage TESTIMONY

Two versions of the same idea, and the people who practise them find each other completely reasonable and everybody else exhausting.

The first has no word for it

Lifelong partnerships form, hold, raise children and end in one death rather than two, and nothing is signed, worn, announced or celebrated. Asked when they married, people from these worlds are not being evasive. The question does not parse. They were not married. They are together, and have been.

The second is purely administrative

Live together long enough and you are married. No ceremony, no announcement, no date anybody could name. The threshold is a duration and the duration is written down somewhere in a municipal code that nobody has read.

These are not cold people. They have every feeling anybody else has. They simply do not perform them in public, and they regard a world that does as a world in which everybody is auditioning. Other cultures find them boring. They find other cultures tiring. Neither has ever been persuaded.

The interruption

Because the second version runs on a clock, it has a loophole, and the loophole has survived every attempt to close it: sleep elsewhere a stated number of nights each year and the count resets.

Which means somewhere there is a person who has spent forty years going to their sister's house for three nights every year, on the same dates, for reasons the family stopped asking about a long time ago.

And the open problem

A species that already regards itself as one enormous family has a genuinely strange time with all of this, and the Restoration has not been able to get a straight answer from anybody about how it works.

Atmospheric masks INTACT

The most common object in the galaxy, because most people are breathing somewhere they did not evolve to breathe.

At the cheap end it is a moulded cup over the mouth and nose with a filter cartridge and a strap, sold everywhere, replaced constantly, and thrown away when the cartridge browns. At the other end it is a machined respirator built into a suit and worn for a working lifetime.

What it tells you about a person

Everything. A mask says which world's air a body was built for, and therefore where that body is standing now and why. A crew stepping off a ramp will hold up a small reader, watch it flash from red to green, and pull their masks off with the relief of people who have just been told they get to be comfortable.

Some species wear them permanently offworld and have done for so long that their faces are essentially a matter of hearsay. A Gashi bounty hunter in a good suit is a pair of gold-black eyes above a piece of engineering, and there are people who have known him for years and could not tell you what is under it.

The etiquette

You do not ask. Not what is under it, not what the air was like at home, and not why he has never taken it off.

Beryllium rifles INTACT

A kinetic weapon that fires a poisoned round, banned across the Royal systems and on Maspin, restricted almost everywhere else.

The metal is toxic. Survive a hit and you carry a cancer risk for the rest of your life, which is what the bans cite and what everyone means when they talk about them.

"You don't just wanna put holes in people. You wanna give them cancer too?"

Why they exist at all

Unlike almost every other weapon in this volume, these can still be made. It is chemistry rather than industry, and a competent chemist with access to the base metal can produce them, which is exactly how they turn up on worlds that have outlawed them.

Crates move under other names. Seizure returns most often find them declared as battery stock, mineral samples, or agricultural chemical.

The breaching kit INTACT

Everything a four-man team needs to get through a door that does not want them.

The charge

A small roll of wool-like fabric. Peel the velcro edges and the underside is a grey, sticky clay. Press the clay over a grenade set to its highest dial, slap the whole assembly against the surface, and pull the six-inch antenna out of the centre of the cloth. When the light on the antenna goes from amber to green, it is armed, and you should not be where you currently are.

Four of them, placed on a rooftop and fired together, will open a building.

The grappling pistol

Slim, light, and it fires a molten orange line rather than a hook on a rope. The claws catch a ledge and melt fractionally into it, welding themselves in place. You tug once to test it. It has never been the tug that killed anybody.

Flashbangs and frags share a body and differ by a dial. The dial is why teams have rules about who carries what, and why one man's mistake with that dial, on a cartel compound, put Corporal Billem's leg out from under him and is still being brought up.

Smoke comes in dented cylinders that smell of phosphorus and are worth more than the rifle when things have gone properly wrong.

Datapads INTACT

A handheld screen, rebuilt from scratch after the Wipe and now made at Saigo and two licensed plants.

You confirm who you are with a thumb on the glass. Off-network it checks you locally and squares up with the ledger later.

They do not talk to anything from before the war. The people who designed them had never used a pre-war device, had no examples to study, and built to their own guesses, which is also why nothing in them anticipates a skeleton key.

Gravity spires INTACT

Towers that burn Corefuel to hold an atmosphere onto a rock that has no business keeping one.

A spire generates a local gravitational field and a pressure envelope around itself, about 1.4 kilometres across. Put three to seven of them in a cluster with overlapping envelopes and you can live on an asteroid: walk outside, plant a garden, hang washing.

They are how the Wake fragment colonies existed at all. The homeworld's own core, refined, keeping the people standing on its wreckage alive.

What breaks

The regulator assembly, always. Nobody can make one; they come out of salvage and pre-war stock, issued quarterly against a settlement's entitlement.

What happens if a cluster goes

The envelope opens over four to eleven hours depending on its size. The safety schedule says get to a hardened structure. It does not say what to do after that.

Guard credits INTACT

The money. A credit is a line in the Guard's ledger, and it is worth something because the Guard says it is.

Nobody outside the accounting division calls them credits. On a dock or in a bar it is Guardcoin, said the way you say the name of a company that owns your town.

And then there is the coin

Struck silver, heavier in the hand than anybody expects the first time, in the same denomination as the ledger and carrying none of its properties. You can put a few of them on a table without a single system anywhere knowing that you did.

That is not a survival from the paper decade. It is current issue, and it is the only part of this arrangement the Guard has never explained in writing. A ledger entry has a sender, a receiver, a date and a reference. A silver credit has a weight.

Which is the whole of it

The Guard built a currency that records everything, and also mints the exception. Every bounty settled on a fringe world, every retained item under Standing Order 41 that somebody afterwards turned into money, and a great deal of what moves through the cartels, moves in metal, because metal does not reconcile.

When the Wipe took every financial record in existence, money went back to paper for about a decade while the accounts were retyped, and then the credit replaced it. It is not backed by metal or grain or anything else. It is backed by the Guard's word and by the fact that member worlds collect tax in it.

Where the ledger works

Wherever Guardnet reaches. Beyond that you settle in paper and hope somebody reconciles it later, at the discretion of whoever you are dealing with.

Which means the answer to whether your savings exist depends on where you are standing. Cut a world off the network and everything its people own becomes a rumour until it comes back.

The ledger rules allow settlement to a world or a district to be suspended by administrative decision. It has happened nineteen times in twenty years, for an average of forty-one days.

Guardnet INTACT

The network being built to replace the one that died, and it is not going quickly.

It carries the credit ledger, service records, licensing and official traffic. It does not carry public communication and was never meant to. If you want to send a letter to someone three systems away you still use a courier ship or a church-owned radio tower, the same as everybody has for sixty years.

Coverage is continuous through the inner member worlds, patchy past them, and absent on forty-four member worlds and every non-member world in existence.

That map matters more than anything else about it. Money is a ledger entry now, and the ledger lives here. Where the network reaches, you have savings. Where it does not, you have a promise.

Holocloaks CONTESTED

Not invisibility. Something worse to be on the wrong end of.

Activated from the gauntlet, the armour's contours dissolve into a rippling distortion and the light bends around the wearer. What is left is a whisper of heat-shimmer moving across a landscape, indistinguishable from the landscape unless you already know to look.

What gives it away

Footprints. The system does not hide the ground, and on ash or sand or snow the prints are perfectly visible for as long as it takes the wind to take them. Standing still, a man in a holocloak is a rumour. Moving, he is a trail.

The gauge

There is a power meter on the gauntlet and it is the only thing that matters. It runs down fast, it does not recover in the field, and every operator who has ever worn one has spent the entire approach doing arithmetic against it.

Restricted issue, and not manufactured anywhere the archive can name.

Hoverboards INTACT

Everybody knows what one is. Everybody has seen one. Nobody can build one.

The repulsor assembly came out of factories that no longer exist, and the design is well understood in the sense that engineers can explain exactly how it works and cannot produce the part. Surviving boards get repaired and traded and the price goes up every single year.

Saigo has tried to rebuild them four times and abandoned it four times. The programme reports are unusually honest about why.

Hyperspace slipstream INTACT

You do not go to the place. The place is brought to you.

That is not a metaphor and it is how every navigational primer in the galaxy opens. A vessel under slipstream does not cross the distance; the space behind it is drawn toward it, and the ship arrives without ever having travelled. What the crew experience is the g-force slamming them into their seats, the stars outside stretching first to white streaks and then to a rush of blue, and then a lurch.

Aboard, it is just the hypercharge

A gauge climbing toward a hundred while somebody reads the number out loud, because on a small vessel the difference between seventy per cent and ninety-nine is the difference between an argument and an escape.

The drives

Seven classes in service. Anything above class four is on the unreplaceable schedule, which means what exists is what exists and there is no facility left anywhere that knows how to build another. Classes one through four are still made, at three plants, at a rate that does not keep up with the ships being lost.

Which is the quiet fact underneath every schedule in this volume: the galaxy is getting slower, by a little, every year, and has been for decades.

The lanes

Every route on record died with everything else. The ones in use now were re-flown by hand over about thirty years by crews going out into unsurveyed dark to find out whether it worked. The survey authority publishes what that cost. It is a long document.

And some volumes you do not enter

The schedules carry standing advisories against transit of certain regions. Reasons are given for most of them.

Magboots CONTESTED

They let you walk up a wall, and almost nobody has a pair.

Sleek, rose-gold, with pointed toes that look far too elegant for what they do. They hum faintly with every step and grip whatever ferrous surface they are set against, which means a man in magboots can climb the outside of a building at a walking pace, clink by clink, and step off the top of it as though he had come up a staircase.

Why they are rare

They are pre-war, and the manufacture died with everything else. What is in circulation is what survived. A pair is worth more than most people's contracts, they turn up mostly as loot, and their owners are extremely aware of both facts.

What they are actually used for

Not war, mostly. There is a wrecked starship the size of a city on a world nobody names, so thoroughly overgrown that people climb it like a mountain, and the steep sections of it are impossible without a pair. Fathers and sons have gone up it together for generations.

They do not like lightning. A storm will fry a pair permanently, and there is no repairing them, and no replacing them either.

Plasma knives INTACT

A blade that is not a blade, carried by everybody who cannot afford to run out of options.

It lives in the forearm gauntlet. A press of the panel and it snaps into being with a hard hiss: a dense, crackling wedge of blue-teal light, throwing its glow across the wearer's armour and the face of whoever is about to have a bad few seconds.

It does not last

A few moments, and then it is gone and the gauntlet needs to cool. That is the whole design constraint, and everything about how it is used follows from it. You do not fence with a plasma knife. You solve one problem with it and then you do not have it any more.

It goes through flesh like the flesh has agreed to it, and it will grind to a stop against bone. It cuts a clean glowing hole through a locked drawer. It cauterises as it goes, which is either mercy or the opposite depending on where it lands.

The bayonet variant mounts under a rifle barrel and burns longer, at the cost of being attached to something two feet long.

The shield variant is the same principle turned flat: a small teal plane of energy that does not block so much as burn. Pressed against something, it does not stop it. It cooks it.

Plasma rifles INTACT

The standard weapon of the age, and nobody can make another one.

The process was worked out on Pashmirské, off the volcanic vents of that world, and for a long period Pashmirské armed most of the settled galaxy. Every plasma rifle now in existence was built before the Wipe. The factories that made them and the charge assemblies they run on were among the first things both sides burned, because that was the whole strategy of the war: not taking ground, taking the ability to build.

So the total number only goes down. Armourers keep them alive by cannibalising the dead ones, and a serviceable rifle appreciates in value against almost everything else. Out on the rim, weapons work as currency. A rifle holds its worth better than money does.

Which makes the Guard's arsenal not just power but a fortune, sitting in racks.

Automatic plasma weapons are legal under planetary statute on nineteen member worlds and illegal under Galactic Standard everywhere. Both are true at once, and which one gets enforced depends on who is asking.

Polaris scrip INTACT

The money in the breadbasket. Excellent money, and only in the breadbasket.

Wages, rent, shopping, licences and local tax are all in scrip. Wages are good and savings are substantial, well above the member-world average, because the system pays properly and there is not much to spend it on.

You can change it for Guard credits at the exchange in Kelton City, at a rate set daily, up to an annual limit per person. Roughly four people in a thousand ever reach that limit.

Nobody is stopped from leaving Polaris. What you cannot do is take twenty years of it with you.

Portaboards CONTESTED

One of the last mass-produced Levitation Matrix devices, and nobody alive knows how to make another.

It floats. That is the short answer and the one most people give. It carries a rider or a load a few feet off the ground, glides over broken country and standing water, and wobbles when the field has to adjust to uneven terrain, which is often.

The long answer is that the Levitation Matrix was a whole class of anti-gravity engineering that came out of the pre-war world and did not survive it. What is left in circulation is what was already built. They are traded, hoarded, stolen, and repaired by people who do not understand the thing they are repairing.

Why an engineer will trade everything he owns for one

Not to ride it. To open it. Take one apart, work out what the matrix is actually doing, and a great deal of what the galaxy currently cannot do becomes possible again.

Several people have tried. So far the boards have survived the attempts better than the reputations of the people making them.

Quantum-thread armour INTACT

The good armour. Pre-war, unmakeable, and getting rarer every year in the most literal way possible.

Nobody knows how to spin the thread any more. Damaged suits are patched from suits that are past saving, which means every repair anywhere reduces the total amount of it in existence. The Guard tracks its remaining serviceable area as a single number, and that number goes down annually.

Ship hulls are armoured with the same material out of the same pool. Every year a committee decides how much goes on hulls and how much goes on people.

Who gets a whole suit is a priority list. Everybody else gets a patched one, a partial one, or the current-manufacture substitute, which is heavier, worse, and available in quantity.

Royal scrip INTACT

The crown's own money. Struck and issued from Maldo, accepted in the Royal systems and in the protectorates, and it is the instrument in which every tax, due and royalty the houses collect is assessed.

What it is worth

What the houses say. There is no metal behind it, no grain, no reserve of anything, and no schedule anywhere setting out what would have to happen for that to change. It is worth something because the Royal treasury will take it back, and the Royal treasury will take it back because it issued it.

The name

Scrip is not the word the ministries use. The ministries say the Royal credit, in every instrument, without exception. Everybody else on every dock in the galaxy says scrip, and has since before anybody now living was working, and the two words have never once appeared in the same document.

Which is the entire political situation in one noun. Polaris pays its farmers in a currency that is excellent and only good in Polaris, and every person in that system knows exactly what that arrangement is. The crown does the same thing across two systems and a string of protectorates, and the difference is that on Maldo it is not sayable.

Against the credit

Not published. There is a rate, it moves, and it is quoted between banks and by nobody in public. The treasury has never printed one and has never been asked in a form it would have to answer.

The Restoration has looked for a stated conversion in nineteen years of ministerial filing and has not found one. What we have found, repeatedly, is contracts written in both units on the same page with no bridge between them, which is what people do when the answer is understood and nobody wants it in writing.

What comes in

Taxes from the Royal systems. Dues from the protectorates. Royalties from arrangements with third parties, of which by far the largest is Astonia, which pays by the head.

And the problem with that

The Astonian accounting is performed by the Guard. The treasury receives a figure and a payment in its own money, and does not receive the returns underneath, and has not, on the record, asked for them.

So the crown's single largest revenue line is a number somebody else worked out, converted at a rate nobody publishes, into a currency the crown values itself.

What it will not buy

Nothing scheduled. Nothing unreplaceable. Maldo steel is worked out and no quantity of Royal scrip will produce another tonne of it, which the maintenance books on every Royal building record in the plainest possible way, one repair at a time.

[Compiler's note: the treasury on Maldo has never failed to honour this money and we should say so. It has also never been asked to honour very much of it at once.]

Schedule of unreplaceable classes INTACT

The insurers' list of things that cannot be made any more.

It exists for a boring reason. You cannot indemnify something by replacing it if there is no replacement, so underwriters had to write down what falls into that category in order to price it. The list gets revised every year.

What is on it

Plasma weapons and their charge assemblies. Quantum-thread armour. Regenerative medicine. Pre-war vaccine stock. Grav-rudder assemblies. Gravity spire regulators. Slipstream drives above class 4. Every kind of drone and remote system. Repulsor transport. Combine drive units. Maldo steel. Certified parent seed lines.

Forty-one additions in the last twenty years. Three deletions, all three after Saigo certified it could build the thing again.

What it means

Everything on this list appreciates against everything not on it, permanently, because the supply only ever falls. Which is why a rifle is a better store of value than money out on the rim, and why the largest holder of scheduled items in the galaxy is the Guard.

[Compiler's note: this is a document about insurance. It is also the most complete description of the present age that anyone has written.]

Sensory tanks TESTIMONY

A tank of floom fluid that you put a dying person into.

It is used for injuries nothing else will touch. What it does is not fully understood by anyone who operates one, including the people who operate them: it brings back function that conventional medicine has already written off, and it does not bring back tissue that is gone. What is missing stays missing.

There are four of these anywhere, three of them on Maspin, and the limit is the fluid rather than the tank.

What patients report

Attendants say the same thing every time. People under immersion dream continuously, and when they surface they describe stretches of experience far longer and far more coherent than the hours they were in the water.

Skeleton keys RECOVERED

A pre-war device that copies everything off a terminal without touching it.

You put it anywhere on the housing and it sticks, magnetically. No port, no cable, no connection of any kind. Then you wait, because it is not fast, and when the indicator turns it is finished.

Nothing detects them

Every security system now in service was built after the Wipe by people who had never seen one and had nothing to design against. Guardnet's published protections do not list the class, because as far as its architects were concerned the class does not exist.

Almost none survive. They are not insured, not scheduled, and not traded openly, and the technical material we hold breaks off after the processor generation.

Space airbags INTACT

The last thing a ship does, and it does it without being asked.

When a vessel's systems work out that the situation is no longer recoverable, they fire the reservoirs. Expanding foam floods the hull in seconds, filling every compartment, every passage, and every space around every crew member, setting to a dense semi-rigid mass that holds a body still through an impact that would otherwise fold it.

It dissolves shortly afterwards. Not on a timer, and not on a command. It simply stops being foam, sags, and drains away, leaving a residue on the deck and a survivor who is generally unconscious.

The unsettling part

The ship makes the decision. There is no lever. By the time a pilot has understood that the situation is unsurvivable, the foam has usually already gone off, which means most people who have been through it did not experience the crash at all. They experienced a pressure, then nothing, then waking up.

Crews are not warm about this. A machine that knows before you do, and acts before you can, is a machine that has already had an opinion about your competence.

Space vaccines INTACT

The reason there is no plague.

A standard course against the major transmissible diseases, given nearly everywhere, and the single most successful thing anyone has managed to keep running since the war. Coverage is above ninety per cent on eighty-eight member worlds. It is below forty on nineteen, and the map of who gets them looks almost exactly like the map of where Guardnet reaches, because the programme runs off the ledger.

What they cannot do

There are forty-one diseases with no surviving formulation at all. The seed stock burned with everything else. Populations that happen to have picked up resistance to any of them are noted, world by world, in the survey material, and that is the whole of the plan.

And the other kind of medicine

The regenerative material, the cure-anything material, is not this. That was pre-war, the facilities are gone, and what exists is a stockpile being spent. A million doses is an enormous number until you are counting people in billions.

The Targath magnetic web TESTIMONY

The reason the Guard stopped underestimating a species that burrows.

How it works

Targaths dig. Not trenches, and not tunnels in the ordinary sense, but a lattice laid down slowly through the crust of a whole colony over months or years, built in the dark, undetectable from orbit and undetectable from the surface. It draws no power while it sits. It reads as geology.

Then somebody switches it on.

What that does

Everything ferrous within its reach is pulled straight down. Ships in low orbit lose the argument first, and come out of the sky in numbers. On the ground it is worse and slower: a soldier's armour, his rifle, his helmet, every plate and fastening on him, all of it dragged flat against the dirt with him inside. He is not injured. He is pinned, awake, in the open.

What happens next is a matter for the people who arrive afterwards, and the accounts of Rudcuff are consistent that nobody was left to say.

The web has not been used since. Whether that is because the Targath cannot build another or because they have not yet needed to is a question the Guard's schedules do not raise.

Torkal bombers INTACT

The aircraft that burned the jungle colonies, now in its seventh generation and no longer carrying anybody.

The second generation is the one people mean when they say the name. Long, heavy, and built to fly low over canopy and unload, and what it unloaded went across the Targath jungle worlds in overlapping lines until there was nothing left standing to overlap. Pilots flew those runs personally, watched an entire ecosystem go up as a sheet of light beneath them, and came home feeling like they had held lightning.

What changed

The ionic calibrators in the old batteries were the constant failure point, and nobody fixed them. They were replaced outright with seismic-magnetic cells, which are enormously expensive and last, and the space that bought was used for something else.

The seventh generation has no pilot

Real computing has been creeping back into Guard airframes for a few years now, quietly, in ways nobody has to sign for. The men who used to fly these things had a terrible job and knew it. The men who built the thing that replaced them are, in several cases, not comfortable with what they did.

And afterwards

They get scrapped. There is a sculpture in a town square on a rock in the Wake field made out of a second-generation airframe, cut up and welded together and painted teal and magenta by somebody who never explained what it was supposed to be. It is the most peaceful thing on that asteroid.

Translator chips INTACT

A Guard-made implant that puts Galactic Standard in your head. It goes in at the neck.

One of the very few things the galaxy has managed to start manufacturing again since the Wipe, which makes it a small triumph and a very profitable line. Guard personnel get one if the job needs it. Everybody else buys one, and they are not cheap.

Each unit is serialised, and the serial ranges are allocated by production quarter, which means any chip anyone finds can be dated to within three months of when it was made.

The scar

The placement leaves a mark, and the surgical notes say so plainly: it is unavoidable at that position. The same notes mention, without further comment, that some patients ask for the implant specifically because there is already something at their neck they would rather people did not look at.

Wingsuits INTACT

Not a garment. A function of the armour, folded flat until you need it.

Strike the chestplate and sheets of material snap taut between the limbs, turning a falling man into something with a wing loading. The suit's temperature regulators take over at the same moment, which matters more than people expect, because the interesting places to do this are interesting for a reason.

What it is actually like

The wind screams past the helmet at a pitch that gets into the teeth. Rain hits the visor and streaks off sideways in trails. The suit fights the air for the first few seconds and then stops fighting it, and after that you are cutting rather than falling, and it is entirely possible to forget what you came down here to do.

The landing is the part nobody practises enough

You flare, you extend, and the ground arrives with more authority than the training tower ever managed. A good landing is a hard skid onto one knee. A bad one is the same thing with a longer skid.

Then you hit the panel and the material folds itself back into the armour, and there is no evidence you ever had it.

Materials

Biodium INTACT

A combustible fuel extracted on Pashmirské. It is not Corefuel and is not comparable to it.

Origin

It is the residue of a rainforest that covered a large part of the world and dried out a very long time before anybody arrived on it. The deposit is finite, is not being added to, and was laid down by an ecosystem that no living record describes.

What it is for

Domestic and light industrial use. Heating, cooking, generators, small plant. It does not fly anything and no vessel of any class runs on it.

What it is worth

Enough. Pashmirské is not a wealthy world and is not a poor one, and the difference is this deposit. It is the reason the administration can pay for what it provides, and the reason the world has not needed to ask anybody for anything since the war ended.
