Corefuel INTACT

A quarter of a litre of it will run twenty haulers for a hundred years. It is refined out of the core of a dead planet, and there is one planet you are allowed to take it from.

Yield

One standard measure, taken as 0.25 litres, is rated by the licensing authority at a commercial hauler fleet of twenty vehicles for approximately one hundred standard years.

Reserves

The Wake fragments are assessed at about five thousand years at current rates. It is not scarce. Nothing about this trade is driven by scarcity.

The licence

Extraction, synthesis, transport and resale are licensed by the Guard Board of Directors and by nobody else. Duty is charged at the point it comes out of the ground and again at the point it is sold.

For GC 4461: 812,443.6 tonnes extracted, 40,622,180 credits in duty, and 3,249,774,400 credits at final market.

Everywhere else

Every world has a core. Getting at one anywhere else means deep drilling, fracturing, or a lucky asteroid, and then it still has to be synthesised. Since GC 4420 there have been eleven applications for a non-Wake licence. All eleven were withdrawn by the applicant.

The process

1 gap

Registered GC 4417 to a single named patentee, K. Avaris, and assigned afterwards to the Board for a consideration of one credit. The registration sets the process out in seven steps. Six of them are redacted in the copy we hold. [RECORD DAMAGED]

What the Maspin say

That planetary cores are alive. That the thing in the tanks is not a mineral. They do not say it as belief, and mystics on four other worlds say something close enough that we have filed them together, under religious testimony, which is where claims go when nothing corroborates them.

[Compiler's note: the market figure above is filed to the credit. The number of people employed in the extraction zone is not filed at all.]

Maldo steel INTACT

The metal the Royal systems are made of, and there is no more of it.

It came out of one world during one industrial century, and it is better than anything now in production: stronger, longer-lived, and with a surface finish that is the reason it got used for statues and railings as well as for beams.

Then the ore ran out.

Every palace, ministry, monument, embassy and lamp post the Royals have raised anywhere is built from a material that cannot be made again. Repairs go in with modern alloys that do not match and never will, and every Royal building is tracked as a slowly falling percentage of its original self.

Knock a wing down and you can rebuild it. You cannot rebuild it out of the same thing.

Flora

Astonian coral INTACT

Reef, standing in open air, where a hedge should be.

Astonia had an ocean and does not any more, and the coral simply stayed where it was. It stands across the whole equatorial belt, eight metres in places, dry, in pinks and oranges and a blue that keeps glowing after dark.

It does not grow. It does not rot either. There is exactly enough water in the sand to hold it where it is, indefinitely.

The colours are wrong on purpose

They look garish to human eyes and they were never meant for human eyes. The fish that lived here saw further up the spectrum than we do, and in that light, what looks lurid to a visitor was camouflage.

People keep it alive

There is a spray bottle by the door in most houses in the settled belt, and misting the nearest formation is a daily thing that everybody does. No law requires it. Ask why and you get a different answer from everyone.

And it protects them

A lifetime spent breathing over these reefs is what Guard medicine credits for Astonian resistance to eleven diseases the rest of the galaxy has no answer for.

Astonian milk INTACT

Dairy from herds that graze on a forage growing nowhere else in the galaxy, and the reason Astonians are built the way they are.

Guard medical survey credits something in this milk for bone density and muscle mass well above the human mean. Take the same animals somewhere else and the effect disappears, because it is the grass, not the cows.

Three worlds have tried to grow that forage off Astonia. All three failed.

Four hundred thousand tonnes of solids go out a year, and the Royal houses take a royalty on every tonne of it under an instrument they signed decades ago.

Fortified wine, made in quantity before the war on four worlds. Two of them stopped. One of them no longer exists.

Comet caps RECOVERED

A mushroom, and the reason a Guardsman keeps one eye on the calendar.

They come up in a small handful of places and travel badly, so what circulates is mostly dried. Taken properly they do what this class of thing does everywhere: the walls get interesting, the hours stop behaving, and somebody in the room announces they have worked out what everything means.

They are the running joke and the running risk on any deployment. Drug tests come round roughly every six months, which sounds generous until you realise everybody knows the date and nobody remembers it.

Legality is a local matter and a live one. Sixty-one separate drug-licensing polls have gone to the Guard franchise in the last twenty years, which means somewhere out there, a great many people have very strong feelings about a mushroom.

Broad flat canopies on bare trunks, named for the red resin that runs when you cut them. Slow, long-lived, and entirely happy in ruined ground.

Fermented kraskor TESTIMONY

The finest thing on Maspin, by the Council's own account, and it is meat that has been left alone for years.

Kraskor flesh is fermented down until it is liquid, or near enough, and then taken the way Maspin take everything, which is absorbed rather than eaten. Grades exist and the good ones are measured in years.

Floom eggs TESTIMONY

Unfertilised eggs, laid on dead ground, full of a blue liquid. On Maspin they are fertiliser. Off Maspin they are the most valuable medicine in existence.

The ordinary use is the important one: a floom drops them on dry grass or a failing garden and a week later the ground has recovered. That is how the settled belt stays fertile without importing anything.

The fluid

Nobody sensible calls it a drug. Calsco calls it the essence of life in its purest form and does not appear to be exaggerating for effect. It is the medium in the sensory tanks and it brings people back from injuries that should have finished them.

Taking it

For a human it is hours of something that is not a high in any recognisable sense. For a Maspin it is not hours. Ask one whether they have ever tried it and you will get a straight no, and the reason, which is that the effect would last the rest of their life.

Control

The Council of Riflo restricts collection, holding and export, and has refused three applications to expand the trade. It is the most valuable thing on the planet, and the body sitting on it is the body that would profit most from letting it go.

Flooms TESTIMONY

The creature Maspin runs on, and the reason the air there is as good as it is.

They are nervous, affectionate, and much smarter than they look. Everyone who has kept them says the same thing, unprompted: a floom decides very quickly what it thinks of a person, and it is almost never wrong. People on Maspin take this seriously enough to act on it.

What they do

They take in ambient life energy the way a plant takes light. Not stealing it, not draining anything, just standing in it.

Then they lay eggs on dead ground: unfertilised, full of a blue liquid, dropped on dry grass and failing gardens. About a week later the ground has come back greener than it was. The Trailblazer concession imports no fertiliser at all and its yields keep climbing.

The local phrasing, given to us word for word by three different people:

Floom is the ecosystem. All things live because of flooms, and floom lives because of life.

Trade

They are exported, in very small numbers. The Council restricts it and has turned down three applications to expand it.

Kraskor INTACT

Big, horned, herd animals on Maspin, with a strong preference for charging first.

They are herded across the settled belt by people made of smoke, which is a sight visitors do not forget, and they are one of the few things this world produces in enough quantity to sell offworld. Four hundred thousand head a year go out live.

The Maspin do not eat them in the form they sell them. What they eat is fermented, and it takes years.

Open Kraskor on its own page

Megafauna of Marfeld INTACT

Forty-one catalogued species over a tonne, nine of them predators, all of them still out there.

Every other world hunted its big animals to nothing. Marfeld never managed it, and that single failure shaped everything about the place: why the towns are walled, why they stay small enough to move, why there has never been a city, and why the world's chief export is people who have already survived something.

The settlements survey them every year, tracking range, movement and density, and pool the results. It is the most consistent piece of science produced on the world and it is done by farmers.

Domestication

In the last two centuries they broke some of the big grazers to harness and bred the aggression out. Those lines are exported now as draught animals, placid as anything.

The animals changed. The culture did not.

Pickled inside-barked mycelium TESTIMONY

A fungus that grows on the inner bark of certain jungle trees, cut out, pickled, and drunk.

It is named beside fermented kraskor in the Council's submissions as one of the two great Maspin foods, which on a world with very little to eat is a real distinction.

Which trees it comes from is not written down anywhere and nobody would tell us. That reticence turned out not to be religious. It is commercial.

Redleaf INTACT

The Monveri crop. A cultivated leaf with a psychoactive resin, legal there by name in their accession terms and legal on twenty-two other worlds by local statute.

Monver taxes it like anything else and enforces nothing, and the line you will hear if you ask, more or less word for word from anyone: soldiers who fight hard should relax hard, and it helps with what fighting does to you.

That is mostly true.

The health there is, every year, a minority for whom it stopped being recreation a long time ago. Nobody has proposed a statute. It is the one subject on that world where a direct question gets a change of topic.

Rockroot INTACT

A tuber that grows in thin soil, in rock cracks, in heat and in frost, and keeps for two years in a sack without anyone doing anything to it.

It is the food of last resort on a dozen marginal worlds and the food of the Path of Root on Marfeld, where a seventeen-year-old with no tools and no supplies is expected to find enough of it to live on.

It tastes appalling. No world in this volume exports it and eleven import it, which tells you everything about who is eating it and why.

Spireleaf INTACT

A low, broad-leaved plant that will grow under a gravity spire, which almost nothing will.

The light under an envelope is wrong and the pressure gradient is worse, and most cultivars simply give up. This one does not. It came out of somebody's greenhouse a long time ago and it is now on every asteroid colony in the field.

It appears in the supply manifests as a seed issue, listed under gardening rather than food. Which means people living on a rock, breathing borrowed air, asked for something to look at, and somebody put it on the ship.

Starfruit INTACT

A sectioned fruit, very sweet, grown on the warm worlds and cut across the sections so it comes apart in stars.

It travels badly. Inner systems get it fresh and the outer worlds get it preserved, which is a difference of about eleven days in transit and, to anyone who has only ever had the jar, an entirely different fruit.

Yinmelon INTACT

A big, heavy, fleshy fruit, mostly processed into a sauce of the same name and shipped in sealed tins by the container load.

It is one of the highest-volume food items moving anywhere, which is exactly why it is also one of the most common things written on the outside of a container holding something else entirely. Customs seizure returns are full of Yinmelon sauce that is not Yinmelon sauce.

The sauce itself is decent. Somebody has a story about a guard at a farmer's market on Monver who took a bribe in the form of a taste and lost a thumb to what was in the tin.

The Astonian dialect TESTIMONY

[NO LIVING SPEAKERS RECORDED]

The way Astonia used to talk. One person wrote it down, and then it was gone.

The survey

4,100 words, a sketch of the sounds, and eleven pages of stories taken down from speakers. Done by a single investigator using a transcription system of their own invention which they never explained. No recording exists. The investigator's name appears on nothing else, anywhere.

How it ended

After the annexation, the schools went to sponsored religious foundations on contract. Residential attendance, and teaching in Galactic Standard. Inside eleven years they had ninety-four per cent of the children.

One generation. That is all it takes.

Our own survey of the world in GC 4457 found no speaker.

Two attempts to bring it back, both by Astonian associations, both working from the same notes because there is nothing else, both suspended.

[Compiler's note: the conscription yield for this world is filed every year, to the person. It is three entries away.]

Crag CONTESTED

The slur. It means non-human, all of them, any of them.

It is not a word for a species. It is a word for a category, and it gets used identically on peoples who have nothing whatsoever to do with each other. A Nhath and a Vitula and a Targath share no biology, no history and no language, and one syllable covers all three.

Where it came from

Nobody knows. There is no first use, no derivation, and nobody who can tell you. It shows up in the recovered material already in general circulation, with no gloss, as though it never needed one.

The exemption

People who use it will very often exempt somebody. This one is different. This one is all right. It is offered as a compliment and taken as one, and it does not reduce how often the word gets used. It is what lets everyone go on using it.

Where it sits

It is not in Galactic Standard law. Nothing prohibits it. Guard notices discourage it in the messes, which are the only official documents anywhere that admit the word exists, and they are notices about language rather than about people.

Non-humans are about a fifth of everyone alive. They are 0.8 per cent of the Guard.

Very little of that gap was decided by anybody. Terraforming was financed to make worlds habitable for humans, and it worked, so the settled galaxy is an environment humans can stand in and a great many other peoples cannot. Those peoples serve offworld in masks, or on medication, or under a specification of some kind, and a soldier who requires equipment nobody else requires is a soldier a unit has to plan around.

The rest follows from arithmetic. Four fifths of the establishment is one species, so the training, the rations, the medicine, the armour and the sizing of every piece of it are built once and built for that species. Nothing in the schedules bars anybody. The schedules simply do not fit them, and there has never been a year in which fixing that was the cheapest thing available to do.

Which leaves an organisation that is 99.2 per cent human without a single instrument anywhere requiring it to be.

Galactic Standard INTACT

What everybody speaks. Nobody made them.

No law imposes it and no instrument requires it. It is the language of the code, the ledger, the shipping manifests and the Guard, and that has been more than enough. If you want to buy something, sue somebody, or get paid, this is the language you do it in.

Where it came from

It is not anybody's first language and never was. It assembled itself out of the large human tongues of the pre-war era, taking whatever was most useful from each, and it went through three stages to get here.

Before the war it was the language of trade, spoken between parties who had no other language in common and no interest in learning one.

During the war it became the language of negotiation, for the same reason and with more at stake. Both belligerents used it. Almost every surviving instrument from that period is written in it, which is why this archive can read them at all.

After the war it became the only one. The Guard needed a single language to administer in, and it did not have to impose one, because the thing everybody already used for contracts and ceasefires was sitting there.

Nobody had to be made to learn it

There is no ministry of language, no standard body, and no penalty attached to speaking anything else. It spread because the alternative was not being paid.

Where it was taught deliberately, it went faster

On Astonia the schools were handed to sponsored religious foundations under the annexation instrument, with residential attendance and instruction in Galactic Standard written into the contract. Inside eleven years those foundations had ninety-four per cent of the children.

That is the only case in this archive where anybody set out to do it on purpose, and it is catalogued separately, because what happened to Astonian speech is not what is happening elsewhere and we do not want the two read as one process.

Guard nicknames INTACT

Nobody in this service is called what is on their file, and how many things a man is called tells you exactly how many people are close enough to take a liberty with him.

Nobody agrees, and the disagreement is the whole system

A name does not shorten once. It shortens differently in every direction, and the versions do not compete or resolve. One staff sergeant in the personnel series is attested, in the same year, as Jim, Jimzy, Jimz, Jimzo, Jimbo and Jimmy. Six people, six words, one man, and not one of them adopted anybody else's.

Which means the nickname is not really about him. It is a record of a relationship, held by the other person.

Who is allowed

Anybody who has earned it, and there is no ceremony for earning it. What there is instead is a very reliable tell: the first time somebody shortens your name in front of the room and nobody looks up.

The full name is the distance

Read the establishment by this and it goes the wrong way from rank. A Special Operations sergeant has six names. A colonel of the covert division has a rank and a surname. The men in this volume who are only ever given one name, in full, every time, are the men nobody has ever been in a room with twice.

Getting it wrong on purpose

A recognised move, and not an affectionate one. You mangle a man's name, hold his eye, and wait to see whether he corrects you. Correcting is not the loss. The loss is the pause before you decide.

Some people never correct anybody, ever, about anything. It is worth knowing which ones.

Short forms that stopped being short

Yakib became Yake so completely that both turn up in the same conversation in the same mouth, and the man answers to either without noticing there were two.

Elsewhere

The Maspin do the same thing and made it the law: the inherited name is long and the one that stuck is the one you give a stranger. Nhathian fuses a three-part name to two syllables for the people who love him and keeps eleven for anybody taking a statement.

Three peoples, no contact, one arrangement. Nobody planned it and it is not in any instrument.

[Compiler's note: the enlistment form has one line for a name. We hold four thousand two hundred and six testimonies and have not once heard a soldier use what is on it.]

The Maspin alphabet TESTIMONY

The written system of the Maspin. Flowing, connected, and executed with a quill.

Character

Informants of other peoples describe the script as elegant before they describe it as legible. Maspin informants describe it in terms of feeling rather than of sound, and the Restoration has not been able to establish whether the system is alphabetic, syllabic, or something for which we lack a term.

Use

Council record, contract, correspondence, and rite. The Council's minute is taken by hand in this script and is not translated.

Availability

No Maspin text is held by this archive. Copies of Council submissions to the Royal treasury exist here in Galactic Standard because the Council prepared them in Galactic Standard, addressed to a body that would not otherwise read them.

Maspin names TESTIMONY

A Maspin has two names and only uses one of them.

The surname comes from whoever raised you, and it is almost always a tree. The jungle has a great many of them, and a family takes one, and the children take it after. You do not have to be born to the household to carry the name. You have to have been raised by it, which on Maspin is the same thing said properly.

The name you actually go by is a nickname, and it arrives in childhood the way nicknames do everywhere. Something you did. Something you kept doing. A word a visiting trader used about you that stuck. A character out of a book you would not stop talking about at nine years old.

Nobody assigns it and nobody records it. It settles on you, and then it is yours, and that is what you tell people your name is.

Ships are not named at all

The reason given is an objection to worldly attachment, and it is given briefly, in a tone that closes the subject.

Councillors are not named either

Sitting members of the Council of Riflo are addressed as the Council and nothing else, and outsiders do not learn their names. What that rule is for is not something anyone here has felt like explaining to us.

Nhath names RECOVERED

Three parts, in a fixed order, and every one of them is a compound.

Kakavai-Shtuv Aroniela-Kipo Deva Strongskull Moonchild, eighty-seventh generation

The given name is your body

A physical trait welded onto the body part it is true about. Kakavai is strong, shtuv is skull, and the man is Strongskull. It belongs to you alone and it passes to nobody.

The family name is what you believe

A spiritual element welded onto a family role. Aroniela is the moon, which is the sacred one, the one raids are timed to. Kipo is child. Moonchild. It goes to the children unchanged and it is the same sound in the four hundredth mouth as the first.

Note what that means side by side. A Nhath's private name describes their skull, and their inherited name describes their relationship to a moon. The flesh is the personal part and the faith is the shared one.

The number is the generation

Base eight, named after the fingers, because a Nhath hand has four: ka, da, ga, ra, ma, ba, va, sa, and then a block prefix for every eight after that. It goes up by one each generation and it never restarts. Higher numbers command more respect, and the recovered examples run past a hundred.

A new clan may be founded at any time and starts at one. Nobody is impressed by a one.

Succession, in full

Kakavai-Shtuv Aroniela-Kipo Deva · Strongskull Moonchild 87 Peus-Maika Aroniela-Kipo Desa · Bighands Moonchild 88

The father's skull and the son's hands. The moon stays where it is, and the number moves one.

How it is actually said

Almost never in full. The formal short form fuses the given name into one word, Kashtuv, and among family and friends it clips again to Kash. A Nhath goes his whole life as two syllables to the people who love him and eleven to anybody taking a statement.

And to strangers

Nhathian has two words for you, marlo and lo, chosen by the standing of the person addressed, and choosing wrong is not a rudeness. But there is no form at all for someone outside the people, because an outsider has no line and no number for the grammar to measure. They are krayd, which serves for they, for other species, and for enemy. It is not an insult. There is no other slot.

[Compiler's note: the Guard's contracts identify these same individuals by a single job code. An eighty-eight generation line and an invoice, for one man, filed in the same cabinet.]

Nhathian RECOVERED

The Nhath language, pieced together from a partial survey, two word lists, and people who remembered some of it. No native text has ever been recovered.

We print it at length because it is the only substantial evidence about this people that was not produced by somebody who was paying them.

How it sounds

Dry and deliberate, one syllable placed after another, with the strangeness carried in the vowels rather than in clusters. Consonants bite, vowels run long.

Us and everyone else

Their word for themselves is their word for we. Every other people in the galaxy calls them by it, which means the entire galaxy addresses them, without noticing, as us.

For everybody outside there is one word, krayd. It does duty for they, for other species, and for enemy. There is nothing neutral in the language for a stranger.

Counting

Base eight, named after the fingers, because a Nhath hand has four. It goes all the way down: tools cut for that grip, eight-sided rooms, eight-hour periods, formations of eight.

Colour

There are no abstract colour words at all. Every one is built off a thing. Red is blood-colour, white is clean-colour, black is night-colour, silver is weapon-colour. Two of them have no equivalent anywhere else: one means the colouring of a healthy prey animal, and one means the colour enemies bleed, which changes depending on who you are fighting.

Opposites are the same word backwards

This is the part that matters.

meaning word and its opposite
truth / lie ver rev
trust / suspicion falo olaf
respect / contempt keen neek
memory / forgetting kan naka
honour / shame kargo kaffe

A lie is not the absence of truth in this language. It is truth pronounced backwards. Hearing both in one sentence is a joke no translation can carry.

Names

Three parts. A given name describing something physical about you, compounded with a body part, not inherited. A family name, inherited unchanged. And a generation number, counted in eights, going up each time.

Higher numbers command more respect. Recovered examples run into three figures.

A name is said in full almost never. The formal short form fuses the given name into one word and the intimate form clips it again. See Nhath names.

One word with an origin

Bezoo, weapon, is the sound a plasma discharge makes. Every Nhath grows up hearing it, and it sits in the basic vocabulary next to the words for water and food.

[Compiler's note: the contracts call these people raiders with no political organisation. We have set the contracts and the grammar side by side. We are not going to say the rest of it.]

Pre-war language families INFERRED

Before the war, several large human cultures held territory across multiple worlds, each with its own language. Some had done so for a thousand years or more. They fought one another periodically without any of them being destroyed.

They ended between roughly four hundred and one hundred years ago. The cause in each case was the collapse of movement: supply chains stopped, trade stopped, and worlds ceased to be able to reach one another. No multi-world human polity survived the war. What survived were planets, some of which acceded to the Guard and some of which did not.

The languages continued to be spoken locally. They ceased to be spoken between worlds.

Evidence

No literature, speech recordings or grammars are held here. The families are reconstructed from suffixes on proper names, which appear in shipping and licensing registers across worlds that have no relationship to one another.

Kanta

The language of the human homeworld and the oldest human tongue attested here. It marked descent. A name ending in -zin, -zon, -jin or -in denoted the son of a named person.

The ending is still functional in some lines. Ninzin, Jayzin and Iradin are inherited family names. In other cases it has become a given name with no patronymic force. Jimzon is a given name meaning the son of Jim. His father's given name was Korjin, meaning the son of Kor.

Kanta has the widest distribution of the three families named here. Its home planet was destroyed in GC 4394 and it has no remaining first-language speakers.

Myatugo

Marked a holding: ground registered to a named party. The suffix is -ton or -tom.

It appears on Kelton, Weton and Kinton. Kelton and Weton are the two planets of the Polaris system. Kinton is four systems distant with no recorded connection to either. All three are agricultural worlds.

Saolai

The clerical and administrative language, used in law, accounting, scholarship and court ceremonial. The suffix is a final -o, -a or -ia.

It appears on Maldo, Creta, Katanzaria, Kitalia, Saigo, Korno and Riflo. Maldo is the Royal administrative capital. Creta is the principal banking world. Katanzaria maintains a civil registry running eleven centuries. Saigo is the chartered university world.

Other families

At least four further suffix groups are attested and some had wider distribution than the three above. They appear as -ar, -or and -vor; as -eld; as -ow; and on two worlds whose registered names carry a diacritic that Galactic Standard does not use and that roughly half of all filings omit.

These families are not named here. Identification would require material produced in the languages themselves, and no such material has been recovered.

Convergence of two suffixes

Myatugo -ton and Kanta -zon are unrelated in origin and have converged in form. Penston, Armstin and Krostin are consistent with either derivation and cannot be assigned. The homeworld's older name, Waketin, is consistent with both simultaneously.

Irregularities

Penston is a personal name carrying a Myatugo suffix. Astrovin is a commodity carrying a Kanta suffix. Cross-borrowing of this kind is normal between languages in contact and is not treated here as evidence against the reconstruction.

Profanity INTACT

Four words do almost all of the work, they are the same four words on every world in this volume, and they are older than anything else still in general use.

What is actually said

Two of them carry the load. One is a verb doing duty as a verb, a noun, an adjective, an intensifier and a piece of punctuation, and in the recorded material it appears in that last role more often than in all the others together. The second is a noun for waste that has quietly become the word for any situation. After those, a distant third for the underworld and a distant fourth for damnation, both of which survive in mouths that have never held the belief either one came from.

Everything else is regional, weak, and disappearing.

The thing worth noticing

Nobody teaches this. It is not in the centrally produced material, has never been printed in a primer, and no foundation anywhere has ever taught it under contract.

It is also, of everything in Galactic Standard, the part that varies least. A Guardsman off Modanick and a dock hand on a world that has never had a garrison reach for the same word, in the same position in the sentence, at the same provocation.

Nobody transmitted it deliberately. It moved anyway, on ships, in messes, between strangers with nothing else in common, and it arrived intact.

Where it is not allowed

Two of the eleven tower proprietors refuse it outright, which is why there are worlds where a broadcast drama sounds like nobody has ever been annoyed.

A separate class entirely

The words this volume catalogues as Crag and Scarg are not profanity and are not treated as profanity by anybody. They are ordinary vocabulary that happens to do harm. Nobody lowers their voice for either, no proprietor refuses either, and no notice anywhere discourages the second one at all.

Which is the whole distinction. The words people apologise for are the ones that mean nothing.

[Compiler's note: our holdings are eighty per cent commercial and administrative paperwork, in which nobody swears at all. Everything in this entry comes from the four thousand two hundred and six testimonies, where they do, constantly, and where nobody once stopped to explain what they meant.]

Scarg INTACT

Rubbish. Refuse. What you throw out.

An ordinary word, in ordinary use, on every world that speaks Standard. It carries no charge and nobody flinches at it.

Except

In a galaxy where nothing can be built any more, the line between rubbish and stock is a matter of who is looking. A dealer in pre-war components and a man carrying a sack to the tip are handling the same objects and using different words for them.

So the word does quiet work. Something is scarg until somebody who knows better sees it, and then it is not, and then it never was.

There are people who make a living entirely in that gap.

On the source tiers

An editorial note.

An editorial note.

This volume is assembled from paper. Every networked record in the galaxy was lost in the event catalogued here as The Wipe. What remains is what was printed, filed, stamped, carried, or remembered, and what could be read off damaged media by people working without funding in rooms that are frequently cold.

We are not historians. Most of us are volunteers. We hold no authority and issue no findings.

Because the quality of our sources varies enormously, every entry in this volume carries exactly one tier tag. The tag describes how we came to know the thing, not whether the thing is true. A tag is a statement about our evidence and nothing more.

INTACT. A physical record survived and was read directly. Ledgers, manifests, municipal codes, construction specifications, insurance inventories, incorporation papers. These entries are the most reliable in the volume. They are also, as a rule, the least interesting, because the documents that survive are the documents institutions took the trouble to keep in triplicate.

RECOVERED. Pulled from damaged media. Where the source is illegible we mark the gap and do not fill it. A passage reading [...] is a passage we could not read. It is not an abridgement.

TESTIMONY. One person remembered it and told us. We record an initial and a settlement. We do not record full names, because several of our early informants asked us not to and we saw no reason to treat the rest differently.

CONTESTED. Two or more surviving sources disagree, and we have printed them together. We do not adjudicate. Where accounts cannot both be correct we say so and stop. Readers who want a resolution will have to find one elsewhere.

INFERRED. We guessed. We have marked every place we guessed. An inference in this volume is generally an arithmetical one: a population estimated from a housing roll, a casualty figure estimated from a structure.

A note on figures. Readers will observe that this volume can state the mass of a shipment to a fraction of a tonne and cannot state how many people lived on the world it left. We are aware of this. It is a property of the surviving record and not of our method. Commercial and military accounting was filed in duplicate, insured, audited, and stored in fireproof rooms. Census material was not.

Cross-references are printed at the foot of each entry. A cross-reference marked [ENTRY NOT RECOVERED] points to something we know is missing. We have chosen to print these rather than remove them, on the reasoning that a reader is better served by a name and an absence than by neither.

[Compiler's note: this volume is incomplete and will remain so. We are printing it now because several of the people who spoke to us for it have since died.]

The abandoned monastic quarters

Nine districts of Shayron that were closed and sealed, and are still standing.

They emptied slowly, over three centuries, as the faiths that filled them stopped sending anyone. There is no conquest in the story, no plague, no disaster. Enrolment simply falls, year on year, until a house has four people in it, and then one, and then the city writes the closure down.

Two of the nine were shut with a single occupant left inside, in both cases because that occupant asked to stay.

The city still maintains the roofs and the drains, inspects every seven years, and finds them empty every time. They are sealed at street level. They are not sealed underneath, because the oldest sewers in the city run beneath all nine and are still in use.

Three of the libraries were never removed. The transfer papers say the books would be collected when convenient.

The Abyss

The hole in the floor of the Elder Tree.

It sits at the centre of the chamber, perfectly round, with nothing around it. No rail, no rope, no warning. Everybody who has stood in that room mentions how strange it is to see a drop like that left completely open, and how quickly you stop noticing.

Nobody has ever described a bottom. No survey has been permitted and none has been requested twice. The Maspin do not treat the depth as an interesting question.

After an interment, blue vapour comes up out of it, and the tree takes it in.

The Academy memorial walls

Cast brass plates on the approach road to the Academy, running in continuous rows, with every name in applied gold leaf.

Names go up in order of loss, once a year, in the eleventh month. Each one gets a surname, initials, a service number and a year. No rank, no unit, no place, because at the moment they went up nobody thought any of that would matter as much as the name.

There are 2,140,880 of them across forty-one walls.

Every plate is perfectly legible and nobody has ever read them all. Three people from this archive have tried. The furthest anyone got was the eleventh wall.

The accounting division

A very large room full of desks, fluorescent light that hums, and people retyping the past.

Every financial record the Guard had died in GC 4401 along with every other computer in existence. What survived was paper duplicates, in cabinets, scattered across a hundred worlds. So the division has spent decades typing twenty years of accounts back in by hand.

Clerical strength went from 411 to over nine thousand during that programme and never came back down.

Nobody has ever audited the result. There is no body with the standing to do it, and the division audits itself. What the Guard wanted out of twenty years of retyping was the twenty years.

Actom

Where the Guard makes soldiers, and where a hundred and forty thousand people a year find out what they are.

There is nothing else on it. No cities worth the name, no industry, no reason for anybody to be there who was not sent. Just training grounds running to the horizon, ranges, obstacle country, and barracks laid out in rows that go on long enough to be visible from orbit.

Fort Actom is the name everybody actually uses, and it is the first line of every service record in the Guard. Basic at Fort Actom. Say it in a bar and half the table nods.

What it is like

Loud. Everything is loud. And it is where the sorting happens: the ones who came out of the Scout Corps at fourteen, the sixteen-year-olds off poor worlds who signed because it was that or nothing, and the occasional accountant who has never held a rifle and is about to.

The intake register is kept by name, age, parent world and prior status, and it is the most complete civil record of a generation that exists anywhere in the galaxy. It was not built to be one. Nobody was counting people. They were counting throughput.

Ancestor faiths

Talking to your own dead. It is the most common religious practice in the galaxy and almost nobody who does it calls it religion.

It is not one faith. It is a shape that has appeared independently on more worlds than anything else in this volume, and the versions share nothing but the direction they face. A shelf in the corner with something on it. A word at a graveside. A place left at the table. Telling them about your day. On Nancast, small faceless iron figures kept in the house.

What they believe

Asked directly whether the dead can hear them, people answer that they can, that they cannot, and that it is not what the practice is for. All three answers come from people doing the identical thing.

Nothing is written down

No world files a return on what people do in their own kitchens, and no authority has ever had a reason to count it. This is the largest religion in the galaxy and it has no records at all.

Apprenticeship

You work for nothing and you leave with a trade. That is the whole arrangement, and most of the galaxy runs on it.

How it is put to you

Plainly, usually across a bench, by somebody with no time to be delicate about it: I will teach you. I cannot pay you. You will leave here able to do this.

And it is not a trick. Most small businesses genuinely cannot pay a second wage. The offer is honest, everybody involved knows exactly what it is, and most people take it, because the alternative is paying somebody else for the same thing.

You can apprentice to almost anything stable

Carpenter, electrician, mechanic, cook, medic, librarian, even police, where it means ride-alongs and a great deal of paperwork. The only requirement is finding somebody willing to take you.

Which is the catch

Nothing here is decided by a qualification. It is decided by whether a person who does the work is prepared to have you in the room, and that comes down to who your family knows. It is a class system that never had to be written down, because it never had to be enforced.

Most people go through two or three before anything sticks

Which produces the characteristic fact about anybody you meet in this galaxy: everybody has a year of something. A year of engines, a year of stonework, a year of setting bones. Half-finished trades, everywhere, in everyone.

It is also how skill survived the war at all. The machines went and the schools mostly went, and the knowledge came through anyway, hand to hand, because that is the only way it was ever really transmitted.

And it is why the Guard fills its ranks without trying

Every recruiter in the galaxy is walking into rooms full of young people who have been told, honestly and repeatedly, that learning something costs them four years of unpaid work.

The Guard pays you to learn.

Aster

A goddess of the Shayron tradition, who is held to act sideways.

The devotion is personal and domestic rather than congregational, and the phrase everyone uses is close to identical: Aster works in ways you are not meant to understand at the time. It is what people say when something has gone badly and they are not ready to call it meaningless.

Whether she is her own figure or an aspect of Tracine is argued about by the people who observe her, and we are not qualified to settle it. Both accounts are held here.

The asteroid colony docking pad

One landing pad per rock, painted azure, and the only door in or out.

A ship comes once a week. It brings food, water, plant consumables, school materials and mail, and it takes away certified Corefuel. That is the whole rhythm of life out there: six days of nothing and one day when the world briefly connects to the rest of the galaxy.

Twice a standard year the orbit puts the fragments somewhere the radio cannot reach for several days. The safety schedule's advice for that period is to work to the published timetable, which is another way of saying wait.

Reader's key

Seen in the manuscript at Ch. 1.

Astonia

The sun does not rise here and does not set. It sits low on the rim of the sky and stays there, and the sky holds pink and yellow at every hour, over sand the colour of brass.

The dry ocean

There was a sea here for most of the world's history. Terraforming and drift took it away across about four hundred years, and the reefs it left are still standing. They stand where shrubs would stand on any other world: eight metres of coral in the open air, dry, pink and orange and a blue that carries after dark.

They do not grow. They do not rot either. There is enough water in the sand to hold them exactly as they are.

The people keep them alive. Households keep a spray bottle by the door and mist the formation nearest them, daily, everywhere in the settled belt. No ordinance requires it. We asked four informants why and got four answers, none of which was the same as another.

Diamond

The mountains are diamondiferous to a depth nobody has bothered to measure, which makes the stone here an industrial material and not a precious one. It goes out by the shipload for cutting tools. Children are given the flawed ones.

The night

The day is too hot to work in, so nothing happens in it. Trade, worship, school and every kind of public life happen after dark, under signage that runs pink and green above streets already lit like a long evening. This is a choice their grandparents made and not a fact of their bodies, and they will tell you so.

The bodies

Two Guard medical surveys, both dated GC 4416, record what everyone here already knew: Astonians are stronger than the human mean and harder to make ill. The first credits the milk, which comes from herds that graze on a forage that grows nowhere else. The second credits a lifetime spent breathing over the reefs, and lists eleven diseases the rest of the galaxy has no vaccine for and Astonians largely shrug off.

Both surveys recommend further study. No further study was undertaken.

The annexation instrument is dated GC 4419.

Schooling

After the annexation, the schools were handed to sponsored religious foundations on contract. The contracts survive and are specific: residential attendance, and instruction in Galactic Standard. Within eleven years they had 94 per cent of the children.

Levy

Astonians do not enlist. They are levied, under a clause of the same instrument. Yield for GC 4461: 41,208 persons. Royalty paid to the Royal houses that year on the same clause: 2,472,480 credits.

The Astonian Annexation

Transfer of Astonia from Royal protectorate to Guard territory, GC 4419. Effected by instrument, with a preceding action.

Stated grounds

Cartel control of the territorial administration, and a public health emergency. The emergency is documented: a wave of fatal overdoses across the principal cities over fourteen months, with a filed figure of 4,118 deaths, and one death of a prominent person which is the subject of most of the surviving ministerial material.

Sequence, as filed

Contested territorial election, GC 4417, with allegations of interference lodged by two parties. Formal warnings to the territorial administration, GC 4418, three in number, held here in full. Orbital interdiction and search and seizure operations, GC 4419. Instrument of annexation, same year.

Effect on cartel revenue

Filed and substantial. Prosecutions in the following three years: 2,411. Assets seized: 880,400,000 credits. The Restoration has verified the reduction in trade against the shipping returns and finds it real.

The Royal position

Astonia was a Royal protectorate. The houses did not contest the annexation. The instrument executed alongside it provides for a continuing royalty to the Royal houses on conscription yield, mineral rights and dairy export, in perpetuity, subject to accounting by the Guard.

The accounting is performed by the Guard. The Royal treasury receives the figure and the payment. It does not receive the underlying returns and has not, on the record, requested them.

Preceding documents

Two Guard medical surveys of the Astonian population are dated GC 4416, being three years before the annexation and one year before the contested election. They are catalogued under Astonians.

Astonian coral

Reef, standing in open air, where a hedge should be.

Astonia had an ocean and does not any more, and the coral simply stayed where it was. It stands across the whole equatorial belt, eight metres in places, dry, in pinks and oranges and a blue that keeps glowing after dark.

It does not grow. It does not rot either. There is exactly enough water in the sand to hold it where it is, indefinitely.

The colours are wrong on purpose

They look garish to human eyes and they were never meant for human eyes. The fish that lived here saw further up the spectrum than we do, and in that light, what looks lurid to a visitor was camouflage.

People keep it alive

There is a spray bottle by the door in most houses in the settled belt, and misting the nearest formation is a daily thing that everybody does. No law requires it. Ask why and you get a different answer from everyone.

And it protects them

A lifetime spent breathing over these reefs is what Guard medicine credits for Astonian resistance to eleven diseases the rest of the galaxy has no answer for.

The Astonian dialect

[NO LIVING SPEAKERS RECORDED]

The way Astonia used to talk. One person wrote it down, and then it was gone.

The survey

4,100 words, a sketch of the sounds, and eleven pages of stories taken down from speakers. Done by a single investigator using a transcription system of their own invention which they never explained. No recording exists. The investigator's name appears on nothing else, anywhere.

How it ended

After the annexation, the schools went to sponsored religious foundations on contract. Residential attendance, and teaching in Galactic Standard. Inside eleven years they had ninety-four per cent of the children.

One generation. That is all it takes.

Our own survey of the world in GC 4457 found no speaker.

Two attempts to bring it back, both by Astonian associations, both working from the same notes because there is nothing else, both suspended.

[Compiler's note: the conscription yield for this world is filed every year, to the person. It is three entries away.]

Astonian milk

Dairy from herds that graze on a forage growing nowhere else in the galaxy, and the reason Astonians are built the way they are.

Guard medical survey credits something in this milk for bone density and muscle mass well above the human mean. Take the same animals somewhere else and the effect disappears, because it is the grass, not the cows.

Three worlds have tried to grow that forage off Astonia. All three failed.

Four hundred thousand tonnes of solids go out a year, and the Royal houses take a royalty on every tonne of it under an instrument they signed decades ago.

Astonians

The people of a world with no sunrise, and the reason the Guard wanted it.

They are stronger than the human mean and they are harder to make ill, and both of those were measured and written down three years before anybody annexed anything.

Strength

Bone density and muscle mass well above the range. Guard survey credits the milk, which comes from herds grazing a forage that grows nowhere else. It is not training and it is not selection. They are simply built that way, and they were built that way before the Guard arrived.

Immunity

A lifetime breathing over the dry reefs leaves them shrugging off eleven diseases nobody has a vaccine for.

Both surveys recommended further study. Neither study happened. The annexation happened.

Since

Astonians do not enlist, they are levied, under a clause of the instrument. Forty-one thousand a year. Their failure rate at basic training is a third of the member-world average, which surprises nobody who has read the first half of this entry.

Astrovin

Fortified wine, made in quantity before the war on four worlds. Two of them stopped. One of them no longer exists.

So every bottle of pre-war Astrovin is a bottle that will not be replaced, and the price climbs every year. Collectors bid on them by house and by year.

It is also, and this is the thing about it, a bottle an ordinary family might have in a cupboard. Most of what cannot be made any more is a rifle or a drive assembly or a suit of armour. This is the one irreplaceable object that turns up in a kitchen, kept back for something worth opening it for.

Atmospheric masks

The most common object in the galaxy, because most people are breathing somewhere they did not evolve to breathe.

At the cheap end it is a moulded cup over the mouth and nose with a filter cartridge and a strap, sold everywhere, replaced constantly, and thrown away when the cartridge browns. At the other end it is a machined respirator built into a suit and worn for a working lifetime.

What it tells you about a person

Everything. A mask says which world's air a body was built for, and therefore where that body is standing now and why. A crew stepping off a ramp will hold up a small reader, watch it flash from red to green, and pull their masks off with the relief of people who have just been told they get to be comfortable.

Some species wear them permanently offworld and have done for so long that their faces are essentially a matter of hearsay. A Gashi bounty hunter in a good suit is a pair of gold-black eyes above a piece of engineering, and there are people who have known him for years and could not tell you what is under it.

The etiquette

You do not ask. Not what is under it, not what the air was like at home, and not why he has never taken it off.

The Autumnals

[ENTRY NOT RECOVERED]

One side of the war that ended the old world, and we cannot tell you a single thing they believed.

Everyone knows the name. It is spoken on every world we have visited, mostly as an accusation, by people who were not born when the fighting stopped. Say it in a bar on the rim and somebody will tell you they started it and we are the ones cleaning up the mess.

Nothing they wrote survives

No charter, no proclamation, no orders, no requisitions, no letters, no ledgers. Not one page produced by that party is held anywhere we have been able to reach. We have appealed publicly three times and received nothing.

What physically exists, in full

One hull section, unpowered, in a salvage yard. One banner in a museum on Sansvor, catalogued as captured colours, with no provenance attached. One uniform tunic in a private collection on Maldo. Two sleeves, no insignia, no maker's mark.

All three are dark, in shades between orange and brown. Nobody can tell us whether that was their colour or whether that is what sixty years does to cloth.

A name

They chose it themselves, which is unusual. The other side used an acronym. A civilisation that names itself after the end of a season has already decided something about where it thinks it is.

Baline

A cold moon that grows nothing, and the place where the food of ten worlds stops being food.

Orbital rings of storage and mile after mile of refrigerated warehousing on the surface. Four hundred and eleven million tonnes under cold at any given moment, held between the harvest that produced it and the sale that will move it.

What that actually means

Everything grown in the Polaris system passes through here, and while it sits in the dark on Baline it is not a crop any more. It is a position. It is held, valued, borrowed against and traded, sometimes several times, without a single sack of it moving.

Nobody is from here

The population is measured in postings rather than families, everybody's residence is tied to their contract, and the registrar has never recorded a third-generation resident. People come, work a rotation in the cold, and go.

Barris

A Trailblazer in logistics, and the man at the festival table who does the introducing.

The work

Soil readings, elevation scans, rainfall patterns. Making sure nobody puts a port down on swamp or on stone. It is the least glamorous job on a concession and the whole thing rests on it.

At a table

He offers his name unprompted, tells you what he does without being asked twice, and then goes round the table naming everybody else and what they are for. He is the one who makes a stranger into a guest, which is a skill, and which nobody has ever thanked him for.

He is also the one who calls for the Yinmelon story, and he has heard it before.

The Battle of Rudcuff

One of the Guard's first, fought by the only two battalions it had, and the day it learned what it had signed up for.

The set-up

A colony held by Targaths. First and Second Battalion, which at that point was the entire army, every one of them a volunteer. The objective was to take the ground. Nobody expected much difficulty.

What actually happened

The Targaths had built a magnetic web through the crust and were waiting. It came on as the fleet made its approach.

The ships in the outer ring went first, dragged out of the sky and into the surface. On the ground the men could not move: armour, weapons, everything pulled flat, pinned in the open with the sky coming down around them. Whether they fought back is genuinely not known.

The reinforcements found nothing

Not a defeat, not a rout, not a line that had broken and run. There was simply nobody left to have any of those things happen to.

Why it is still spoken about

Because it was survivable for exactly one reason: the second wave was late. And a man who came in with that second wave has spent thirty years carrying both halves of that, the guilt and the gratitude, and now sits in a chair with an old map on the wall behind him.

He calls them real heroes. He also, without noticing he is doing it, gets nostalgic about it, in the specific way of a man remembering the last time his job was simple.

Berji Kegeron

also: Kegan · Berj

The tallest man on Castle Team by a clear head, and the least interested in acting like it.

Blond hair, tightly curled, cut short. Green eyes at the far end of the range, the sort people comment on and he waves off. Broad through the shoulders and imposing out of armour right up until he moves, which he does with a loose, excited, faintly lanky energy that undoes the whole effect. Green visor.

Lieutenant. Monver

Forested, mountainous, locally governed, extremely proud of itself, and deeply relaxed about what people do on their own time. He fought a war on his own ground with the Planetary Defence Force before he was ever Guard, on the side that won and then merged in.

What he actually is

A cook, a beach person, and a light and tasteful druggie. He does not believe in hierarchies and is not especially interested in ethics either. What moves him is his people: his friends, his family, and keeping them safe. He will do things he would rather not discuss to that end and will not pretend the cause had anything to do with it.

He is engaged. She is a botanist with the Guard's scientific service, and what they have in common is growing things, cooking them, and smoking the ones that are for smoking.

He talks in stories rather than principles, and he is the one who says the thing that lands. You can't hate yourself into being better. And the old Monveri line about a ship in harbour being safe and belonging somewhere else entirely.

His enlistment runs out shortly and he has not filed anything about extending it.

Beryllium rifles

A kinetic weapon that fires a poisoned round, banned across the Royal systems and on Maspin, restricted almost everywhere else.

The metal is toxic. Survive a hit and you carry a cancer risk for the rest of your life, which is what the bans cite and what everyone means when they talk about them.

"You don't just wanna put holes in people. You wanna give them cancer too?"

Why they exist at all

Unlike almost every other weapon in this volume, these can still be made. It is chemistry rather than industry, and a competent chemist with access to the base metal can produce them, which is exactly how they turn up on worlds that have outlawed them.

Crates move under other names. Seizure returns most often find them declared as battery stock, mineral samples, or agricultural chemical.

Biodium

A combustible fuel extracted on Pashmirské. It is not Corefuel and is not comparable to it.

Origin

It is the residue of a rainforest that covered a large part of the world and dried out a very long time before anybody arrived on it. The deposit is finite, is not being added to, and was laid down by an ecosystem that no living record describes.

What it is for

Domestic and light industrial use. Heating, cooking, generators, small plant. It does not fly anything and no vessel of any class runs on it.

What it is worth

Enough. Pashmirské is not a wealthy world and is not a poor one, and the difference is this deposit. It is the reason the administration can pay for what it provides, and the reason the world has not needed to ask anybody for anything since the war ended.

The Blind Day

Blindfolded, cuffed together, and turned loose for a full day in front of everybody they have ever known.

The rite

The couple is bound at the wrist and blinded, and must live an entire ordinary day like that. Eat. Move. Get from one place to another. Every single thing requires the other person, and neither can see what the other is doing.

Two things are being said at once, and the rite does not bother to separate them: your fate is chained to theirs now, and you will have to trust this person when you have nothing left to go on.

The families set the tasks, and the tasks are meant to be funny rather than cruel. This is the community's one licensed opportunity to make the couple look ridiculous, and it is taken up enthusiastically. Cook a meal for both families, neither of you able to see the fire. Cross running water on stones. Carry something fragile across town. Find an object a sibling has hidden, and the sibling is permitted to lie exactly once.

The last task is dressing each other

Ceremonial clothes are laid out, and each dresses the other blind.

They walk into the ceremony wearing whatever they have made of one another, and nobody straightens a thing. The crooked collar is the point. Every wedding portrait on that world has one.

Then the blindfolds come off

That is the first time they see each other married, and it is where the ceremony begins. The whole day was the prelude.

Peeking is not an annulment

It is worse. It is remembered.

The breaching kit

Everything a four-man team needs to get through a door that does not want them.

The charge

A small roll of wool-like fabric. Peel the velcro edges and the underside is a grey, sticky clay. Press the clay over a grenade set to its highest dial, slap the whole assembly against the surface, and pull the six-inch antenna out of the centre of the cloth. When the light on the antenna goes from amber to green, it is armed, and you should not be where you currently are.

Four of them, placed on a rooftop and fired together, will open a building.

The grappling pistol

Slim, light, and it fires a molten orange line rather than a hook on a rope. The claws catch a ledge and melt fractionally into it, welding themselves in place. You tug once to test it. It has never been the tug that killed anybody.

Flashbangs and frags share a body and differ by a dial. The dial is why teams have rules about who carries what, and why one man's mistake with that dial, on a cartel compound, put Corporal Billem's leg out from under him and is still being brought up.

Smoke comes in dented cylinders that smell of phosphorus and are worth more than the rifle when things have gone properly wrong.

A pilot with Nova Squadron, and the squadron's worst comedian. He tells jokes constantly. Roughly one in three lands, which he takes as encouragement.

Squadron nights are a real fixture on a mothership, and somebody has to put a name down for the stage. He put his down for a song called Dark Holiday, and put Kelsa's next to it.

The Burial Moon

Grass to the horizon, a few footpaths, and small chapels at intervals. Nobody lives here except the people who cut the grass.

What it costs

In a galaxy of small crowded worlds, this is an entire moon given to the dead. That is the whole point and it is not sentimental: the annual maintenance appropriation is 8,204,600 credits and it has been granted in full every year since the establishment.

The numbers

Interred to date: 2,140,880. Surveyed and unallocated: 9,411,000.

How you get here

You wrote it down when you signed. Every person entering Guard service records their rites at enrolment: cremation or interment, faith or none, next of kin. A standard plot costs nothing. A custom monument, a custom plot, or more than two family members attending are chargeable, and the schedule of charges is filed.

Which means that somewhere there is a form where an eighteen-year-old ticked a box about their own body, and the Guard has kept it, and will honour it.

When it does not work

The establishment is built for individual services. There is one paragraph permitting a combined service at the caretakers' discretion when the numbers exceed what the moon can hold.

It has been used. The return for its use records attendance as a figure and the number of people commemorated as a range.

The Burial Moon chapels

Two hundred and fourteen small stone buildings scattered across a moon of grass, about four kilometres apart, so that wherever a plot is there is one within walking distance.

Each holds forty people. Each is unheated, and belongs to no faith at all: a rail, a table, a cupboard, and nothing else on the walls. That is deliberate. Any rite a person wrote on their enrolment form at seventeen can be performed in one of these rooms without moving a single thing.

Services are booked through the caretakers. The average attendance is six.

C.O.R.D.

Compact of Realms in Defense · vernacular: the Cord

Defensive bloc formed by established institutional powers in response to the spread of the Autumnal movement. Belligerent party to the Great War. Dissolved by the destruction of its constituent members.

Formation

2 gaps

The founding instrument survives in two partial copies, both fire-damaged. The recoverable text opens: "The undersigned realms, being severally threatened in their [...] and having no confidence in the sufficiency of separate defence [...]" The list of signatories is legible in nineteen places and illegible in what appears to be a further thirty to forty.

Structure

A compact of sovereign parties, not a state. Contributions were assessed against each member's own accounting and collected by the member itself. There is no recovered evidence of a unified command. There is a considerable quantity of recovered correspondence about establishing one.

The Wipe

1 gap

Attributed to C.O.R.D. by the Guard and by general account. The stated reasoning, which appears in Guard educational material and in no C.O.R.D. document we hold, is that the object was to cripple Autumnal coordination. No order authorising the event has been recovered. [NO SURVIVING PRIMARY SOURCE]

The Restoration observes that the name is an acronym, that the Autumnals named themselves, and that this difference is remarked upon by informants across a dozen unconnected worlds without prompting.

Calsco Fritt

also: Cal

Seven feet of Katanzarian in a fur hide, with cross-draw revolvers, tribal tattoos, and a laugh you can hear from the other end of a settlement.

He runs the Trailblazer concession on Maspin: the port, the medbay, the flooms, the deal with the local council. He is very good at it, and he is good at it because he is a superb reader of people who has had a lot of practice.

He negotiates with a floom tucked under one arm, stroking it absently while he talks, and the effect on the other side of the table is exactly what he intends it to be. Gold holowatch. Greyleaf, constantly.

He is theatrical, manipulative, warm, and genuinely funny, usually all four inside one sentence. He lectures on politics entirely in metaphor, and when somebody asks him to drop the metaphors he is wounded about it and does it anyway, badly.

He also butchers people's names on purpose, and waits to see whether they will correct him.

Why he is out here

He was a chieftain on Katanzaria and he is not one now. Three versions of how that happened circulate on his own world. One says he failed a ritual obligation. One says he lost a duel. The third says he was simply out-manoeuvred in the electoral half of the succession, which is lawful, carries no dishonour, and is the only one of the three that would leave no mark on a world that writes everything down.

He would rather people believed either of the first two. Those happen in an arena.

Home

He is married, to a woman he describes as fierce and brilliant and beautiful, and he cannot go back to her without either a title or something heroic to his name. He is working on it.

The Capital District

The ceremonial heart of Shayron: the Castle, the processional way, three great squares, and the old mosaic quarters that are still lived in.

No industry is allowed inside the boundary and none has ever been. There is no exhaust here and no engine noise. The streets are hand-laid stone kept under permanent contract, the planting is jasmine and citrus by schedule, and the light comes in low and gold most of the day.

Almost nobody who works here lives here. The resident population is small and works in food, hospitality, restoration or the household. On an observance day the district holds two hundred thousand people, and the day after, it goes back to being very quiet.

Captain Medarco

An officer they served under years ago who was a bastard the entire time, and the only reason this archive knows his name is that one of them still does the impression.

What survives

Not a service record, not a posting history, not a photograph. A posture: shoulders back, chin up, and a voice pitched into the flat bark of a man reading out an announcement he did not write.

"Attention. Captain Medarco speaking. As you know, there has been way too much fun in our division. New rules, straight from the top. Any enjoyment is strictly prohibited on this mothership. Under no circumstances are we to engage in any, and I mean any, shenanigan behaviour."

It is performed standing on a table, drunk, with a crumpled napkin held under the nose as a moustache, and it goes on considerably longer than that.

The charge sheet, as delivered

The emergency exit signs swapped for arrows pointing at the laundry chute, and a cadet who went down three decks before anybody found him in the socks. Drop and give me forty. And no more throwing microwaves out of windows when you lose at cards, the last one having still been plugged in.

Every item on that list is something the men in the room did, which is why the bit works and why it has survived a decade of telling.

The thing about him

Nobody performing this is being cruel about a man they hated. They are quoting a man who made a stretch of their lives worse and is now a bit they can do at a table, which is the only revenge available against an officer and is more than most of them get.

And why it lands in a room he has never entered

Because everybody there has met him. Not him specifically. The other one, on their first posting, under a different name.

Cargo cults

The faiths that grew where the ships stopped coming.

Why they are worse here

The historical version of this happens to people who saw wealth arrive and then leave. What happened in GC 4401 was different in scale: populations that had instant medicine, interstellar travel and constant communication lost all three inside a day, and a good number of them lost every outside contact permanently.

They are not imagining a golden age. They remember it. Some of them are old enough to have used it.

What they do

Keep the landing grounds clear, and nothing lands. Maintain dead machines with real care. Hold observances at the feet of relay towers that no longer speak. Set goods aside against a return. Treat any surviving pre-war object as sacred rather than merely valuable, which is a distinction that stops mattering after two generations.

The characteristic object is a piece of pre-war manufacture, non-functional, whose purpose nobody alive knows, around which an entire account has grown up.

One thing we will say plainly

This archive has received two credible reports of communities holding ordnance in this way. We reported both. We were not told what happened next.

The cartels

Not one organisation. Between nineteen and thirty of any size, depending on what you count, operating wherever the Guard's reach runs out.

Substances, weapons, transit, protection, labour supply, licensing fraud. The usual list, at scale.

How they took Astonia, which is the case everyone knows because it ended in an annexation and the papers came out. They came in through the nightlife, then the property, then the lending, and then they bought the municipal offices and eventually the territorial government.

Not one shot was fired at any stage. It was all transactions, which is why there is a paper trail.

And they behaved themselves at home. Astonia under the cartels was orderly, because Astonia was where the money came from. What the same organisations did elsewhere was not orderly at all.

The contested part

Guard material presents the cartels as an outside threat to the member worlds. The prosecution returns show that most of the substances, weapons and transit involved were Guard-made or Guard-licensed at some earlier point, and had left Guard hands somewhere along the way.

The returns do not record how.

Cillus Vot Shayron-Skoln

A prince of the blood who wanted to be a war correspondent, and got what he asked for.

Ginger, a deep earthy orange rather than a bright one, shaved close at the sides with just enough length on top to curl. Clear skin. Tall and toned without being strong, and not thin either. His eyes read as big without actually being big, and that is the whole problem with his face: it announces, from across a landing pad, that nothing has ever happened to him.

Softly spoken. Endearing before he has said anything worth being endeared by.

He grew up behind castle walls on Shayron with everything arranged for him, and left specifically to find out what the galaxy actually looks like. What he found was worse than he had pictured.

How a Royal ends up with a Guard squad

The Royal forces and the Guard are close. They train together, exercise together, and lend each other people, in the way two friendly militaries always have. A Royal journalist embedded with Guard formations is unusual but not strange, and he volunteered for it expecting routine work: a few weeks with a line unit, some morale footage, a report home about ordinary business.

He shoots footage of squads for exactly that purpose, and at one point he shoots Squad 412 celebrating with looted goods.

What he wears

A religious pendant, given rather than bought, and he does not take it off.

Civilian dress

Nobody here dresses like the end of the world. Everybody is a little poor, so everybody buys things that last.

The standard set, which you will see on any street on any member world:

Trousers, hard-wearing, cut much the same everywhere and stitched differently on every planet, which is how people tell at a glance where a stranger got dressed. An undershirt. A shirt over that. And a coat, thin or thick depending on the sky. Boots, good soles, and the design of the sole is a local matter people have opinions about.

The pockets, and why

Every coat has a lot of them. Chest, shoulder, a slot for a pen, the arrangement a soldier would recognise. Not a comic number. A tasteful number, and always more than you would design for one person.

Nobody chose this as a style. It is what happens when a garment has to be made in one run and sold to a farmer, a clerk and a mechanic at the same time. You cannot tool up for three coats, so you make one coat that does not fail any of them, and a coat that does not fail any of them has pockets.

Which means the most ordinary object in the galaxy quietly contains the entire manufacturing situation, and nobody wearing one has ever thought about it.

The shirt is where the person is

It is the only garment anybody chooses, and the reason is that it is the cheapest thing they own.

A moonball club. A university. A town, a district, a whole planet. A religious mark. A geometric pattern. A print loud enough that somebody's mother has commented on it. A piece of art somebody liked enough to wear.

Club badges turn up thousands of light years from the club, which is the one solid piece of evidence that at least some leagues are followed across worlds by people who will never attend a match.

Worn technology, because there is not enough of it

Devices are scarce and expensive, so they are carried on the body rather than left anywhere: readers, lamps, meters, translators, whatever somebody has scrapped together or found second hand. None of it matches. A person's kit is a record of what they could get.

Bags

Satchels and packs, nearly universally. People are moving, and people who are moving carry everything they own on the strap.

Off duty, a soldier dresses like where he is from and not like the Guard, which is why a bar full of them looks like a bar full of eleven different worlds and not like a unit.

And then some worlds ignore all of it

Great volumes of fabric, pastels, garments in variety and colour that would be absurd anywhere else and are simply Tuesday there.

[Compiler's note: what is described above is a statement about what gets manufactured, not about anybody. Average the galaxy's people and you get a person who does not exist. We have printed the coat because the coat is real. The person wearing it is their own business.]

The Coal Run

A heated span with water on both sides, and the couple starts at opposite ends.

The rite

They run toward each other. The marriage exists the instant their lips meet in the middle. No words. Nobody officiates. Either it happened or it did not, and every person present saw the exact moment.

Opposite ends is the entire design

Either one of them can stop. If one stops, the other is left standing alone on the far side, in front of everybody, and there is no version of that which can be smoothed over afterward. Both have to keep going. That is the vow, and it is made with the legs.

The surface is something genuinely unpleasant and genuinely survivable, and it varies with what the world has: superheated grating over an exhaust manifold, plasma venting on a timed cycle so that the run has a window, or a cooling Corefuel channel, which is to say they run across the thing the galaxy is powered by.

The falling

Usually one of them goes in the water. This is the part that makes the culture.

The other jumps in after them. Voluntarily, immediately, and without being asked. And then everybody else wades in and carries the pair of them across.

Nobody is embarrassed. Nobody has failed. It is fun, it is half the reason people turn up, and the lesson gets stated by the crowd instead of by a priest: you were never going to finish this on your own, and nobody expected you to.

A wedding where nobody fell in is considered a slightly boring wedding
