The Collective

the faith has no name of its own. This heading is ours

When you die your soul joins every other soul, and that accumulation is God.

Not a god who was there first and made everything. God is what the dead have built, is still being built, and you are going to be part of it.

Which makes being good urgent

If people are cruel, God becomes cruel, and then everyone who dies afterwards goes into a cruel God. Adherents do not talk about this in terms of sin or reward. They talk about it the way an engineer talks about a structure that everybody is adding to whether they mean to or not.

Praying means addressing the entire dead history of your own kind. Not asking. Contributing.

Where you find it

Scattered, unorganised, out on the cold moons, and among raider populations that will not accept contact of any other kind. Missionaries carried it from Sonaff. Versions of it turn up on inner worlds and we are not certain they are the same faith.

A distinction

The Maspin returning to the ocean under their crust is not this. They are describing something they consider a physical fact, not an afterlife.

The colony recovery detail

The Guard element that walked the Corefuel colony after the raid, and the two men in it who matter.

The soldier who lifted the floorboard

He did it because it was the next board. He was not searching for anybody. That is the whole thing: a routine sweep of a burned house, done properly, by somebody who had no reason to expect anything under there.

The officer

He read the station chief off a scan, marked him killed in action, and closed the family out on an assumption spoken flatly enough that it was clearly not the first time he had said it.

"There's probably not even a body left after those ion bombs."

He was wrong about one of them.

Comet caps

A mushroom, and the reason a Guardsman keeps one eye on the calendar.

They come up in a small handful of places and travel badly, so what circulates is mostly dried. Taken properly they do what this class of thing does everywhere: the walls get interesting, the hours stop behaving, and somebody in the room announces they have worked out what everything means.

They are the running joke and the running risk on any deployment. Drug tests come round roughly every six months, which sounds generous until you realise everybody knows the date and nobody remembers it.

Legality is a local matter and a live one. Sixty-one separate drug-licensing polls have gone to the Guard franchise in the last twenty years, which means somewhere out there, a great many people have very strong feelings about a mushroom.

Corefuel

A quarter of a litre of it will run twenty haulers for a hundred years. It is refined out of the core of a dead planet, and there is one planet you are allowed to take it from.

Yield

One standard measure, taken as 0.25 litres, is rated by the licensing authority at a commercial hauler fleet of twenty vehicles for approximately one hundred standard years.

Reserves

The Wake fragments are assessed at about five thousand years at current rates. It is not scarce. Nothing about this trade is driven by scarcity.

The licence

Extraction, synthesis, transport and resale are licensed by the Guard Board of Directors and by nobody else. Duty is charged at the point it comes out of the ground and again at the point it is sold.

For GC 4461: 812,443.6 tonnes extracted, 40,622,180 credits in duty, and 3,249,774,400 credits at final market.

Everywhere else

Every world has a core. Getting at one anywhere else means deep drilling, fracturing, or a lucky asteroid, and then it still has to be synthesised. Since GC 4420 there have been eleven applications for a non-Wake licence. All eleven were withdrawn by the applicant.

The process

1 gap

Registered GC 4417 to a single named patentee, K. Avaris, and assigned afterwards to the Board for a consideration of one credit. The registration sets the process out in seven steps. Six of them are redacted in the copy we hold. [RECORD DAMAGED]

What the Maspin say

That planetary cores are alive. That the thing in the tanks is not a mineral. They do not say it as belief, and mystics on four other worlds say something close enough that we have filed them together, under religious testimony, which is where claims go when nothing corroborates them.

[Compiler's note: the market figure above is filed to the credit. The number of people employed in the extraction zone is not filed at all.]

Corporal Billem

The man who was in charge, and the reason somebody else ended up in charge.

What happened to him

He was breaching a door on a cartel compound when one of his own people put a fragmentation grenade through a house that should have taken a flashbang. Every gas tank in the building went up. A second later the rounds came through the door he was standing in, and took his leg out from under him.

He killed the man who shot him before he sat down, and reported it in one word that does not appear anywhere else in this archive.

"I frosted the fucking Crag that shot me, so it's clear here."

How he took it

Mask off, back against a wall, one hand pressed hard into his own thigh, and furious. Not at the wound. At the man who caused it, who was standing four feet away and is described in the record only as Private Dumbass.

"Look I'll be fine, but I just cannot keep up with you."

That sentence is the whole of him. He is bleeding, he is not getting up, and the part he chooses to say out loud is an apology for slowing the assault down.

What it cost, and what it did

Six or seven hostiles were still holed up in the compound. He could not go. So a staff sergeant took three men forward and finished it, and the returns for that action read zero Guard fatalities, the principal captured alive, the compound intact, followed by the phrase that gets him into this volume at all: all without a corporal.

He stayed on the net the entire time, running the evacuation from the floor.

"Copy that. EVAC is about an hour out. Regroup at entry."

Afterwards

The ankle is described by a friend as being in about a million pieces, and the same friend reckons he is quietly relieved: he had been going out every other week for a long time, and a stretch in a hospital bed is the first uninterrupted rest anybody has been able to give him.

[Compiler's note: the grenade is attributed in one place to a private on his own team and in another to a named man on the team that came to help him. Both accounts are held here. Somebody, on the day, decided to cover for somebody.]

The Council Chamber of Riflo

Stone floor, woven banners, and bioluminescent vines kept trained along the upper walls, so the whole room has a faint blue underlight before anyone lights anything.

A ceremonial bowl sits in the centre. When it is lit at the opening of a session, every seated councillor's flame answers it, each one a different colour, and the room reads at a glance as a set of individuals rather than a body.

The floor hums

Everyone who has stood in that chamber says so, and none of them says it as a figure of speech. The stone carries the mood of the room. Anger, amusement, doubt, all of it comes up through your feet before anybody speaks.

Records are taken by hand with feathered quills. Gavels are used. A vote is not counted; the flames change colour, and unanimity is all of them going white at once.

The Council of Riflo

Governing council of the settled belt, Maspin. Composition is by seat rather than by election, and the Restoration has not established how a seat is filled.

Address

Councillors are addressed as the Council and by nothing else. They do not give their names to outsiders and they do not appear to use them with each other in session. This is a rule of the body, not a courtesy, and no visitor has ever been given the reason for it.

Seats

Nobody outside Maspin knows how many there are or how you get one. Seats are not elected in any sense a visitor would recognise, are not obviously inherited, and are not explained. What is known is that one of them belongs to the Trailblazers, has since GC 4451, and is held by a human, which suggests the body can add a seat when it decides to.

This is a remote world that has had very few long-term visitors and no interest in being surveyed. Almost everything in this entry comes from people who were guests.

Proceedings

Catalogued under the Council Chamber. Decision is expressed through the councillors' flames. Unanimity is described as their merging to a single white.

Competences, as reported

Taxation and remittance to the Royal treasury. Land and concession. Labour, including the administration of indenture. Rites and observance. Relief.

Relief

The Council's own submissions to the Royal treasury are held here in copy and record fourteen applications for assistance over nineteen years following eruption, quake, flood and crop loss. No reply to any of them is held by this archive, and the Council states that none was received.

Indenture

Administered by the Council. The Restoration notes, from the Council's own registers, that indentured persons are in a number of recorded cases assigned to establishments controlled by the family of a sitting councillor. The registers record this openly, there being no provision under which it would need to be concealed.

Crag

The slur. It means non-human, all of them, any of them.

It is not a word for a species. It is a word for a category, and it gets used identically on peoples who have nothing whatsoever to do with each other. A Nhath and a Vitula and a Targath share no biology, no history and no language, and one syllable covers all three.

Where it came from

Nobody knows. There is no first use, no derivation, and nobody who can tell you. It shows up in the recovered material already in general circulation, with no gloss, as though it never needed one.

The exemption

People who use it will very often exempt somebody. This one is different. This one is all right. It is offered as a compliment and taken as one, and it does not reduce how often the word gets used. It is what lets everyone go on using it.

Where it sits

It is not in Galactic Standard law. Nothing prohibits it. Guard notices discourage it in the messes, which are the only official documents anywhere that admit the word exists, and they are notices about language rather than about people.

Non-humans are about a fifth of everyone alive. They are 0.8 per cent of the Guard.

Very little of that gap was decided by anybody. Terraforming was financed to make worlds habitable for humans, and it worked, so the settled galaxy is an environment humans can stand in and a great many other peoples cannot. Those peoples serve offworld in masks, or on medication, or under a specification of some kind, and a soldier who requires equipment nobody else requires is a soldier a unit has to plan around.

The rest follows from arithmetic. Four fifths of the establishment is one species, so the training, the rations, the medicine, the armour and the sizing of every piece of it are built once and built for that species. Nothing in the schedules bars anybody. The schedules simply do not fit them, and there has never been a year in which fixing that was the cheapest thing available to do.

Which leaves an organisation that is 99.2 per cent human without a single instrument anywhere requiring it to be.

Crescent City

Capital of Pashmirské, on the long peninsula that closes the northern ocean.

The peninsula is the reason the city is where it is and the reason it was fought over for as long as it was. It is approachable along one axis and is bounded by water on the rest, which made it defensible by whoever held it and expensive for whoever did not.

It changed hands during the war. How often is not agreed. The lowest figure given by any informant is four and the highest is eleven.

Condition

The city was never destroyed and was never repaired. What stands is a century and a half of small-arms and light ordnance damage across a fabric that was substantially complete before the fighting started, patched where a building was in use and left where it was not.

Now

It is the seat of the administration and holds the cabinet, the ministries and the residence. It is not a large city by the standards of this volume and it is the only one on the world with a population that has grown in each of the last returns.

Creta

Green mountains, lakes you can see the bottom of, and spring that does not end. Four continents, four governments, and more money than any of them will discuss.

Four countries, one policy

The continents govern themselves and have agreed on foreign policy by permanent convention, renewed without amendment forty-one times. What they argue about instead, in the record and in public, is fishing quota, water rights, and the correct preparation of two dishes.

Neutral, and armed about it

Creta was not invaded, not blockaded and not bombarded, through the entire war. Its own account credits universal service sized to make occupation expensive, and a standing refusal of basing rights to anybody.

Both belligerents also banked here throughout. We record that as a second fact and not as a correction to the first.

Service is eleven months and universal. The force has no long-range transport, no expeditionary doctrine, and no legal power to acquire either.

The vaults

Cretan deposit records survived the Wipe because they were on paper in rooms built to survive things. The four governments state that they are complete. They are not open to this archive, to the Guard, or to anyone else. Applications are answered promptly and in the negative.

The giving

Endowment records are public and precise. Between GC 4403 and 4462 Cretan foundations paid for 1,206 libraries, 411 hospitals and 89 university faculties on other worlds. Where the underlying capital came from is not published.

[Compiler's note: this society works from three rooms. Two of them were paid for by a Cretan endowment. We record that here because it seemed dishonest not to.]

Custodial labour

Prison work. Not a camp exactly, and not a prison exactly either.

A sentence can be extended by administrative decision on grounds set out in a schedule. The grounds are broad, the decision is not appealable, and the numbers are unambiguous: 41,206 terms extended over twenty years, against 88 reduced.

Where

Two Guard installations take most of it. One of them mines magnetic ore. What that ore is for does not appear anywhere.

Who

The rolls are kept by species. Non-humans are about a fifth of everyone alive and about three fifths of these rolls. Targath turn up at a rate the population numbers cannot account for.

Why it is defended

Guard material puts it in terms of the bigger picture: the work needs doing, the sentences exist anyway, and member states that fall behind on their obligations can be reminded that both of those things are true.

Daiser

Caretaker of the Council's temple at Riflo, and the sharpest person in the building.

He is introduced to offworlders as the Gatekeeper, which is what the job is called and not what he is. He opens the great oak doors, receives you, and shows you where to stand, and it is very easy to treat him as furniture for the first ten minutes.

"He's not just a gatekeeper. His name is Daiser. He's... like you. Someone surviving the pressure. Don't add more weight to his shoulders."

A Maspin: smoke and vapour, water where the eyes should be, an ember behind it all that brightens when he is enjoying himself, which is often.

The situation

He is indentured. Sentenced to work off a debt that exists on paper and nowhere else, with seven years still on it and no wage to buy it out with. His holder is an establishment controlled by his own uncle, who sits on the Council. Everybody involved regards this as normal, including, most of the time, Daiser.

"We call it indentured servitude. Where I work off an imaginary debt until I can pay it off and be free, which is actually fucking hard without a paycheck."

The way out is his uncle dying or a lottery that does not exist.

Before that

A chemist, and a properly trained one. He can make things most people cannot get, including weapons that are banned on his own world.

How he talks

Two registers, switched instantly. Street with anyone he likes. An elaborate, over-polished formal voice for anyone with authority, deployed with a completely straight face, which is its own kind of insult.

He has never flown. He has never been off Maspin at all. He can fly, though, and when asked where he learned he says a book or two, which is either a joke or the most alarming sentence in the temple.

Datapads

A handheld screen, rebuilt from scratch after the Wipe and now made at Saigo and two licensed plants.

You confirm who you are with a thumb on the glass. Off-network it checks you locally and squares up with the ledger later.

They do not talk to anything from before the war. The people who designed them had never used a pre-war device, had no examples to study, and built to their own guesses, which is also why nothing in them anticipates a skeleton key.

The Dead Moon raiders

White cloaks in a whiteout, black masks with nothing on them but metal eyepieces, long rifles with bayonets fixed.

Not a species. A faction, drawn from several populations of the cold outer moons, and beyond that nobody knows how it is put together. No structure, no leader, no territory, no demand has ever been recorded. They do not hold ground and do not appear to want any.

Everybody who has survived contact says the same thing about the way they move, which is that they are in no hurry. They come out of the storm at a walk.

The one thing that stops them

Missionaries reached those moons out of Sonaff, and a number of raider populations hold the same faith as communities they are otherwise permanently at war with. There is at least one recorded case of a raider breaking off in the middle of an action on seeing a devotional pendant.

Not surrender, not mercy, not law. A pendant.

The death benefit

650,000 credits, and everything he owned.

It is paid to whoever is named on the contract, it is paid in full, and it is paid on schedule. The Guard is scrupulous about this in the way it is scrupulous about all of its commercial obligations, which is to say completely and without warmth.

That is the figure for a man of rank on a second or later contract. Further down the establishment it is smaller, and it is subject to the same instalment machinery as everything else, which means a widow on a poor world inherits a filing obligation along with the grief.

The estate goes with it. Personal effects, retained materiel, whatever is in the cabin, crated and shipped to the named address.

Six and a half times a good year's pay

Which means the arithmetic is available to anybody who wants to run it, and some people run it. A man from a poor world with a large family can work out exactly what he is worth alive and exactly what he is worth dead, and the second number is larger, and there is no version of this document that hides that from him.

"I've fought next to you on every battle, but I will put my life on the line before my career. If I die, my family gets paid."

He is not being morbid. He is quoting a figure.

Debt absolution

A marriage between two families cancels every debt between them. Instantly, entirely, by custom, with nothing signed.

The stated reasoning is warm

The families are one now. A debt between them is a debt owed to yourself, and therefore meaningless.

The practical reasoning is not

A ruined man with a daughter and a creditor has, available to him, a single move that clears the ledger.

Why it is not used constantly

Because everybody can see it. It is lawful, it is free, and a family that visibly engineers one is finished socially. Not prosecuted. Finished. Everyone within a hundred miles understands exactly what was traded and for how much, and it does not get forgotten, and it attaches to the children.

So it happens rarely. And when it happens, the whole district knows within a day.

What it produces

A parent forbidding a good marriage because the debt is income and they would rather keep collecting. A couple genuinely in love whose wedding will look like a transaction no matter how they conduct themselves. Somebody borrowing deliberately, at ruinous rates, to force a family's hand. And, most often, a spouse who is loved perfectly well and will never once be certain whether they were chosen or written off.

In a post-war economy where debt is the ordinary condition and collection has been contracted out to people with weapons, the custom is everywhere and is deeply, quietly resented.

The decontamination doctor

Whoever is on shift at the far end of the Maspin decon cycle, waiting for you to be finished being sick.

The cycle is thorough. Most first-timers come out of it on their knees, and this one has watched enough of that to have a routine: he waits, he lets you get there yourself, and then he offers a hand and a smirk he does not fully suppress.

"First time, I take it? Won't take long to get used to. Mind over matter, unless you've got a severe parasite, scales, or plasma burns."

The list at the end is the useful part. Those three are the ones that do not get better with practice.

The Destruction of Wake

The most talked-about event in living memory, and the one nobody can agree on.

What the Guard says

One ordnance deployment, Autumnal forces, GC 4394. Over in under an hour. Responsibility stated flatly, with no source cited and no unit named. It appears as settled fact in every piece of Guard educational material.

What the people say

We collected thirty-eight accounts across eleven settlements and six worlds, all of them from people who were children then or repeating a parent. Every single one describes something that took days. Two to nine of them. Six say the sky changed colour before anything was heard. Four describe evacuation orders. One describes those orders being cancelled.

An hour and nine days are not two versions of one event.

We note, and draw nothing from it, that the account was published by the party that later received the exclusive licence to mine the remains, and that there is nobody left on the other side to answer it.

How many died

Between 900 million and 4 billion. Neither number rests on a document. Both rest on people.

The Detonation

At the moment of the union, something is destroyed, loudly, on purpose.

A cannon. An enormous firework. A structure brought down under control, chosen in advance and often chosen carefully. Whatever the world can manage, the requirement is that it is sudden, that it is loud, and that it cannot be undone.

It is not celebratory noise

That is the thing outsiders get wrong. This is joy deliberately punctured, at its own high point, by the memory of catastrophe. The bang is not applause. It is a correction.

What it says

Nothing lasts. This will not last either. We are doing it anyway.

On worlds that came out of the war with a continent bombed flat, or a capital that is now a beautiful ruin with the sky coming in through it, the rite is not symbolic and nobody there needs it explained. Everyone in the room has seen the real version of what is being staged.

And the sound is the memory

Which means at every wedding on such a world, there is a portion of the crowd who flinch, who know they are going to flinch, who came anyway, and who are held by somebody standing next to them for a second afterward.

Diontesheempluntornskalla (Dan)

A councillor of Riflo, and the one who will actually talk to you.

The full name is real and he does not expect anyone offworld to attempt it. Dan is what he offers, immediately, with no ceremony about it, which is exactly how Maspin names work: the long one is inherited, and the short one is the one that stuck.

His seat is harmony

Not defence, not trade, not rites. His job on that Council is the agreement between people, and he holds it because he believes real strength is empathy and restraint rather than the other thing.

He is the one who collects the Gift of Memory at the festival, and he takes his time about it.

"Wine allows humans to feel very deeply."

The discharge ceremony

The Guard does not simply stop paying you. It gathers everybody up and says so out loud.

Two venues

Either an auditorium aboard the mothership, which is efficient and means nobody travels, or a proper ceremony on the ground.

The ground option is held on one of the junction worlds. Not a capital and not anywhere important, just one of the places that exists mostly as a place other places connect through, with routes running everywhere and nothing much at the centre of it. They are chosen for exactly that: it is the shortest total journey for the largest number of families, which is the sort of decision this organisation is extremely good at making.

Outdoors, when the weather on that world permits. Rows of chairs. A stage. Names read out.

What it is for

A contract ending is a commercial event and there is no reason at all to hold an event about it. They hold one anyway, because a soldier who leaves quietly tells people it was nothing, and a soldier who leaves in front of his mother tells them it was something.

Several people in this record are within a year of standing in that field.

Dometré Polaris

A prince of the blood who appeared once, in one room, agreed to terms on behalf of a Royal house, and cannot be found in any register anywhere.

What is on the record

He was received in full session at the Council Chamber of Riflo and addressed by the centre councillor as Prince Dometré Polaris, negotiator for the House of Kafkee, Flamebearer. The Council took the minute in its own hand and in its own script, as it does, and has never amended it.

"May your shadow burn long."

The terms he agreed

Ten million in Royal scrip, against long neglect. One unit of Royal soldiers, to hold the shipping lanes against piracy. And a Gift of Memory.

The first two are ordinary instruments. The third is not something a Royal house has ever been asked for, and there is no precedent anywhere in this archive for a crown party accepting one.

The problem with the name

Polaris and Kafkee are separate houses. A Polaris carrying a Kafkee ceremonial office is not forbidden and is also not filed, anywhere, in any register we hold, for anybody. The Royal lists carry no Dometré. They also carry a very great many thin-blooded claimants who are entitled to a seat and a small maintenance and appear on no list at all, which is precisely why this entry is contested rather than closed.

What the room made of him

Not much, at first. One elder stated she had already seen his face, in a vision, kneeling, in the posture of a servant. Another observed that his father had stood on the same floor and lied without his flame so much as flickering. He was tested on songcraft, on the ground that the Royals were once said to sing at every rite, and an exemption was produced on his behalf from the Elder Harmonists.

"Your tongue wears the sand of other stars, boy. Not Polaris rain."

Then his pendant answered theirs, and the room changed. What was said afterwards is recorded as a rare sign, for the family, and as sacred, he may be.

The beard

He wore one. The Royal court requires its household and its blood to go clean-shaven, by long ceremonial rule, and has for as long as there has been a court. Nobody in the chamber raised it. Everybody outside it has.

Since

No soldiers arrived. No payment was made. The Council has not withdrawn the minute, has not written to any house, and declines to discuss the matter with this archive.

[Compiler's note: a man walked into the one room on that world where a decision happens, gave a name, and left with an agreement. We can tell you what he promised to the credit. We cannot tell you that he exists.]

Dorch Rawlden

Son of Grai Penston Rawlden, aged about twenty-three. He holds a junior post in the municipal administration of Crescent City and has held no other.

Standing

He was born outside marriage, at a time when his father was already a senior figure, and to Entonia Yalenti, a journalist working within the limits the statutes allow, who had been attached to his father when both were young, and who is dead. She died of a cancer attributed to industrial contamination in the town where she and Rawlden were both raised. Rawlden has the same disease. The administration promotes monogamy as stated policy on the grounds that it is stabilising, and he is the publicly known exception to it.

He carries his father's name. On a world where children born outside a marriage frequently do not, this is generally read as an acknowledgement rather than as a courtesy, and it is the only formal thing anybody can point to in his position. No instrument defines his standing and no office is reserved for him.

The post

Dorch is responsible for scheduling refuse collection across several districts of the capital. It is unimportant work, it is done adequately, and he applied for it himself against open advertisement.

Informants who deal with the administration are consistent that he is given nothing of consequence, and equally consistent that this is not a punishment or a precaution. He has never asked for anything of consequence. Several describe him as tired in a way that is unusual at his age.

What he is reported to want

To live offworld under his own name and be no relation to anybody. This is said by people who know him and is not said by him in any account held here.

Why he has not gone

He is frightened. Of the galaxy, from what reaches him about it, and by several accounts of his own world as well.

He is also, so far as this archive can establish, the one person on Pashmirské who could leave without asking. Everybody else who has departed in the last decade was put on a ship and told not to return.

Sources

Four informants, three of them former municipal employees and one deported under the second chance. None has described a conversation with him lasting more than a few minutes.

Dorrow

The mills. Grain arrives raw from Weton and leaves as flour, oil and cake, and the difference between those two states is where the money in this system is made.

Throughput, GC 4461

1,188,400,000 tonnes in. 1,141,220,000 tonnes of finished product out.

The processing margin is the largest single margin in the system. It is realised on Kelton, where the product is sold, and not here, where it is made.

Dorrow has the second-highest output value of the ten inhabited bodies and the second-lowest household income.

Dragon's blood trees

Broad flat canopies on bare trunks, named for the red resin that runs when you cut them. Slow, long-lived, and entirely happy in ruined ground.

Which is why Sansvor is full of them now. They have come up inside two rail terminals, an exchange and eleven civic buildings, and in every case the municipality entered them as a maintenance item and then left them alone. The canopy of the north terminal is a tree.

The resin sells as a varnish and a dye. It is the world's largest surviving export by value, which says more about the world than about the resin.

Dreamwalking

The belief that the soul is tied to the body rather than kept inside it, and that in deep sleep or unconsciousness the tie goes slack.

While it is slack the soul can be moved. Including, adherents say, through time.

The mechanics they describe

Consciousness has something like weight, and that weight pulls it back toward its body. Overcome the pull and it goes elsewhere. A stretch of unconsciousness earlier in your life leaves the body unoccupied for that long, and that unoccupied time stays available afterwards. Two days in a coma at twenty buys you two days at forty, and while you are using them you are twenty.

They also hold that this was once done with instruments rather than by accident, and that a device existed for pointing a soul somewhere rather than merely loosening it.

Where it turns up

Among Maspin practitioners working with floom preparations, in two monastic traditions on Shayron, and in the folk medicine of four worlds with no connection to each other.

Why we have not dismissed it

Religious testimony is normally consistent about meaning and wildly inconsistent about mechanism. This is the other way round. The accounts agree in detail about how it is supposed to work and disagree about what it is for, and we do not know what to make of that.

The Elder Tree

One tree, hollow at the base, going up into cloud. Inside it there is a chamber with mosaic walls and a chandelier, and in the middle of the floor there is a hole.

Inside

Every account agrees on the room: the mosaic, the light hanging above, humans and Maspin standing together with no arrangement made for either, and the opening at the centre with nothing around it.

Height

Nobody has measured it. Every informant describes the crown entering cloud. Trailblazer survey work in the surrounding concession recorded canopy heights across the district and stopped at the edge of the ceremonial ground, by agreement.

What it is for

The dead go into the hole. Blue vapour comes back up afterwards and is taken into the tree. The Maspin hold that what goes down returns to the ocean beneath the crust and that the tree drinks from it.

One thing we can add

The district around this tree is exceptionally fertile, and nothing is imported into it.

Attributed to C., Base Delta, and to four Maspin informants who asked to be recorded together.

The Elder Tree interment rite

How the Maspin bury their dead, which is not burial.

The chamber fills. Somebody starts singing and the room takes it up. The person being interred walks to the edge of the opening in the floor and sings over it. Then the hood comes down, the necklace comes off and is set on the ground, and they step backward into the hole.

Blue steam comes up afterwards and the tree takes it in.

The stone from the necklace goes into the wall.

Everyone attends

Humans, Maspin, anybody who is there. Nothing is arranged differently for outsiders and nobody is warned in advance what they are about to watch. Two of the three visitors who described this to us had no idea what was happening until it had happened.

They walk

Every account has the person going to the edge unassisted and stepping back on their own. We asked, as plainly as we could manage, whether the timing is chosen by the person being interred. They understood the question perfectly well. They did not think it was an important one.

Even graves grow flowers, I may sink like a stone, For what we know, for what we know, But you'll never be alone.

The enlistment rites form

Six questions you answer on your first day, about your own body.

Burned or buried. Which faith, from a list of eighty-eight, with a blank line if yours is not on it. Whether your family wants you sent home at their own cost. Two names. Your signature. The date.

You cannot start without filling it in, and once filed it is kept forever, because decades later it is the document somebody reads to find out what to do with you.

It can be changed at any time by writing in. Fewer than two people in a hundred ever do.

[Compiler's note: it is a good form. It is well drafted and it is honoured. The volunteer transcribing the GC 4444 series stopped for the day when she noticed what the ages in the third column were.]

Entonia Yalenti

A journalist of Pashmirské, mother of Dorch Rawlden, and the only person in this part of the record whose account of the town was published anywhere.

The work

Journalism on Pashmirské operates within statutory limits on speech, and Yalenti worked inside them. What that permitted is narrower than the word suggests elsewhere in this volume. She is not reported to have been obstructed, and she is not reported to have tested it.

The town

She and Rawlden were raised in the same place. The air and the water there were contaminated by industrial discharge across a long period, and both of them developed cancers of a kind that presents unusually early.

The contamination was a condition of the war. Nothing could be done about it while the fighting continued. It was cleaned by Rawlden's administration once he held the capital, at public expense, and completely.

The people who grew up drinking it are a separate matter and were not cleaned.

The relationship

She and Rawlden were attached to one another when both were young and separately again, much later, for approximately two weeks. Dorch Rawlden is her son.

She did not marry, did not hold any position in the administration, and is not recorded as having sought either.

Death

She died of the disease. The date is not held here.

Three shipping schedules, one insurance schedule, and a man who used to drive supplies out there.

Nothing else. No survey. No population figure. No accession instrument. Nobody in this archive has been.

1 gap

It takes deliveries. Somebody organises convoys out to it, which means there are people there who need feeding and equipment that needs parts, and the routes are difficult enough that leading them counts as a line on a service record.

That is the whole of it. A place that exists because things are sent to it, known to the galaxy as a destination on a manifest and to almost nobody as a place.

Fermented kraskor

The finest thing on Maspin, by the Council's own account, and it is meat that has been left alone for years.

Kraskor flesh is fermented down until it is liquid, or near enough, and then taken the way Maspin take everything, which is absorbed rather than eaten. Grades exist and the good ones are measured in years.

The Council's formal submissions describe it, alongside pickled inside-barked mycelium, as a staple delicacy of the cuisine. That is the highest praise any food gets in a Maspin document.

None of it is exported. What leaves this world is live kraskor, in a form the Maspin themselves would not touch.

Field aliases

The names men use when their own have become a problem, and the reliable comedy of watching them pick one under pressure.

A good alias is boring. It sounds like somebody's cousin. It survives being said out loud to a customs officer who is not listening. The ones that get used are almost never the ones that get chosen carefully.

Smelvin Klombo

Invented years earlier for a drinking trip on Zonar, retired, and then brought back into service because it was the only one its owner could remember. It works, in the sense that nobody has ever repeated it back without pausing first.

Dometré Polaris

Arrived after a failed first attempt at James Predator, which was abandoned mid-sentence. Polaris is a Royal surname and reasonably common on Shayron, which is either excellent cover or an extremely expensive mistake depending on who is checking.

Grugg Treeleaf

Assigned to a man who was unconscious at the time and had no say in it whatsoever. Nobody has yet had the heart to tell him under what circumstances it was decided.

The rule everybody forgets

The alias is the easy part. The hard part is the story attached to it, and the story is where people die: a farmer with plasma scars, a prince with a beard, a native of a world that has not had a hurricane in two hundred years describing this year's hurricanes.

Floom eggs

Unfertilised eggs, laid on dead ground, full of a blue liquid. On Maspin they are fertiliser. Off Maspin they are the most valuable medicine in existence.

The ordinary use is the important one: a floom drops them on dry grass or a failing garden and a week later the ground has recovered. That is how the settled belt stays fertile without importing anything.

The fluid

Nobody sensible calls it a drug. Calsco calls it the essence of life in its purest form and does not appear to be exaggerating for effect. It is the medium in the sensory tanks and it brings people back from injuries that should have finished them.

Taking it

For a human it is hours of something that is not a high in any recognisable sense. For a Maspin it is not hours. Ask one whether they have ever tried it and you will get a straight no, and the reason, which is that the effect would last the rest of their life.

Control

The Council of Riflo restricts collection, holding and export, and has refused three applications to expand the trade. It is the most valuable thing on the planet, and the body sitting on it is the body that would profit most from letting it go.

Flooms

The creature Maspin runs on, and the reason the air there is as good as it is.

They are nervous, affectionate, and much smarter than they look. Everyone who has kept them says the same thing, unprompted: a floom decides very quickly what it thinks of a person, and it is almost never wrong. People on Maspin take this seriously enough to act on it.

What they do

They take in ambient life energy the way a plant takes light. Not stealing it, not draining anything, just standing in it.

Then they lay eggs on dead ground: unfertilised, full of a blue liquid, dropped on dry grass and failing gardens. About a week later the ground has come back greener than it was. The Trailblazer concession imports no fertiliser at all and its yields keep climbing.

The local phrasing, given to us word for word by three different people:

Floom is the ecosystem. All things live because of flooms, and floom lives because of life.

Trade

They are exported, in very small numbers. The Council restricts it and has turned down three applications to expand it.

Foundation Day

The Guard's birthday, and the best-documented event in this volume by an enormous margin.

Same date every year since GC 4406. Assembly at nine, an address by whichever Director is nearest, a parade, a flyover if there is a fleet in the system, food for everybody, and a broadcast in the evening. It is not a religious holiday and the Guard is clear about that.

It is also observed almost everywhere. Twelve member worlds hold it on a different local date, for harvest or weather reasons, each by a written dispensation, each of which we have.

Why we hold so much of it

Because the Guard photographed itself. We have the incorporation papers, the register of all fifty-six observances, the parade orders, the vendor licences, the road closures, the catering invoices, and 4,192 photographic plates.

Attendance at the main event last year: 218,406, counted at the gate.

The Friend

the Maspin shaman

Ask for the shaman on Maspin and you will be corrected. He would rather you called him Friend.

He smiles in a way people describe, without prompting and in almost the same words, as soft and ancient.

What he does

Nobody outside is clear. He is present at the festival, he is consulted about people who are dying, and the Trailblazer surgeon at Base Delta credits him with stopping a man from bleeding out through a hole in the heart, and then walking that man back to a vehicle afterwards.

Finding him

You do not. Ask a Maspin child where the shaman is and you will get a straight answer:

"You don't find the shaman. The shaman finds you."

Two things that unsettle visitors

He knows names he has not been told. And he has been known to leave something at the medbay for a person before that person arrived on the world, with instructions about who to say it came from.

Galactic Standard

What everybody speaks. Nobody made them.

No law imposes it and no instrument requires it. It is the language of the code, the ledger, the shipping manifests and the Guard, and that has been more than enough. If you want to buy something, sue somebody, or get paid, this is the language you do it in.

Where it came from

It is not anybody's first language and never was. It assembled itself out of the large human tongues of the pre-war era, taking whatever was most useful from each, and it went through three stages to get here.

Before the war it was the language of trade, spoken between parties who had no other language in common and no interest in learning one.

During the war it became the language of negotiation, for the same reason and with more at stake. Both belligerents used it. Almost every surviving instrument from that period is written in it, which is why this archive can read them at all.

After the war it became the only one. The Guard needed a single language to administer in, and it did not have to impose one, because the thing everybody already used for contracts and ceasefires was sitting there.

Nobody had to be made to learn it

There is no ministry of language, no standard body, and no penalty attached to speaking anything else. It spread because the alternative was not being paid.

Where it was taught deliberately, it went faster

On Astonia the schools were handed to sponsored religious foundations under the annexation instrument, with residential attendance and instruction in Galactic Standard written into the contract. Inside eleven years those foundations had ninety-four per cent of the children.

That is the only case in this archive where anybody set out to do it on purpose, and it is catalogued separately, because what happened to Astonian speech is not what is happening elsewhere and we do not want the two read as one process.

Galactic Standard law

The code that runs everywhere, sitting on top of whatever your own world does.

A member world writes its own statutes and the Guard leaves them alone. It can strike any of them at any time and in fifty-three years has done so forty-one times, thirty-eight of which were about tax or port dues, because that is what the Guard actually minds about.

The part that matters

The code applies everywhere. Enforcement does not, and nothing in the code requires it to. There is no provision for complaining that a law was applied to you and not your neighbour, and no body that would hear it.

So automatic plasma weapons are lawful under local statute on nineteen worlds and unlawful under the code on all of them, and both facts sit there until somebody needs one of them. A world can run for decades doing something openly and then find out it was illegal the whole time, on the day that becomes useful.

The laws are not there to be applied. They are there to be available.

Slavery

Prohibited absolutely, in the strongest language in the entire code. There is no inspectorate, no penalty schedule, and no enforcement mechanism attached to it.

The Gashi

Green-skinned, and nobody can agree on whether that skin is reptile or amphibian.

Up close it settles the question no better. It has the fine dry grain of scale in some lights and the give of something that would rather be damp in others, and the Gashi themselves find the question tedious in the way any people find it tedious when strangers open with it.

What they wear

Robes and tunics, cut long, and over them a great deal of decorative gear that is built to move: panels, sashes, hanging lengths of fabric weighted at the ends so they swing and settle rather than hang dead. A Gashi walking across a room is doing something that a human walking across a room is not.

The hair

All colours, every variety, and no two families the same. What is consistent is the quality of it. Gashi hair grows thick, holds a shape, takes a comb, and looks in every case as though it has just been finished by somebody very good, which is not a thing they work at and is very annoying to everyone else.

What they do

Artisans, overwhelmingly, in the broad sense rather than the narrow one. Chefs, painters, teachers, engravers, people who make the small good version of a thing that could have been made badly and cheaply instead. It is a whole world, so it is also farmers and clerks and mechanics, but the culture is built around art and sophistication and it judges accordingly.

Which makes the ones who go into other lines of work interesting, because the sophistication does not come off. It just gets applied to something else.

The gem mosaic wall

The inside of the Elder Tree is covered in coloured stones, and every one of them is a person.

When a Maspin is interred, the stone is taken off the necklace they wore in life and set into the wall. There are thousands. Nobody has counted them and nobody has been asked to.

There is no order to it. Not by date, not by family, not by anything. A stone goes wherever there is room. There are no names, no dates, and no inscriptions of any kind, so a family cannot come back and find their own.

Asked about that, they say it is not what the wall is for.

The gem-setting practice

Every Maspin wears a stone. When they die, it goes into the wall.

It is taken off the necklace they wore in life and set by somebody from the household, or by a councillor, wherever there happens to be room. No inscription, no date, nothing written at all.

Asked how a family finds their own stone afterwards, they said that they do not, and looked mildly puzzled that anyone would want to.

The Gift of Memory

You do not tell a Maspin what happened to you. You give them a tear and they feel it.

Do not tell. Share a tear.

At the festival someone comes to collect it. You hold a memory, a real one, whatever moves you, and it goes into a single tear, and that is taken. Love, grief, joy, the worst thing you have ever seen. The kind does not matter.

It has to be true

A memory picked for effect is detectable, is an insult, and the Maspin will not explain how they know.

What it is for

It is how they come to understand another person. They do not assume understanding and they do not ask for it. It is given once, deliberately, and it costs the giver something to hand over.

The Council asks for one from foreign parties. It sits in the minutes alongside credits and shipping like any other term of an agreement, because to the Maspin it is one.

Several cultures in this volume forbid a person from ever speaking about certain things. When someone from one of those worlds gives this gift, they have not found a clever way around their own rule. They have broken it.

Glazberries

Small teal berries with a hard glossy skin, bitter enough raw to make you pull a face, and good cooked or fermented.

They grow wild on several jungle worlds and are farmed properly on Kinton. Their real distinction is that almost everybody can eat them: they agree with humans and with most surveyed physiologies, which is rare enough that three separate services put them in the standard field ration.

Grai Penston Rawlden

styled Kon-Grai

Grai Penston Rawlden is the sole governing authority of Pashmirské. He is approximately fifty-eight years old. He commanded the principal military formation on the world during the later part of the hundred and fifty year conflict and holds no office that existed before him.

Origins

Rawlden was raised poor, in a town whose air and water were contaminated by industrial discharge across a long period. Everybody there drank it. Nobody there had the means to do anything else, and while the war continued nobody at any level had the means to do anything about the discharge either.

Before the capital

Rawlden was a general. His background is logistics rather than command in the field, and accounts credit his standing at the end of the war to the fact that he had spent decades keeping formations supplied in conditions where supply was the difficulty.

The civil population was aware throughout that the war was continuing. When he offered stability, he was permitted to remain.

Accession

Rawlden did not win the war. The two powers that had funded the conflict destroyed one another, after which the money and the resupply ended and the fighting declined over approximately sixty years. He held the capital when it stopped. The consolidation that followed was carried out largely by administration rather than by force, against factions that were by then without ammunition, without a patron and without any further offer to make.

Title

Rawlden is styled Kon-Grai, a Nhathian term for a leader, formed from kon, north, and grai, stone. He is not Nhath and has never met one. No contract, correspondence or recorded contact exists between him and that people. He appears to have taken the term from reading.

Accounts of him consistently note that he reads a great deal and that the Nhath are a long-standing interest of his.

He does not speak the language. He has perhaps a few dozen words of it.

Nhathian provides no neutral term for a person outside the Nhath. Krayd serves for they, for other species and for enemy. A person outside that people using their word for a leader is making a claim the language has no form for. Nobody on Pashmirské raises this and nobody has been recorded asking Rawlden about it.

Rawlden's given name is Grai, which is the same word as the second element of the title. It has not been established whether the resemblance influenced his choice.

He also uses the term Fonty, from the Nhathian Fon-Ty, meaning a subordinate. He writes it without the hyphen.

Administration

Rawlden governs with a cabinet. Appointments are made on loyalty to him and on a record of completing work, and he does not tolerate corruption in any part of the administration. Bribery is not a route to anything under his authority, and informants from several trades confirm this without prompting.

He lives modestly. No residence, household or personal holding of any scale is attributed to him by any account held here.

Marriage

Rawlden is married to Sershanti Rawlden, formerly Kinsley, and has been throughout. The administration promotes monogamy as stated policy on the grounds that it is stabilising.

He conducted an affair lasting approximately two weeks, acknowledged it rather than denying it, and separated from his wife for a period. They reconciled. He offered a divorce and she declined it. Accounts from people close to the household are consistent that the refusal was a decision about position rather than about him, and that the marriage has been maintained since as a working arrangement that both parties present as a stable one.

Entonia Yalenti

A journalist, working within the limits the statutes allow for that work, and attached to Rawlden when both were young. She is dead.

She and Rawlden were raised in the same town. Both developed cancers of early onset, and the account given by both of them is that the air and the water there were contaminated by industrial discharge over a long period.

Family

Rawlden has one son by Yalenti, Dorch Rawlden, aged about twenty-three, born outside the marriage and a publicly known exception to the policy. His standing is not defined by any instrument. He holds a junior post in the municipal administration of Crescent City and is catalogued separately.

Every account agrees on two things: that Rawlden regards the affair as a wrong he committed, and that he loves the boy.

Manner

Rawlden speaks without notes. Every account describes him as quick, dry and unusually well constructed in the moment, to the extent that listeners routinely assume he has prepared and rehearsed. Nobody has produced a text of anything he has said.

The amnesty

Soldiers of the defeated factions were offered amnesty on taking an oath, and the offer was general rather than case by case. It was honoured. Informants from three of the former factions confirm this.

The faction leadership was deported. Rawlden has allowed it to be understood that a number of them were killed. None were.

Government

Rawlden's stated position is that a population which has been at war for a hundred and fifty years does not require political ideals, and requires food, water, shelter, safety and an absence of shelling. He has said publicly that taxes are collected, that obedience is expected, that certain liberties are not available under his authority and that some of his subjects are afraid of him. He does not describe the arrangement as democratic, free or just and has not claimed a mandate for it. He has also stated that he wants the position and intends to keep it. Accounts agree that he presents none of this as a responsibility reluctantly accepted.

The address

No complete text of Rawlden's principal public address has been recovered. It survives as a set of fragments, quoted by people who were present, of which three recur in almost every account.

The first concerns a widow whose husband had been her sweetheart at school, died badly, and called for his mother at the end, and who was told afterwards that he had died for freedom. Rawlden's stated objection is that the sentence returned nothing to her.

The second concerns young soldiers who were told they were about to die for a democracy in a war none of them had voted in.

The third is a single line and is the fragment most often quoted.

"You have food. You have water. You have a roof. Nobody is shooting at you. What the fuck else do you want?"

Informants agree that the passages between these fragments describe injuries and deaths from the conflict in detail. Those who have discussed the address state that the descriptions are placed immediately before the list of provisions he supplies, and are intended as a comparison.

The remediation

One of the earliest acts of the administration was the cleaning of the contaminated ground and water in the industrial districts, including the town Rawlden was raised in. It was carried out at public expense, it was completed, and it is not commemorated anywhere.

Nothing in it reaches the people who grew up drinking the water. That population is now in middle age.

Observance

Speech is restricted by statute, dress is regulated in certain respects, and attendance at a calendar of public festivals is compulsory.

The festivals do not concern Rawlden. There is no portrait of him in a public building, no honorific in daily use, and nothing addressed to him. What they commemorate is the world as it was before the war, at its furthest extent and its most accomplished, and the observances are constructed to be moving.

Expansion

Rawlden has raised the possibility of territorial expansion in cabinet and has not acted on it. The stated reason is that the population is not ready.

Dissent

Rawlden's stated policy on political dissent is imprisonment under strict conditions or public execution. Neither is carried out. Persons removed for dissent are subjected to a staged execution and then deported, and the practice is catalogued separately.

The distinction is not published and Rawlden has never corrected the public account. The reputation is maintained deliberately and the killing is not.

Health

Rawlden has a cancer of a class that was routinely preventable before the war and for which no formulation now survives anywhere. It is attributed to the town. Yalenti was raised there also and died of the same thing.

He did not know he had it when he went to war. It was present and undiagnosed for a long period, and it accelerated after he took the capital.

There is no treatment. What there is instead is machinery. His legs have failed progressively and he uses prosthetics. Several organs have been replaced with mechanical substitutes and his heart is regulated. The replacements are engineered rather than grown, they are not a close fit, and they impose limits on what he can do and for how long. He is maintained rather than cured, and by any ordinary description of the term he is on life support.

None of it is public. The effort of keeping it from being public is itself considerable, and every account of him at a public event describes a man who appears entirely well, for as long as the event lasts.

He is on record, from before any of it, as objecting to prosthetics. He has not withdrawn the position and has never been asked to reconcile it with his own body.

The condition is not public. It is recorded here on the testimony of three people who have no connection to one another, two of whom were deported and one of whom was not.

Security

There have been repeated attempts on Rawlden's life. Informants put the number between nine and nineteen and agree that most were poorly prepared. The former faction leadership is offworld, alive, and in several cases has said publicly what it would like to see happen to him.

He is described by everybody who has been near him as careful in a manner that is proportionate to this rather than in excess of it.

Relations with the Guard

There is no relationship. No application, refusal, incident or complaint is recorded in either direction. Rawlden is reported to hold a low opinion of the organisation and to have no intention of acting against it.

His own account of himself

Rawlden describes what he does as wrong and does not qualify it. His position, given consistently and without being asked, is that a world of this kind will produce a certain amount of harm regardless, that it is better carried by one person who has agreed to carry it than distributed among many who have not, and that he has agreed. He does not expect anything afterward and says so.

Informants divide on this. Some hold that it is the most honest thing any of them has heard from a person in power. Others hold that a man who enjoys authority as plainly as this one does has found an unusually good reason to keep it, and that the two accounts are not exclusive.

Sources

No document issued over Rawlden's name is held here. There is no portrait, no service record and no account of his life prior to his holding the capital. The material in this entry comes from people who have met him, and their accounts are unusually consistent with one another.

The Grand Mothership Dining Hall

Warm tans and golds, in a ship that is otherwise white and blue all the way through. It is the only room aboard that does not look like a machine.

Ornate chandeliers hang from a ceiling high enough to make the space feel like weather. The sleek white structural beams are still there, still glowing faintly with the ship's own light, but everything hung on them and set beneath them is amber, tan and gold. Long tables and deep booths run the length of it, and the noise is a constant weather system of laughter, cutlery and shared war stories.

What is actually on the tray

Grilled white meat, dusted with teal and red flakes. A garnish of yellow spireleaf sprouts arranged on the side by somebody who was told to arrange it. Circular tan grains, soft and steaming. A tall glass of opaque pastel-yellow chai.

It is good. That is the surprising part. The bread comes out of the ovens hot enough to smell from the elevator, and the spices are real, carried aboard from a dozen worlds by people who missed them. A man can come off six weeks of ration bars, walk through those doors, and be undone by the smell before he has even sat down.

It seats the entire embarked complement in three sittings, and it cost more to fit out than the medical wing, which is in the accounts and has never been commented on.

You are required to come out of armour to eat. The standing order gives the reason as morale, and it is correct: it is the one hour of the day when a unit stops looking like a unit and starts looking like five people who know each other.

Graves

The oldest of the five sent to Sonaff, which is why he ended up in charge of them.

Nobody appointed him. There were five people in a blizzard outside a sealed hangar, not one of them infantry, and he was the one who had been in longest, so he gave the orders.

"Plan? Stay in position, shoot anything you see that isn't me."

That is the entire plan, and given what he had to work with it is not a bad one.

Gravity spires

Towers that burn Corefuel to hold an atmosphere onto a rock that has no business keeping one.

A spire generates a local gravitational field and a pressure envelope around itself, about 1.4 kilometres across. Put three to seven of them in a cluster with overlapping envelopes and you can live on an asteroid: walk outside, plant a garden, hang washing.

They are how the Wake fragment colonies existed at all. The homeworld's own core, refined, keeping the people standing on its wreckage alive.

What breaks

The regulator assembly, always. Nobody can make one; they come out of salvage and pre-war stock, issued quarterly against a settlement's entitlement.

What happens if a cluster goes

The envelope opens over four to eleven hours depending on its size. The safety schedule says get to a hardened structure. It does not say what to do after that.

The Great War

also known as: the War · the Last War · the Long Account (Katanzaria)

Two powers went to war and both of them ceased to exist. Nothing succeeded either one. Everything in this volume is dated from it and nobody can tell you why it started.

When

It stopped in GC 4402 and no source disputes that. It started somewhere between GC 4386 and GC 4393 depending on which world you ask, a spread of seven years. Some of that is worlds dating the war from the first fighting in their own sky. Not all of it is.

Why

Every world has an answer. No two answers agree. No document has been recovered that would let anyone prefer one.

Our view, marked as inference and held loosely: this is not lost data. There was never one story to lose. INFERRED

How it was fought

Look at the requisitions and the damage assessments and the targets come up in the same order every time: shipyards, weapons manufacture, plasma extraction, medicine, banks. Ground taken and ground lost barely appear.

They were not trying to hold each other's worlds. They were taking each other's capacity to make things, and they succeeded, and that is why a galaxy that can still fly cannot build a ship.

Who was on which side

We cannot draw the map. The best evidence is tax filings, because allegiance was decided by whom you paid, and they give roughly 65 worlds one way and 72 the other with everything else neutral, split, or paying both.

Nineteen worlds appear in the collection records of both parties in the same year.

The two atrocities

The Wipe, laid at C.O.R.D.'s door. The destruction of Wake, laid at the Autumnals'. In both cases the accusation is made by the other side, and in one of those cases the other side is not there to answer it.

[Compiler's note: we have been asked several times to produce a map. We have not produced a map.]

Greyleaf

Cured leaf, rolled and smoked. The most common vice in the galaxy and the cheapest.

Grown on forty-one worlds, sold everywhere by the packet, legal in every jurisdiction in this volume, and issued as part of the Guard ration. It is what two people share on a wall at the end of a shift.

It also turns up in the cause-of-death column on every member world that keeps one.

Grugg Treeleaf

Carried in unconscious, admitted under a name he did not give, and that is the name he has now.

What happened

A medevac out of jungle country on Maspin, with three men in it and one of them past speaking. Somebody else supplied his name on the radio. The base took it down, the medbay admitted him under it, and every subsequent line of his treatment, his theatre time and his discharge sits in that file under that name.

He was not asked and could not have answered. By the time anybody could have corrected it, it had been written eleven times.

The name itself

Treeleaf is a Maspin surname in the ordinary Maspin pattern, which is to say a tree, taken by the household that raised you. It is unremarkable and it is local.

Grugg is not a Maspin word, is not a Maspin sound, and does not occur anywhere else in our material.

So the name is half of one world and half of nowhere, joined at a medevac, and there is no arrangement under which a person would have arrived at it themselves.

Condition on admission

The record is specific about the injury and vague about the man. Facial. Extensive. He lived.

Since

No follow-up, no transfer, no next of kin contacted, and no correction ever filed. The file is closed and correct and in that name.

[Compiler's note: three men gave three names on one call and only one of them was in a condition to be lying. This archive is a great many files exactly like this one, and we normally do not notice, because normally there is nobody left to be wrong about.]

The Guard

A police force on a small world with a port, which is now the largest thing in the galaxy. It did not fight the war. It was incorporated four years after the war stopped, by people who had.

Founding

The incorporation instrument survives and names nine founders by name and prior title. Four were general officers of armies that no longer existed. Five held commercial interests in shipping, insurance and salvage.

It constitutes the body as a chartered corporation selling security to subscribing worlds. That is what it is. Everything since has been growth.

The mark

A skinny blue trident. It is painted on the hull of every station and outpost the Guard has ever touched, stitched onto the chest of every polo, and stamped on the crates that come off the supply run. On a good many worlds it is the only piece of galactic government anybody has ever actually seen.

The first world is not named in the instrument, and we have not been able to establish it.

What you get for joining

Defence, and free movement of persons between every member world.

Read the accession debates and it is the second one they talk about. We hold eleven in full, and in nine of them the right to go somewhere is the argument that carries the vote. That is what a galaxy remembers after it has watched borders decide who lived.

What you give

An assessed share of revenue, and people. Your own laws, religion, holidays and government stay yours. Planetary law can be struck by the Guard at any time and almost never is, because the Guard wants the money and not the argument.

Not an army, a company

There are no branches. Flight, ground, engineering, medical and administrative divisions share the same hull, the same mess and the same seniority list. Nobody serves in a national contingent; absorbed formations enter as individuals, which is why no formation in the establishment is older than the Guard itself.

Not enlistment, contract

Fixed term, completion bonus per operation. Units bid for the work that is going, and units with strong completion records win what they bid on. Acceptance rates are filed by unit.

Nobody is assigned. Everybody applies.

Standing order 41

Materiel at a cleared objective is recovered rather than destroyed, and a schedule sets out what the recovering personnel may keep. The schedule has been widened twice. Retained items are not entered anywhere, on the stated ground that entering them would be disproportionate.

Enforcement

Galactic Standard law is universal and binding. Nothing in it requires enforcement to be even, provides a complaint for uneven enforcement, or names a body to hear one.

The laws are not there to be applied. They are there to be available.

The Guard Academy

Where the Guard raises the people it will employ.

Two ways in. The ordinary one is an application at the usual age from a member world. The other is wardship: when an action leaves a child with nobody, and the Guard was there, the Guard takes the child.

Over the last twenty years that is 41,880 children. The average age when they come in is seven.

They get a real education, better than most worlds manage, plus service instruction from about twelve and a specialist stream from fifteen. Poetry, mathematics, languages, the lot. Eleven periods across the entire course are spent on the history of the Great War.

Ordinary entrants join the service at a rate of about six in ten. Wardship entrants join at ninety-four in a hundred, which is not surprising, because the Academy is the only home they have.

The Guard Board of Directors

Seven people run the galaxy. They elected each other, and any of them can be removed by the other six.

That is the whole constitution and it has never been amended. No member world confirms them. No citizen votes on them. There is no term, no appeal, and nobody outside the room to appeal to.

What they hold

The money. Every exclusive licence the Guard owns, including Corefuel. Every senior appointment. Authorisation of any operation above a certain size. Standing orders. And the power to strike any law on any member world.

Who they are

People with commercial interests, undeclared, because nothing requires them to declare and nothing requires Guard contracts to be advertised. One seat has always gone to a general, which the founding document does not require and which has happened every time anyway.

What the minutes look like

In nineteen years, 1,411 resolutions. 1,388 of them carried without a division, which means nobody asked for a count. There is no way to record a dissent on the form and nobody has ever asked for one to be added.

Seven people who can each be fired by the other six will agree with each other about almost everything. Not because they are told to. Because none of them wants to be the one who objected.

Guard burial rites

Whatever you wrote on the form when you signed, the Guard does. That is the promise and it is kept.

Cremation or burial, your faith or none of them, a plot on the Burial Moon at no cost, your remains transported, and two family members brought out at the Guard's expense to stand there.

Anything beyond that is chargeable: a custom stone, a particular plot, a third relative, or sending you home to your own world instead.

When there are no remains

The obligation is discharged with a service and no interment, and the name goes onto the memorial walls at the annual addition like everyone else.

When there are too many

One paragraph in the schedule permits a single combined service, at the caretakers' discretion, when the numbers are past what the moon can handle.

It has been used.

The Guard corridor

A hallway on the mothership lined with small chapels, one per faith, rentable by the hour.

How it works

The paperwork is the marriage. You file first, at a desk, and you are married when the clerk stamps it. Everything after that is a service you are purchasing.

Then you pick a door. There are a great many doors. The enlistment rites form lists eighty-eight faiths and the corridor makes a decent effort at all of them, which means a stretch of identical hatchways opening onto rooms that share nothing but their dimensions: incense in one, water in the next, a bare wooden bench, a stained-glass panel lit from behind, an altar with a sun on it.

There is a price list

It is posted. It is not expensive and it is not free, and the difference between the rooms is entirely a matter of how much is in them.

The room at the end has nothing in it

No symbol, no furniture, no fee.

It is the busiest room in the corridor by a wide margin, and it has been for as long as the mothership has been flying. Some of that is money. Some of it is eighty-eight faiths and none of them being yours. And some of it is two people who have thirty-one hours of shore leave and no interest in explaining themselves to anybody.

Guard credits

The money. A credit is a line in the Guard's ledger, and it is worth something because the Guard says it is.

Nobody outside the accounting division calls them credits. On a dock or in a bar it is Guardcoin, said the way you say the name of a company that owns your town.

And then there is the coin

Struck silver, heavier in the hand than anybody expects the first time, in the same denomination as the ledger and carrying none of its properties. You can put a few of them on a table without a single system anywhere knowing that you did.

That is not a survival from the paper decade. It is current issue, and it is the only part of this arrangement the Guard has never explained in writing. A ledger entry has a sender, a receiver, a date and a reference. A silver credit has a weight.

Which is the whole of it

The Guard built a currency that records everything, and also mints the exception. Every bounty settled on a fringe world, every retained item under Standing Order 41 that somebody afterwards turned into money, and a great deal of what moves through the cartels, moves in metal, because metal does not reconcile.

When the Wipe took every financial record in existence, money went back to paper for about a decade while the accounts were retyped, and then the credit replaced it. It is not backed by metal or grain or anything else. It is backed by the Guard's word and by the fact that member worlds collect tax in it.

Where the ledger works

Wherever Guardnet reaches. Beyond that you settle in paper and hope somebody reconciles it later, at the discretion of whoever you are dealing with.

Which means the answer to whether your savings exist depends on where you are standing. Cut a world off the network and everything its people own becomes a rumour until it comes back.

The ledger rules allow settlement to a world or a district to be suspended by administrative decision. It has happened nineteen times in twenty years, for an average of forty-one days.

The Guard franchise

Everybody votes, the votes are counted honestly, and the count is published. There is no fraud in this entry.

Every Guard citizen of age gets one vote. Citizenship of your own planet gets you nothing here; you can hold local office on it and still not vote in a Guard poll. Registers are kept by the worlds and audited by the Guard, and fifty-three years of returns exist for every world and district, with the question printed in full.

What gets voted on

Over the last twenty years: 88 polls on roads and transit works, 61 on drug licensing, 44 on municipal boundaries, 39 on holidays and observance dates, 31 on harbour works, 22 on schools, and 106 on assorted local statute.

What does not

Appropriations. Licensing. Who sits on the Board. Standing orders. Whether an operation happens.

Turnout averages 79.4 per cent and has been climbing for a decade. People vote because voting works. The things they vote on are the things nobody upstairs minds losing.
