Guard nicknames

Nobody in this service is called what is on their file, and how many things a man is called tells you exactly how many people are close enough to take a liberty with him.

Nobody agrees, and the disagreement is the whole system

A name does not shorten once. It shortens differently in every direction, and the versions do not compete or resolve. One staff sergeant in the personnel series is attested, in the same year, as Jim, Jimzy, Jimz, Jimzo, Jimbo and Jimmy. Six people, six words, one man, and not one of them adopted anybody else's.

Which means the nickname is not really about him. It is a record of a relationship, held by the other person.

Who is allowed

Anybody who has earned it, and there is no ceremony for earning it. What there is instead is a very reliable tell: the first time somebody shortens your name in front of the room and nobody looks up.

The full name is the distance

Read the establishment by this and it goes the wrong way from rank. A Special Operations sergeant has six names. A colonel of the covert division has a rank and a surname. The men in this volume who are only ever given one name, in full, every time, are the men nobody has ever been in a room with twice.

Getting it wrong on purpose

A recognised move, and not an affectionate one. You mangle a man's name, hold his eye, and wait to see whether he corrects you. Correcting is not the loss. The loss is the pause before you decide.

Some people never correct anybody, ever, about anything. It is worth knowing which ones.

Short forms that stopped being short

Yakib became Yake so completely that both turn up in the same conversation in the same mouth, and the man answers to either without noticing there were two.

Elsewhere

The Maspin do the same thing and made it the law: the inherited name is long and the one that stuck is the one you give a stranger. Nhathian fuses a three-part name to two syllables for the people who love him and keeps eleven for anybody taking a statement.

Three peoples, no contact, one arrangement. Nobody planned it and it is not in any instrument.

[Compiler's note: the enlistment form has one line for a name. We hold four thousand two hundred and six testimonies and have not once heard a soldier use what is on it.]

The Guard nurses

Two of them, on the same ward, and the most frightening thing about them is how ordinary the work is.

A man comes off a transport screaming and thrashing. They take an arm each and pin him to a thin mattress, and they do it the way two people carry a table through a doorway they have carried tables through before. No hesitation, no signal between them, nothing said.

Then the respirator, then the sedative, then the next one.

Guard pay

It is a very good living, and almost none of it arrives while you are alive to spend it.

The structure

A contract runs a fixed term and pays 95 per cent of the total on completion, as a single lump sum. In the meantime you draw 1.3 per cent a year.

The stated justification is that the Guard already provides everything: your quarters, your meals, your medical care, your safety. You have nothing to spend it on, so it is held for you. The real reason is that the Guard is the only employer in the galaxy worth the name, and nobody has anywhere else to go.

It matters enormously whether it is your first

A man on his first contract has never been paid. Everything he has earned is a number held somewhere else, and it stays a number until the day the term closes. A man on his second or third has already been through it once. The first contract cleared, the money is his, and everything since has been on top of that.

Which sorts the establishment into two groups that do not understand each other at all. Ask a Spec Ops sergeant what he is worth and he will tell you, because he has seen it land. Ask a first-term rifleman and he will tell you what he was promised.

What that looks like in hand

A Spec Ops captain's contract is worth about 110,000 credits a year, untaxed, because no member world has the standing to assess a Guard contract and the Guard does not assess itself. Over a full term that is a fortune. What actually reaches him each year, before completion, is roughly the price of a good coat.

So the money is real, and it is also a rumour. It exists as a number in the accounting division, and it becomes yours on one specific day and not a day earlier.

What is not held back

Whatever you retain at a cleared objective under Standing Order 41 is yours immediately, is entered nowhere, and men at that level do not lose much of what they pick up. The Guard is entirely comfortable with this. A soldier with a bag of somebody else's gold is a soldier who is not asking about his balance, and a soldier holding stolen property is a soldier who cannot easily complain about anything.

What it looks like from the other side of the ledger

A single Spec Ops operation ends a criminal system, or takes a cartel principal, or hands control of a whole sector to somebody who will pay for it. The Guard books that against 110,000 a year, most of which it is still holding.

A million credits over a decade, against what a decade of that produces, is not generosity. It is the best purchase in the accounts.

Getting it out

For the ranks that matter, payment is clean and fast, because those are the men the Guard intends to keep.

For everybody else it is a process. The sum is not large to begin with, perhaps sixty thousand for a full term in a clerical grade, and it does not arrive as a lump sum. It arrives in instalments, against forms, to a confirmed mailing address, which must be a fixed address on a member world, which a man who has spent four years aboard a ship does not have. Each instalment requires the previous one to have cleared. Each form requires a countersignature from a department that answers correspondence quarterly.

Nobody is refusing to pay. That is the elegance of it. Every step is legitimate and every step takes eleven weeks, and a surprising number of people simply stop filing.

And the term that follows from it

Note what the payment schedule rewards. The contract costs the Guard almost nothing until the day it ends, and everything on the day it ends. Which means the cheapest possible outcome, for a man in his final months, is one where the day never comes.

Nothing about that is personal. It is arithmetic, done on paper, by people who have never met him. That is the part that should worry you.

Guard quarters

One room, one bed, one door, and the same box for everybody at that level.

Spec Ops personnel get a single cabin to themselves. Not a suite, not a set of rooms, and a captaincy does not enlarge it. Offered upgraded quarters on the top floor or beside the Captain's Club, at least one man has turned both down on the grounds that everything he owns fits in a backpack.

What the rooms differ in is everything else.

One of them is empty on purpose

Immaculate, organised past the point of tidiness and into starkness. Nothing on the walls. A bed made properly every morning. A functional desk. Two plants on the windowsill under the soft glow of a lamp, which are the only living things in the room and are kept alive with the same discipline as everything else.

On the desk there is a grey stone off a colony road, which for years sat there in solitude, and for a few weeks sat beside a small velvet box. That is the whole inventory. A man can live in a room for eight years and leave nothing in it that would tell you his name.

The closet holds a crisp blue polo with the trident on the chest. Behind the door, on a bad week, an astrovin bottle with a few inches left in it, and black paint on the desk from a helmet repainted by hand at three in the morning.

One of them is full

Same cabin, same dimensions, same standard-issue bed.

Strands of light snake along the walls, flickering between blue and purple and green. Stolen and scavenged logos hang as faint holographic projections. A ceiling projector turns a slow aurora across the ceiling in violet and emerald, and the floor shifts colour under every step. The lighting is dim, and all of it is deliberate.

The shelves are a museum of Standing Order 41: defunct pistols with cracked barrels, scavenged gears, gold chains, battle-worn foreign helmets, and a few dented ashtrays still dusted with redleaf. There is an enormous beanbag in one corner. The whole room smells of synthetic flowers doing a poor job of covering the earthy musk of redleaf smoke, which has got into the furniture and is not coming out.

Cluttered, but lived in. Messy, but intentional.

The room the team gathers in is the second one. Nobody ever decided that either.

Guard rank structure

An ordinary army ladder, with two things bolted onto it that are not ordinary at all.

Privates at the bottom, sergeants in the middle doing the actual work, captains and colonels above them, and the Board of Directors at the top where the ladder stops being a ladder and becomes a company.

The ship exception

Command a vessel of a certain class and you may be rated a Commodore, which sounds naval and grand and sits at roughly the same height as a captain of infantry. It exists because the Guard absorbed several fleets that already had the word and found it cheaper to keep it than to argue.

The exception that matters

You can leave the ladder and re-enter it at the bottom.

A soldier accepted into special operations comes in as a Special Operations Private. It is the lowest rank in that arm and everybody starts there, whatever they were before.

And a Special Operations Private outranks a captain.

What that actually buys

Not the right to do as you please. Something narrower and stranger: nobody stops you. You are not asked where you are going, or why you are on that deck, or what is in the case. Doors that require a reason for other people do not require one from you. It is a privileged freedom rather than an unlimited one, and it is the single most valuable thing the Guard gives anybody, because it cannot be bought and it does not appear on any pay schedule.

Which is why a promotion to captain, for a man already inside special operations, is a smaller event than it looks from outside.

Guard rations

What you eat when you are not in the dining hall, which is most of the time.

The good one

Meal 25, the Brellovine pasta kit. It heats properly, it tastes like something a person made, and it is the currency of every field kitchen in the Guard. Men will trade three of anything for one.

The other ones

The Tipa sandwich, which is fine, which is the most anybody has ever said about it. Frozen guomo sticks. And the protein wafer: dry, nearly flavourless, sold by the sleeve at every commissary, and the single most stolen item in the establishment.

The wafers are not stolen because anybody wants them. They are stolen because they are the easiest thing to take, and because a cadet who hands them out behind a latrine wall to four other children is not distributing food. He is distributing the fact that he did something.

Off the supply chain

Anywhere with a market, the good stuff is local: rockroot by the sack, glazberries, spice bundles tied with string, weeflowers for somebody's wife, charcandies for somebody's children. Yinmelon sauce comes in a can heavy enough that nobody picks one up expecting it to be light.

And what a colony eats

Seared tofu. Mashed rockroot. Spireleafs on the side, which no child on any world has ever finished voluntarily.

Guard training

There are two of these and they are not the same experience at all.

The short one

Sixteen-year-olds off poor worlds with no schooling behind them and no particular aptitude in front of them, run through in the minimum time the schedule allows. They are taught to hold a rifle, follow an order, and stand where they are put. It is ordinary infantry training and it produces ordinary infantry, and the Guard needs a great many of them and is not pretending otherwise.

Before either of them, the Scout Corps

A summer programme for cadets with nowhere to go between academic years. Which is to say: for orphans.

They clean their uniforms and their bunks until the whole billet smells of starch and metal polish, pack a bag, and march across country in formation. Rain or shine. Some days they fire at distant targets, and the cheer when somebody actually hits one is louder than the rifle was. When it rains, the drumming on the ponchos makes the world feel far away and almost safe. When the heat is bad they pass canisters between them like contraband.

Thirty minutes a night are set aside for writing letters home. Most of the children draw, or scrawl messages from families they have invented. Nobody comes to collect the post.

They are not beds, only frame cots and thin mats, and it does not matter, because the insects outside hum like a lullaby and every child there is tired enough to forget what is supposed to come next.

It is where most of them meet the first friend they ever have.

The long one, which is most of the establishment and everything above it.

Sleep deprivation as a working condition rather than an incident. Being told, continuously and by people who are good at saying it, that you are nothing. Physical work past the point where the body has stopped cooperating. And the arrangement that does the actual damage: at every hour of it there is an invitation to stop, and no mechanism that lets you.

You can want to quit as much as you like. Wanting is free. There is nowhere to hand the wanting in.

That is the whole design. They are not trying to find out whether you can be made to want to leave, because everybody can. They are trying to find out what you do for eleven more weeks once you do.

Afterwards

Nobody who came out of it discusses it much, and the people who came out of the short one are aware that there was another door.

Guardnet

The network being built to replace the one that died, and it is not going quickly.

It carries the credit ledger, service records, licensing and official traffic. It does not carry public communication and was never meant to. If you want to send a letter to someone three systems away you still use a courier ship or a church-owned radio tower, the same as everybody has for sixty years.

Coverage is continuous through the inner member worlds, patchy past them, and absent on forty-four member worlds and every non-member world in existence.

That map matters more than anything else about it. Money is a ledger entry now, and the ledger lives here. Where the network reaches, you have savings. Where it does not, you have a promise.

Hada Mariner

Long service, clean record, and a retirement date.

Three years on the same flight line with the same four people, and the most competitive of them by a distance. She had been working a barrel roll for a while and landed it, and was told at the bar that she had finally landed it, and did not let that stand.

At the bar she takes the seat next to whoever is sitting on their own. She reads a situation fast, says the useful thing rather than the kind one, and offers, unprompted, to wingman.

She is going to Maldo, to one of the ex-Guard communities there, on a square with ornate geometric stonework that she has apparently described to people more than once.

Maldo is the old Royal capital: a city built out of a used-up world, which stopped making anything a long time ago and is now a nice old town that people retire to and take souvenirs from. A person spends a career on a ship that never stops moving and picks somewhere that has already finished.

The Halgo family

Maspin locals near the Trailblazer base, and the household the medevac dispatcher guesses first.

Nothing about them is on record except that. When a call comes in from that stretch of country, the voice on the other end says, without checking anything:

"Is it the Halgo family again?"

Which tells you the shape of them without a single name. Somebody in that house is always doing something. It has been going on long enough that a bored woman on a radio has stopped needing to look it up.

The High Castle

The crown's house on Shayron. Four wings around a court, raised across two centuries in four separate building campaigns, none of which matched the last.

The bones of it are Maldo steel, shipped in from the old capital while that world still had an industry. The eastern towers are the oldest section standing and carry more of the original metal than anything else in the building.

That matters more than it sounds. Maldo ore is worked out. There is no more of that steel anywhere, so every repair since has been made in some other alloy that does not quite match, and the maintenance records track the building as a falling percentage of itself.

The court and the western wing open to the public eleven days a year. The rest is the household's.

The High Council

The senior ministers, the service chiefs, and the heads of the great houses, sitting on Maldo. Ordinarily they advise. They do not legislate and they do not command.

Except

The High Emergency Council Act says that if the sovereign proclaims an emergency, everything the crown and parliament hold passes to this Council.

The Act is precise about the proclamation and precise about the transfer. It says nothing about how long it lasts, how it ends, who reviews it, or what would revoke it. Parliament on Maldo has noticed this out loud four times, most recently in GC 4438, and amended it none.

And the geography

The Act moves power to a body sitting on Maldo. The sovereign proclaims from Shayron. Those are not in the same system.

It has never been invoked.

Holocloaks

Not invisibility. Something worse to be on the wrong end of.

Activated from the gauntlet, the armour's contours dissolve into a rippling distortion and the light bends around the wearer. What is left is a whisper of heat-shimmer moving across a landscape, indistinguishable from the landscape unless you already know to look.

What gives it away

Footprints. The system does not hide the ground, and on ash or sand or snow the prints are perfectly visible for as long as it takes the wind to take them. Standing still, a man in a holocloak is a rumour. Moving, he is a trail.

The gauge

There is a power meter on the gauntlet and it is the only thing that matters. It runs down fast, it does not recover in the field, and every operator who has ever worn one has spent the entire approach doing arithmetic against it.

Restricted issue, and not manufactured anywhere the archive can name.

House Polaris

The family that took a star's name, and now owns what grows under it.

They were working that system a thousand years before they were royal. The oldest instruments are commercial and show a family adopting the name of the sun they happened to be under. They have not held land there in a very long time and they hold the licence on everything the system produces.

Royalty on the Polaris harvest last year: 411,880,600 credits. That is more than the entire assessed revenue of nine member worlds.

The bit that bothers people

The star, the system, the shared calendar across ten inhabited bodies, and the family collecting on all of it carry the same word. Nobody in the breadbasket can name the sun that feeds them without naming the house that owns the shelf it sits on.

Out on the moons the older common word for the sun is still in use in daily speech. It appears in no contract, no ledger and no filing, and three separate people told us the same thing about it: you do not use it in front of buyers.

Household crowning

The couple are crowned. Not figuratively.

The rite

Two crowns, held above the heads of the pair or set on them outright, and from that moment they are sovereign over their own household. It is stated in exactly those terms. Their home is their territory, their decisions within it are theirs, and no one outside it holds authority there.

The crowns themselves are usually family property, worn by a great many heads across a great many generations, and are frequently not worth very much.

Why it works where it works

On worlds where an actual crown sits an hour's walk away in an actual palace, the rite is not modest. It is a claim. Every married couple on that world has been sovereign of something, briefly, in front of witnesses, and the distance between them and the family in the castle is a matter of scale rather than of kind.

Nobody in authority has ever objected, because objecting would require saying out loud what the objection is.

And there is a joke in it that the Royals do not always hear

The house that holds the throne came up from metalworkers. The galaxy's most exalted family and the couple crowned in a kitchen with two dented heirlooms are, at the origin, in the same trade.

Housing

Buying is the easy part. Keeping the roof on is the problem.

There is no galactic housing system and there never was. Some worlds run housing blocks. Some worlds you can buy a house outright for very little. Some worlds bury the whole business in paperwork and some have none at all. The honest answer to how a person gets a home is the answer it has always been: you get a job, and you get a bad house or a good one.

What is different here is that a building is not a thing you own. It is a thing you are maintaining, against a supply chain that no longer exists.

The structure is fine. Structures last. It is the regulator, the seal, the pump, the coupling, the part in the middle of the thing, and none of it is made any more. It comes out of salvage or pre-war stock or it does not come at all, and a person can spend nineteen consecutive quarters filing correct requests for a part that is simply gone.

So the shape of a home is the shape of its repairs

Patched roofs. A window that was replaced with something that was not a window. Improvised fittings, done well, by somebody who apprenticed for a year and worked the rest out. Whole streets where every house has the same failure at a different stage.

And a world can lose

Not to a war or a disaster. Just to arithmetic, quietly, over decades, as the parts run out faster than they can be found, until the roofs are open and there are cathedrals with weather coming through them and children being taught properly in a building that is losing.

Crowded apartments, everywhere, on nearly every world. Busy-crowded rather than desperate-crowded. People manage.

Hoverboards

Everybody knows what one is. Everybody has seen one. Nobody can build one.

The repulsor assembly came out of factories that no longer exist, and the design is well understood in the sense that engineers can explain exactly how it works and cannot produce the part. Surviving boards get repaired and traded and the price goes up every single year.

Saigo has tried to rebuild them four times and abandoned it four times. The programme reports are unusually honest about why.

Humanist supremacy

That humans are a superior order of thing, that spreading through the stars is theirs by right, and that whatever was done to get here needed no excuse.

It is not a religion anyone joins

There is no body, no clergy, no rite, no text, no register. There is nothing to sign.

It is also the single most widely expressed belief in this volume. It turns up unprompted in testimony from every human world we have surveyed, almost always from people who would tell you flatly that they hold no religious position of any kind.

How it sounds

Recorded word for word, on worlds with no contact with one another: that we are a near-perfect design. That the stars were left for us. That whatever happened, it got us here.

Nobody teaches it and nobody argues with it

No institution in this archive professes it. No institution in this archive contradicts it. Guard educational material describes human achievement in terms we have difficulty telling apart from the doctrine, and files it under history.

Humans

Four out of every five people alive. Present on every inhabited world in this volume except eleven.

Where from

Wake, by general account, on the strength of pre-war genetic sampling that we have the conclusions of and not the method. The technique is lost, so the finding cannot be checked, and at least one very populous world rejects it outright. That is why this entry is filed as contested and not because the question is genuinely open.

Colour does not matter here

Human populations vary continuously in colouring, height and feature, everywhere, and no world in this archive organises status around it. No statute anywhere in our holdings mentions it. Every planet is mixed and nobody thinks about it.

What humans sort each other by instead is world, bloodline, profession and service, and those they enforce, sometimes at law. A Modanicker will not let you hold municipal office. Katanzaria will not give you standing without lineage. Marfeld will not call you a man until you have walked into the country alone.

The word

Crag, for anyone who is not human, is a human coinage in general human use, and it is universal for exactly the reason the first line of this entry gives. When four fifths of everyone is one thing, that thing stops noticing itself.

Hyperspace slipstream

You do not go to the place. The place is brought to you.

That is not a metaphor and it is how every navigational primer in the galaxy opens. A vessel under slipstream does not cross the distance; the space behind it is drawn toward it, and the ship arrives without ever having travelled. What the crew experience is the g-force slamming them into their seats, the stars outside stretching first to white streaks and then to a rush of blue, and then a lurch.

Aboard, it is just the hypercharge

A gauge climbing toward a hundred while somebody reads the number out loud, because on a small vessel the difference between seventy per cent and ninety-nine is the difference between an argument and an escape.

The drives

Seven classes in service. Anything above class four is on the unreplaceable schedule, which means what exists is what exists and there is no facility left anywhere that knows how to build another. Classes one through four are still made, at three plants, at a rate that does not keep up with the ships being lost.

Which is the quiet fact underneath every schedule in this volume: the galaxy is getting slower, by a little, every year, and has been for decades.

The lanes

Every route on record died with everything else. The ones in use now were re-flown by hand over about thirty years by crews going out into unsurveyed dark to find out whether it worked. The survey authority publishes what that cost. It is a long document.

And some volumes you do not enter

The schedules carry standing advisories against transit of certain regions. Reasons are given for most of them.

Indentured servitude

Working off a debt. Legal everywhere, including on the worlds that advertise themselves as slave-free.

The distinction that makes it lawful is that you are not owned. You owe. The debt can be one you took on, one somebody assigned to you, one you inherited, or one a court handed you instead of a prison sentence.

How you get out

You do not get paid, so the debt comes down by the value of your labour at a rate somebody else sets. We looked at eighty-eight indenture registers. In sixty-one of them the instrument does not state the rate at all.

Recorded terms run from eleven months to thirty-one years. The middle of that is nine.

Who runs it

Whoever the local authority is. On Maspin that is the Council of Riflo, whose own registers show indentured people assigned to households belonging to sitting councillors, written down plainly in the ordinary column, because nothing requires anyone to hide it.

What the Guard says

That it is going to be ended, and that the priority is first finishing membership and building a uniform register, after which measures will follow. That position has been published in materially identical words in GC 4429, 4437, 4448 and 4459.

The Ivory Guards

The ceremonial line on Shayron, and the most photographed soldiers in the galaxy.

Pristine ivory armour. Long ceremonial coats that fall past the knee. Helmets built tall enough to add most of a head, kept immaculate, and never once seen with a scuff on them.

They stand exactly fifty metres apart. Not roughly. Every gap on the approach is the same gap, and the sameness is doing the work: a line of men that regular reads as a fact about the place rather than a decision anyone made.

Whether they can fight is a question nobody asks, which is the point.

J.LOT

A belt formation with nothing in it worth having: no settlement, no licence, nothing to mine.

What it does have is rock, in quantity, at speed, in a pattern that makes flying through it fast a genuinely stupid idea. The navigational schedules carry a standing advisory against powered transit at speed.

It appears in the Guard's disciplinary returns eighty-eight times in eleven years, always as the location, always in a charge about unauthorised use of a vessel. Young pilots have been doing this for as long as there have been young pilots.

Jax Sheel

The pilot. Officially one of twelve attached to the platoon. In practice, when Castle Team goes anywhere, Jax flies them.

Wavy raven-black hair and a thick, well-kept moustache that has no business on a face that young. The Guard runs clean-shaven almost everywhere, exemptions take months of argument, and his was simply never challenged. It is a small, cheerful act of not conforming and it suits him completely.

He came into the team through Yake, trains with the twelve, and drinks with the five. Nobody has ever formally decided he is a member of Castle Team and everybody treats him as one.

Before that

He served a custodial sentence and worked it off underground, cutting magnetic ore at one of the two installations that take most of that labour. The conviction does not survive scrutiny and the file does not pretend very hard. He was an embarrassment somebody wanted somewhere quiet, and he had no standing to say so.

He does not bring it up. It is in the record, which is a different thing from being known.

Steady in the air and warm on the ground. He is the one who talks, without making it heavy, about having been pulled out of his own lowest patch by people who bothered.

Jimzon Avaris

also: Jim · Jimzy · Jimz · Jimmy · Jimzo · Jimbo · Jizzbo · Jizzin

Twenty-six. Spec Ops Staff Sergeant, and the man the rest of Castle Team follows without anyone ever having decided that.

Short brown hair. Stubble he never quite gets on top of. He thinks he looks like nobody in particular, and he is wrong about how much that is true.

Two marks he cannot walk past a mirror without finding. His nose was broken in a fistfight that got away from everybody and set crooked, because nobody thought to have it fixed. There is a thin burn line across his left cheek where the hair does not grow, from too much to drink, a handful of fireworks and the certainty of being twenty and finished with the Academy. Nobody else notices either one.

His armour is black and deliberately unshined, with a blue visor. He paints it himself, by hand, every time.

He wears glasses some of the time, and there is no pattern to when.

His right ear does not always work. He mentions it once, to a stranger, as an explanation for not having heard something, and then moves straight on. Nobody who has known him for years has ever raised it.

What he gets called

Everyone who likes him has a different name for him and not one of them agreed with any other.

Jimzy is the colony name. Two people used it and both of them were on that rock: his mother, pointing at a star and telling him it was where he was born, and the neighbour with the sweets. Nobody has called him that since he was eight.

Jim comes from the people who knew him before he was anybody, and it is what he gets in the sentences that are about to be difficult. Jimz is his own team, and it is the one used when somebody has noticed he has gone quiet. Jimmy is the radio.

And then there is Calsco Fritt, who has called him Jimzo, Jimbo, Jizzbo and Jizzin, on four separate occasions, and has not once used the right one. He waits every time for the correction. It has never come.

A promotion to Captain is sitting on somebody's desk. He failed officer school once already, years ago, and has not mentioned that in a while.

Where he is from, and where he is from

Born on Modanick and has never once set foot on it. What he knows about his own birthworld is a bedtime story his mother told him: always warm, always daytime, trees taller than houses. She was describing a place she had loved as a student to a boy sitting on a rock, and she made it better than it is.

He grew up on the Corefuel colony in the wreckage of Wake, where his father ran the station. The family was two months from moving to Creta.

What he carries

A grey stone he picked up on the colony road when he was seven. He has had it ever since and it is smooth because he rubs it. His mother's Royal service pistol, cleaned since he was old enough to be shown how. A gold holowatch, a gift from a general, shined and with an audible tick to it. An engagement ring in a velvet box that has not been opened in front of anybody.

What he is like

Impulsive to the point of recklessness, and funnier in private than anyone outside the team would believe. Table impressions, at length, standing on the furniture. A napkin moustache and a captain they all served under once. A microwave that went out of a window. He reads his own silence as steadiness and does not notice that everyone around him reads it as absence.

He is casually bigoted about non-humans in the ordinary, unexamined way of somebody raised where he was raised, and he is unthinkingly kind to children, and he would be embarrassed to have either one pointed out.

He also uses Crag the way everyone he grew up with uses it, and thinks nothing about it at all.

Johnny Plasma

The man who founded the Guard, who never existed.

The story: after the war, one man with no rank and no property walked from world to world settling quarrels, facing down warlords, teaching people how to keep order, and moving on without taking payment. He founded the Guard and refused every office in it. In most versions he is still out there walking.

Nobody believes it

Not the children who are taught it, not the instructors teaching it. Everybody knows. It is in the standard curriculum at two points and it is universal across the member worlds anyway.

Why bother

Because the alternative is the incorporation instrument, which survives, and names nine actual founders: four generals of armies that no longer existed and five men with money in shipping, insurance and salvage.

A founding myth makes you a nation. That document makes you a company.

Karagash

A Gashi bounty hunter, and the most reasonably priced frightening thing in the sector.

Seven feet. Strong through the shoulders and the arms without any of the bulk that usually comes attached, so the size does not register properly until he is standing next to something you know the height of. His hand closes on a wrist like a vise closing, and he is fast in a way that people who have watched it are not able to describe afterwards without their voice changing.

The face

He wears a mask across the lower half of it, a breathing apparatus rather than a disguise, and it has been there long enough that the shape of him without it is not a thing many people have seen. Above it, gold and black eyes with no pupil anybody has ever managed to find. You can tell exactly when he looks at something, because the light comes off them differently when they move.

The rest

Black suits, cut for a human frame and made to fit his, and he wears them well. A bandolier across the chest, which is not strictly necessary and is clearly a thing he enjoys. And ginger hair, deep and well combed and frankly gorgeous, which on a Gashi is normal and on a seven-foot masked man in a black suit is the detail people bring up first.

The work

He hunts for hire. He is extremely good at it and he does not extend mercy, and he is also not angry, ever, about any part of it. The two usually travel together and in him they simply do not. He takes the job, states the price, does the job, collects, and wishes you a good one.

Nobody knows why he went into this line rather than one of the ten thousand respectable ones a Gashi is expected to want. There is speculation and none of it is worth repeating. The likeliest answer is the one that never gets proposed, which is that he tried it and liked it.

And one detail nobody can account for

He works out of a spool of equipment carried at the hip. On the single occasion anybody got a proper look at what came off it, it was a length of green rubber garden hose, torn out of a wall spigot by hand and still clumped with wet dirt.

He offered no explanation. He was not asked twice.

He is, for what it is worth, modestly priced.

Kaspian

Maspin name: Kadam

Older than the species that names him, and older than the one that made it.

What he was

One of the people who lived on Wake before humans, back when it was a world and not a debris field. His remains went down with it: a skull, somewhere under what used to be the mantle, now scattered with the rest of it across a stretch of empty sky.

What he is

A skull pulled up out of desert sand, wreathed in a thin purple flame that defines its edges rather than consuming them. Lightning comes down to it slowly, like honey rather than a strike, and the sound it makes is a ceremonial drum instead of thunder. A translucent body of shifting starlight phases into place around it, tall and unhurried, with two points of gold where the eyes belong.

On Maspin they call him Kadam, and he is carved into the great gold doors of the Palace of Riflo: an elongated figure hovering just off the ground, arms out, handing a small burning sun down to the Maspins kneeling below. It is a copy of something much older, polished and re-gilded by every generation that inherits it.

Ask a Maspin what it means and you get knowledge, or power, or a shrug. Ask a shaman where they learned what they know, and the answer is him. Ask whether he is real, and even they are not sure.

The name is not his

Asked what he is called, he says he has never had a name in the sense other people have them, and that his people are called Kaspian. Everybody since has used it as though it were his, including this volume, because there has never been anything else to use.

One line is recorded

Nobody has been able to tell us what it refers to.

The queen will return to many moons.

Katanzaria

Stone terraces, long tables, wine, and a monumental architecture raised on foundations nobody here laid. Governed by chieftains. Insists, officially and generally, that its people did not come from Wake.

The disagreement

Katanzaria holds that its people grew here and are related to nobody. The pre-war genetic surveys we hold in summary place them inside the human range with no distinguishing marker at all. Both are printed. They cannot both be right.

There is a complication, and it is not a resolution. Katanzaria does have ruins older than its settlement, built in a way its own masons did not use and cannot copy, and a great deal of what stands here stands on them. That the ruins are not human is established. That the people are not human is not.

Honour, which is not a decoration

What is said about you after you die is the working currency of public life here, and the world's institutions are shaped around that. Katanzaria keeps the most complete civil registry in this archive, running eleven centuries, because a name is an asset and assets are recorded.

Succession

Chieftains, not kings. A title passes within a family but not by birth order: a brother, a cousin or a nephew may take it, and the recorded test is whether the family will be provided for. Alongside the martial component there is an electoral one, and titles have demonstrably moved by each.

Duelling

Recognised in statute, restricted by it, and much rarer in the record than in conversation. Twenty-two registered in the last century. Informants describe considerably more.

Kaz

A bounty hunter, and a voice giving orders in a room the record does not describe.

The trade he is in is an old one and a legal one in most of the places it operates, which is why it has stayed as big as it has. Somebody wants a person found, the price is agreed, and no part of the arrangement requires anybody to explain themselves to a government. There are Guard warrants that get worked this way. There are also plenty that do not.

Of Kaz specifically there is very little: no world, no species, no description, no list of jobs. He works with at least one other person, whom he addresses by name and does not appear to entirely trust.

Kelsadria Vot Feentor-Jayzin

goes by: Kelsa

A pilot with Nova Squadron, and the most organised person in any room she is in.

Pale blonde, worn up in a bun nearly always. Very fit, in the unremarkable way of somebody who does the work and does not discuss it. Striking eyes, and they are never idle: there is always something going on behind them, and it usually arrives on her face a second before she decides whether to say it.

She reads stern for about a minute. She is not. She laughs softly and easily once she has decided you are worth the trouble, and after that she is one of the most expressive people on the flight line.

Underneath, behind the ears, it is dyed a soft light purple. Pinned up in a hurry you might catch a streak of it. Down, which is almost never, it is the whole story.

Royal blood, thinly. House Feentor, Jayzin line, which is the kind of descent half the galaxy can claim: it comes with a seat, a small maintenance, and no money worth the name. She has never drawn either.

Sansvor

She grew up in a beautiful ruin. Gaslamp streets, cathedrals and libraries still standing with the roofs open to the sky, museums nobody catalogues, art nobody looks at, and weather coming in through the gaps. She went to school in something like a bombed-out palace with eight other children in it. The teachers were good. The building was losing.

Every adult around her had a theory about what the world should become. None of them had a roof.

So she wanted a roof. She heard a teacher had flown in the war, got her licence, and joined the Guard for a pension and citizenship for her family on a world where things get fixed. Not patriotism. Arithmetic.

She dumps her shots on the floor at the bar and pulls the disgusted face along with everybody else. She sings karaoke under protest and then sings it properly.

Disciplined, methodical, always with a plan and a fallback. The exact inverse of the man she was going to marry, which is why it worked when it worked: she kept him from flying off the handle and he got her out of her own head. When it stopped working, his unpredictability left her with nothing to stand on and her need to know what came next started to feel like pressure.

She said it out loud once, testing how it sounded: Kelsa Avaris. I like the sound of that. He never gave her the ring. It is still in the box.

Her enlistment ends within the year.

Kelton

One city on the whole world, and beyond it small towns and a great deal of empty ground. Nothing edible is produced here.

What the city makes is the promise that a harvest will be bought, stored, insured and delivered, and the paperwork that makes the promise enforceable. The exchange, the seed registry, the water allocation office, the quarantine authority, forty-one embassies and every insurer writing agricultural risk in the system are all inside it.

Crop laboratories

1,188 registered variant lines, developed here rather than on the worlds that grow them. Licence revenue for GC 4461: 96,440,200 credits.

The arrangement

A farmer on Weton may plant what she likes, harvest it, and sell it. Water, seed, storage, milling, shipping and sale each require an instrument issued in this city.

Everything that decides what happens to the food is in here: the exchange, the harvest ledger, the licensing office, the seed registry, the water allocation desk, quarantine, the port, the crop laboratories, forty-one embassies, and every insurer writing agricultural risk in the system.

King Matthew

The reigning King of the Royal systems, and the man giving the address at the Queen's Anniversary for the fourth year running.

He holds the ordinary powers of the crown, and one that is not ordinary at all. He alone can proclaim an emergency under the High Emergency Council Act, and on that proclamation everything the crown and parliament hold passes to the High Council sitting on Maldo.

The Act says how the powers go across. It does not say for how long, how they come back, or who reviews it. This has been raised in parliament four times and amended none.

It has never been invoked.

Kinton

Fruit, and the geography of who gets it fresh.

Warm, wet, and green all the way round, with forty-one named varieties on the export list and a grading system that Kinton takes far more seriously than anybody buying does.

The distinction that matters

Kinton fruit reaches the inner member worlds fresh. It reaches the outer ones as preserve. That is the entire difference between the centre of the galaxy and the edge of it, expressed in whether your fruit is wet or in a jar, and it is visible in the freight schedules and in nothing else anybody would think to look at.

Which is why a piece of fresh Kinton fruit, on a rock in the middle of nowhere, is not really fruit. It is somebody having gone to a great deal of trouble. Guard supply crews carry them out to the far colonies and hand them to children, and those children remember the colour of them for the rest of their lives.

Kitalia

They saw the water coming and they built above it. Pylons driven two kilometres to the seabed, and cities standing on top of them, and no land in use anywhere on the world.

The engineering

A glacial melt they could see coming two centuries out, and an answer that worked. This is the most completely documented infrastructure in the archive, because the works were financed from offworld and the financiers wanted certification at every stage: seabed surveys, weld schedules, inspection intervals, unit costs, all of it.

Foundations run 1,180 to 2,340 metres. Design load 4.1 million tonnes. Certified to 260 knots sustained. They are, by every measure we can apply, magnificent.

Living on one

Dense and vertical, because there is no outward. The platform is the civic unit: your roll, your rate, your school, your council. There is no countryside and no farming of any consequence, and the whole arrangement rests on the assumption that the structure holds.

Population by platform

Not filed anywhere. Each platform kept its own roll, on itself.

Burial

There is no ground. What Kitalians do instead is done over water, and is catalogued separately.

The Kitalia Platform Collapse

Loss of one platform city, Kitalia, GC 4461. The structure entered the water. It was not recovered and has not been raised.

The structure

INTACT. Commissioned GC 4388. Foundation depth 1,610 metres across 214 pylons. Design load 4.1 million tonnes. Certified storm tolerance 260 knots sustained. Last full inspection GC 4459, passed without qualification. Construction cost 1,204,000,000 credits. Insured value at loss 1,411,000,000 credits, settled in full.

Cause

Charges at the pylon heads, placed by cells operating on the world. The Guard investigated, identified four cells, and cleared them out. What this archive holds is the summary; the working material behind it was never released, which is ordinary.

The dead

Not established. The platform roll was held on the platform.

The Restoration's estimate is inferred from the structure and not from the population, there being no surviving record of the population. Taking certified residential floor area against the mean occupancy density returned for comparable platforms in the last decennial survey, the figure falls between 9,000 and 26,000 persons. We publish the method with the number because the number is a guess.

There is no rubble field. There are no recovered remains. The register of missing persons compiled by the surviving platform administrations is open and is still receiving entries.

[Compiler's note: we can tell you what the structure cost to the credit. We cannot tell you how many people were standing on it.]

Korjin Avaris

Chemist, engineer, and the man who worked out how to turn the core of a dead planet into fuel.

He invented the Corefuel synthesis process. Everything that flies, anywhere, runs on the back of what he did in a workshop on a rock, and the licence was signed over to the Guard for a consideration of one credit.

He ran the extraction station in the Wake field himself. He knew everyone on the colony, he called them by name, and he worked the same hours they did.

What he was like at the end

Triumphant. He hit quota, called the entire settlement off work, and ordered a festival for two days later. He had a wife he was plainly still delighted by and two sons, one of whom did not live past five.

His younger boy asked him, that night, for a spaceship. He did not hesitate for even a moment.

"Even a spaceship. We're gonna get you one."

His contract paid on completion of the full year's quota and not a tonne before, which is how these contracts are always written.

The family was two months from moving to Creta.

Korno

Where things get made, and where engineers go when they are done being shot at.

Not a beautiful world. Grey skies most of the year, low workshops running to the edge of every town, and the constant background sound of small precise machinery. What Korno does is components: the brackets, couplings, regulators and fittings that every other world needs and nobody else can be bothered to fabricate to tolerance.

The apprentice register is the largest single document the planet keeps, and it is the reason people come. Sign on, and a Guard engineering division takes you for a term with a real workshop and a real instructor. It has run under a standing arrangement for thirty-odd years and it works, which makes it almost unique.

That is the shape of the Korno dream, and it is a modest one. A workshop, a bench, a trade, and nobody shooting at you. There are men in the Guard right now counting the months.

Lerroni

Warm water, cheap rooms, and eleven days a year when it is the loudest place in the galaxy.

The coast is the whole economy. Long shallow bays, sand that goes on for miles, bars built out of whatever washed up, and an entire service industry that exists to separate very young people from money they have just been paid.

The eleven days

Lerroni's arrival figures are flat all year and then vertical. Four hundred thousand people in a week and a half, and the peak lines up exactly with the Guard Academy recess, because of course it does.

For most Guardsmen it is the first place they ever went that nobody ordered them to. Which is why grown men still say the name with a particular tone, and why somebody, somewhere, is always trying to get a ship pointed back at it.

The name is also, for reasons nobody has adequately explained, extremely difficult for some people to pronounce.

Liles Ninzin

Old enough that his knees are a joke between the two of them. A general long enough to be respected, and now the one seat on the Guard's Board of Directors that is not a commercial interest.

He is the man who lifted the floorboard

He was on the patrol that reached the Wake colony after the raid, and he found a boy under his mother's body when everyone else had written the settlement off.

He and his then-girlfriend took the child in. They were barely out of college and doing what they could for someone with nowhere else to go. His eighth birthday was the first one he had with them: a small cake, a cheap dinner, and laughter that felt borrowed and was meant kindly.

They were always kind, and the kindness is what made the distance worse.

Now

He runs interference for Jimzon constantly and cannot say why in those words. He offers him a captaincy, quarters, a ship of his own. He refuses to authorise the hunt for the Nhaths, and then authorises it anyway, off the books, with leave time and no paper trail: I don't need proof that I gave this the OK.

He notices things. The bottom row of a man's medals in the wrong order, at a glance, across a room.

He is old enough now that his knees are a running joke between the two of them, and old enough to get nostalgic about the Battle of Rudcuff without noticing he is doing it, in the specific way of a man remembering the last time his job was simple.

What he says he wants, delivered like warmth:

"One day I'd like us both to be on the Director Board, together, away from the mess of combat."

He is on a board of seven where every member can be removed by the other six, and where nobody's dissent has ever been written down.

The little girl in the waiting room

A child in the medbay at Base Delta, with a puzzle in her lap, waiting for her father.

She looks up at whoever comes in, blinks, tilts her head, and crosses the room with the kind of confidence only children and fools have. Then she sits down opposite you, uninvited, and starts.

"Are you a clown?"

She is a hard audience. Told a joke, she does not laugh. Shown a costume flower that honks twice, she does not laugh at that either. Her mouth holds a perfect little frown.

Then she explains why she is there.

"My teacher told me my daddy lost his leg. He isn't here yet. My teacher said he walked on a mine." "Mommy was too."

Her father is a Trailblazer who stepped on a mine. Her mother was one.

"Daddy really likes his legs. I think he's probably sad now."

She will laugh, eventually, at a bad enough joke. How much do rainbows weigh? Not much, they are actually pretty light.

"I will, mister. You're a funny clown."

We do not have her name. We are not looking for it.

Magboots

They let you walk up a wall, and almost nobody has a pair.

Sleek, rose-gold, with pointed toes that look far too elegant for what they do. They hum faintly with every step and grip whatever ferrous surface they are set against, which means a man in magboots can climb the outside of a building at a walking pace, clink by clink, and step off the top of it as though he had come up a staircase.

Why they are rare

They are pre-war, and the manufacture died with everything else. What is in circulation is what survived. A pair is worth more than most people's contracts, they turn up mostly as loot, and their owners are extremely aware of both facts.

What they are actually used for

Not war, mostly. There is a wrecked starship the size of a city on a world nobody names, so thoroughly overgrown that people climb it like a mountain, and the steep sections of it are impossible without a pair. Fathers and sons have gone up it together for generations.

They do not like lightning. A storm will fry a pair permanently, and there is no repairing them, and no replacing them either.

Maldo

They did not build the capital on a beautiful world. They built it on a used-up one, out of the used-up world itself, and every ministry and monument here is made of the ground it stands on.

Five lives

An ordinary green world. Then ore, and a boom. Then a century of heavy industry that made the surface uninhabitable and the sky a colour people still describe. Then the ore ran out and everyone left. Then the crown arrived, because a ruin is free land and the material was already lying on site.

The city

Built in a documented order, and the building registers survive complete for all sixty-one years of it: capital, then parliament, then monuments, then embassies, then houses spreading outward from all four. 3,308 principal structures.

The catch

All of it is Maldo steel, and there is no more Maldo steel. The ore body is worked out. Every repair to a Royal building anywhere is made in some other alloy, and the maintenance you can walk a street and watch it happen, building by building, as less and less of what you are looking at is original.

Now

Population has fallen in each of the last four decennial returns. Working-age people leave; pensioners arrive. The largest single category of registered business on the world is the sale of antiques and reproductions to visitors.

The capital of a monarchy is a nice old town that people retire to and take souvenirs from.

Maldo steel

The metal the Royal systems are made of, and there is no more of it.

It came out of one world during one industrial century, and it is better than anything now in production: stronger, longer-lived, and with a surface finish that is the reason it got used for statues and railings as well as for beams.

Then the ore ran out.

Every palace, ministry, monument, embassy and lamp post the Royals have raised anywhere is built from a material that cannot be made again. Repairs go in with modern alloys that do not match and never will, and every Royal building is tracked as a slowly falling percentage of its original self.

Knock a wing down and you can rebuild it. You cannot rebuild it out of the same thing.

Marfeld

A world that never lost its big animals. Everywhere else hunted them out. Here they are still in the country, in numbers, and everything about how people live on Marfeld follows from that one fact.

Weather

Two months of heat that kills, two months of cold that kills, and the turn between them comes fast enough that people plan for it the way other worlds plan for a storm. Nothing grows reliably. The diet was a hunting diet for most of the world's history and the cooking still tastes like one.

Why the towns are the size they are

A settlement here has to be big enough to wall and small enough to move, because the predators come through on the season and a wall is a delay, not an answer. No town on Marfeld has ever exceeded forty thousand people. No city has ever existed. Nobody local finds this remarkable.

What they sell

Marfeld sells men. They appear in the muster rolls of every army in the surviving record, in every period, listed by name and settlement and rate of pay, because Marfeld has kept that book for eleven centuries and keeps it still. They are contracted as professionals and paid as professionals, and the world is quite clear that this is a trade and not a tragedy.

Guard recruiters have had a permanent office here since GC 4409. That is three years after the Guard existed and twenty-two before Marfeld joined it.

The bombing

Three times. The first took out the surface of half the northern continent during the war, and no target assessment held by this archive lists Marfeld in that sector at all. The second and third are catalogued as incidental to fighting between other parties.

Casualty figures for all three exist and disagree with one another by a factor of ten.

They rebuilt each time. Their own account of it is not grief and not defiance. It is closer to the way another world would talk about a bad winter.

[Compiler's note: we asked forty-one men from this world to describe the trial. Every one of them declined. Two apologised.]

The Marfeld beard

On Marfeld they say hair remembers.

The beard starts growing during the trial, because a boy out there has no way to stop it. When he comes back it is his, and what it is is a measurement: how long he was out, written on his face by his own body while it was happening.

You may trim it, shape it, braid it, dye it. Men do all of those and take real care over it.

You do not shave. Shaving is not a haircut on Marfeld and it is not a fashion choice. It is the renunciation of your family and your bloodline, and there is no lesser version of it. There is nothing in between.

Which is why Marfeld men in foreign service spend months arguing with grooming regulations rather than pick up a razor, and why a Marfeld man who is clean-shaven has either done something enormous or is not who he says he is.

One complication

The Royal court requires its household and its blood to go clean-shaven, by long ceremonial rule. Nobody has ever reconciled the two.

The Marfeld coming-of-age trial

At seventeen, a Marfeld boy is put out into the wild with his clothes and nothing else, for weeks.

He is not told beforehand what he is walking into. Not the season, not the country, not which of the three paths he is taking. Blood is the hunt, Root is the forage, Sky is the climb, and which one you get is not yours to choose.

Where it comes from

It used to be the first hunting season. You went out with a group, for months, and you came back with meat because the settlement needed the meat. What the modern version keeps is the exposure. What it removed is the group.

What people will tell you

Only the parts that happen to other people. Boys who drew winter and crossed frozen rivers on strips of bark. Boys who sewed hides around their feet to keep the toes. Summer, and the insects, and the blisters.

What nobody will tell you

Their own. No man who finishes the trial may speak of it, and the rule holds even between men who both went. It is absolute and it is kept.

We asked forty-one Marfeld men about it. All forty-one declined. Two of them apologised.

The original version killed boys. You do not talk about it because some of the ones who walked out with you did not walk back, and the ones who did came home carrying something they had no words for. The silence started as grief and hardened into a rule.

Marriage

There is no galactic marriage. There is a galactic filing, and then there are several hundred entirely unrelated things people actually do.

The one universal

On nearly every world, the legal marriage and the real one are different events, and only one of them is witnessed by anybody who matters.

The Guard needs a name on a tax filing. That is the whole of its interest. Everything else, the braid and the run and the pool and the day spent in blindfolds, happens somewhere else, in front of different people, and is the part anybody would tell you about if you asked them when they got married.

On occupied worlds this gap is not an accident. The occupier's ceremony is the one on paper. The other one is done quietly, at home, and is never mentioned to anyone in a uniform.

What the good ones have in common

The rites that travel, that survive an occupation, that get carried to a new world by refugees and still work there, all share at least one of four things:

  • The marriage is completed by a physical act rather than a spoken word. The seventh step. The ninth sip. The last seed. The closed circle. There is a moment everybody present can see, and either it happened or it did not.
  • The contract comes first and outranks the ceremony. The party is a party.
  • The legal and the true marriage are separate events, as above.
  • There is a visible exit, and everybody knows where it is.

Which direction the money moves tells you who is scarce. Some worlds pay the bride's family and some pay the groom's, and nobody involved thinks of it as demographics, and it is demographics.

A note on the war

Sixty years ago several hard-hit worlds passed emergency measures permitting plural households, on grounds that were entirely about arithmetic. Most were never repealed. They are now a fossil: perfectly legal, rare, mildly embarrassing on some worlds and proudly traditional on others. The Guard has no view, provided one name goes on the filing.

And a note on citizenship

Marriage into a member world is one of the two routes to Guard citizenship. The other is enlistment. Which means there is an entire category of marriage in this galaxy that is an immigration instrument, an entire office that audits them, and an unknown number of couples who started as paperwork and did not stay that way.

The marriage braid

You do not buy it. You grow it.

The rite

On marriage, a small braid is started in the hair and is never cut for as long as the marriage lasts. It can be hidden, tucked, kept tiny, or worn out where everybody can see it, and there is enormous variation in how: burned at the ends, dyed, beaded, wrapped in thread. What is constant is that it is braided extremely tight, and that keeping it is your job.

A neglected braid is a public statement, and everybody reads it as one.

Why it beats a ring

A ring tells you somebody is married. A braid tells you how long, because it has been growing the whole time. You can read a marriage across a room, in a market, at forty paces, without asking a single question.

The cut

Divorce is a cut. You sever the braid, you bring it to the town council, they run a fast confirmation that the hair is yours, and it is over. That is the entire procedure. It takes an afternoon. It can be done in a temper, at midnight, by somebody who will feel differently on Thursday.

And you may never marry that person again

One cut is permanent. You can marry somebody else, as many times as you like. Never them.

Which produces a specific and entirely avoidable category of person: somebody who did a five-minute thing in a bad hour, twenty years ago, and has had to live inside the consequence ever since. Every world that keeps this rite has them. Everybody knows one.

On a death, you cut it, and you keep it. What is done with it afterward varies and informants become reluctant when asked.

The forgeries

The confirmation step exists for a reason, and the reason is that somebody, at some point, arrived at a council with somebody else's hair.

Maspin

Jungle to the horizon in every direction, and under it an ocean nobody has seen. Far enough out that most of the people born here will never leave, and poor enough that most of the ones who could, do not.

The ground moves

Eruption, quake, storm and flood are annual here rather than exceptional. The Council's own submissions to the Royal treasury, which we hold in copy, list within one nine-year stretch: four eruptions, eleven significant quakes, two monasteries lost to water, and burned crop across an area the submission does not put a number to.

The fruit

Remote worlds cannot sell bulk, so Maspin sells what only Maspin has. The fruit here comes in flavours that do not occur elsewhere and it travels badly, which is precisely why the offworld rich pay what they pay for it. Everything else the world exports is an animal or a plant that also grows somewhere closer.

The ocean underneath

The Maspin hold that the water beneath the crust is alive, that they are made from it, and that they go back into it. They do not present this as belief. They present it as the way the world is put together, in the tone another people would use for the tides.

Survey material confirms a large subsurface body of water. It says nothing else at all.

What it costs to be here

Maspin remits to the Royal houses, and the figure is filed to the credit: 10,000,000 in Royal scrip in the most recent solar rotation returned.

Against that we can set no disbursement, no relief, and no acknowledgement of receipt. The Council's file records fourteen requests for assistance across nineteen years. We hold no reply to any of them, and the Council says none came.

Labour

Maspin calls itself a slave-free territory, and the declaration is accurate as the law defines the word. Indenture is lawful here and is administered by the Council itself.

Reader's key

Seen in the manuscript at Ch. 17 · Ch. 24.

The Maspin

Bodies of smoke and vapour, about the height of a human child. Where the eyes should be there is water, held somehow, and it moves. Inside the head there is an ember, and it brightens.

They have no mouths. The voice arrives anyway, from somewhere further in.

Faces

The features shift with feeling, continuously, the way a fire does. Other peoples report that you learn to read this with practice and cannot read it at all before. Every human informant who has spent a season among them says the same thing: it is not that Maspin are hard to read, it is that they cannot stop being read.

Sparks

Snap the fingers and they come, enough to light a cigar. This is universal, nobody here finds it worth mentioning, and every visitor mentions it.

Eating

Mostly they do not. They take byproduct from the plants around them the way other people take oxygen, with rather more water vapour in it. What they do eat is liquid or close to it: fruit pulped and watered and drunk, absorbed into the smoke of the body rather than swallowed.

Nothing in the diet is chewed. Everything is fermented, pickled, pulped or brewed.

Family

They have families, and the shape of one is not what other peoples mean by the word. Ask a Maspin who their family is and the answer takes in the household, the settlement, and eventually everybody, and they are not being poetic about it.

Nobody outside has ever got further than that. Maspin is a long way out, most Maspin never leave it, and very few outsiders stay long enough to be told anything that is not a courtesy. What is known about how a Maspin household actually works is roughly what a visitor picks up in a season, which is not much, and everybody who has written about it has been a visitor.

Dying

They hold that they are made from the ocean under the crust and that they go back into it. What that looks like in practice is catalogued under the Elder Tree, and it is not a metaphor.

Work

Fruit, kraskor, floom husbandry, port labour, temple and civic service, and the professions. Among our informants were a chemist, a caretaker, a councillor, and a clerk who keeps the tide tables at Riflo port and asked us twice whether we needed anything else.

Status

Indenture is lawful on Maspin and is administered by the Council. A number of the people in this entry are serving one.

The Maspin alphabet

The written system of the Maspin. Flowing, connected, and executed with a quill.

Character

Informants of other peoples describe the script as elegant before they describe it as legible. Maspin informants describe it in terms of feeling rather than of sound, and the Restoration has not been able to establish whether the system is alphabetic, syllabic, or something for which we lack a term.

Use

Council record, contract, correspondence, and rite. The Council's minute is taken by hand in this script and is not translated.

Availability

No Maspin text is held by this archive. Copies of Council submissions to the Royal treasury exist here in Galactic Standard because the Council prepared them in Galactic Standard, addressed to a body that would not otherwise read them.

Maspin children

Glowing eyes at knee height, and a giggle that visitors describe as wind moving through a hollow tree.

They eat like the adults, which is to say they take food into a body made of smoke and vapour, and the food evaporates into the shimmer as it goes. Watching this happen, more than one human visitor has been left genuinely puzzled about how any of them manages a fork.

They bounce when somebody interesting walks past. They are not shy. And they will tell you things the adults will not, generally without being asked.

"You don't find the shaman. The shaman finds you."

Maspin dietary practice

Mostly they do not eat. They stand among plants and take what comes off them, the way everyone else takes oxygen, with a good deal more water vapour in it.

When they do eat it is liquid, or close enough. Fruit gets pulped and watered down and drunk, which for a body made of smoke means absorbed rather than swallowed. Most things can be taken that way if they are broken down far enough first.

Nothing is chewed

Everything in the cuisine is fermented, pickled, pulped, brewed or reduced, and the good stuff takes years.

There is a wine. There is fermented kraskor and there is pickled inside-barked mycelium, and those two are what the Council names when it wants to impress somebody.

The strange part is what they sell. Kraskor go out live and whole to worlds that will chew them, and the famous Maspin fruits get shipped intact to people who bite into them.

Maspin names

A Maspin has two names and only uses one of them.

The surname comes from whoever raised you, and it is almost always a tree. The jungle has a great many of them, and a family takes one, and the children take it after. You do not have to be born to the household to carry the name. You have to have been raised by it, which on Maspin is the same thing said properly.

The name you actually go by is a nickname, and it arrives in childhood the way nicknames do everywhere. Something you did. Something you kept doing. A word a visiting trader used about you that stuck. A character out of a book you would not stop talking about at nine years old.

Nobody assigns it and nobody records it. It settles on you, and then it is yours, and that is what you tell people your name is.

Ships are not named at all

The reason given is an objection to worldly attachment, and it is given briefly, in a tone that closes the subject.

Councillors are not named either

Sitting members of the Council of Riflo are addressed as the Council and nothing else, and outsiders do not learn their names. What that rule is for is not something anyone here has felt like explaining to us.

Mead cards

The card game of choice in Guard messes, played in partners, across a table, for nothing.

Two against two. You sit opposite the person you are playing with and you do not get to talk to them about your hand, which is the entire game: everything you want to say has to be said by what you choose to put down. Good partners develop a shorthand over a few hundred rounds. Bad partners develop a grudge.

It travels well because it needs a deck and a flat surface, and a mothership is a place with very few flat surfaces and a great deal of time.

The universal breach of etiquette is narrating your own hand. Everybody knows it is a breach. Everybody does it eventually.

The medbay doctor

A Guard physician on a busy ward, working at the speed of a man who has done this exact thing all week.

He is not unkind. He is simply not present. He reads a file the way you read a delivery manifest, glances at the body attached to it, and gives instructions to the room rather than to the patient.

"Some fight in this one. You, grab the gas."

The bedside manner arrives as a joke, and it is meant well, and it lands like a dropped tray.

"You'll be back to killing Crags in no time."

A woman's voice on the far end of Calsco's radio, and the flattest, most reassuring sound in the sector.

She does not ask what happened. She asks whose house it is. Emergency work on a small colony eventually becomes neighbourhood work, and after enough years the two are the same job.

"Is it the Halgo family again?"

Megafauna of Marfeld

Forty-one catalogued species over a tonne, nine of them predators, all of them still out there.

Every other world hunted its big animals to nothing. Marfeld never managed it, and that single failure shaped everything about the place: why the towns are walled, why they stay small enough to move, why there has never been a city, and why the world's chief export is people who have already survived something.

The settlements survey them every year, tracking range, movement and density, and pool the results. It is the most consistent piece of science produced on the world and it is done by farmers.

Domestication

In the last two centuries they broke some of the big grazers to harness and bred the aggression out. Those lines are exported now as draught animals, placid as anything.

The animals changed. The culture did not.

Meram Kest

A Second Sergeant of the Royal Shayron Defence Force, under a name that is not the one he was given.

The name is issued rather than inherited. It is what the Crown puts on his papers when he is working somewhere the Crown would rather not be seen working, and it is a real name in every sense that matters to a customs officer and no sense at all that matters to his mother.

He recites the oath the way soldiers do, front to back, without needing to find the start of it:

"I serve the people of Shayron and uphold the dignity of the"

What he is like

A man who very badly wants there to be a procedure. He asks for the code phrase. He wants to know which part of this is the official part, because if he can find that, then the rest of it is something he can be told what to do about.

He also has somebody he answers to whose name he was not supposed to say.

Michael Vousin

A Trailblazer, and formerly a student at Saigo, which is the best engineering school in the galaxy and the place trying to rebuild computers from nothing.

He was partway through and he left. Not thrown out. Left.

Now he builds ports on worlds the shipping lanes forgot, for a body that went unpaid for seven years and did the work anyway. He talks about machines the way people from Saigo do, which is to say more than anyone asked.

The thing he will not let go of is that the artificial intelligence everyone agreed to be finished with is quietly turning up again in Guard hardware, in small ways, in places where nobody has to sign for it.

The military police

Not a duty roster. A service, with its own ladder, its own specialisations, and a doctrine that is simpler than anybody expects.

What is in it

Detectives working actual cases. Riot control. Border and port guards. Prison staff. Investigators who do nothing but paperwork and are worse news than the ones who carry batons. It is a developed institution with a career in it, and a man can spend thirty years inside it without ever standing at a gate.

What they can do, on paper

Enter any quarters. Detain anybody. Charge anybody.

What they can do in practice

Whatever their rank supports.

A newly qualified MP who walks unannounced into the quarters of a special operations captain will discover that the corridor, the duty officer, and every witness available respects the captain considerably more than it respects him, and that the incident goes badly in a way no regulation predicted. To touch somebody at that height you go up your own chain first and let your captain of military police make the request. Everybody involved knows this. It is not written down anywhere.

The doctrine

They care about instability. That is the whole of it.

Get drunk enough to be a nuisance and you will be told to keep yourself together, by somebody who has said it four hundred times and does not care what you do next. Bring something in from a world you were not supposed to bring it in from, some restricted cheese or a bottle or a plant, and you get a warning and your afternoon back. They genuinely do not care.

Do something that threatens the stability of the arrangement and you have an opponent, permanently, with detectives and prisons attached.

The rules are not what they enforce. Order is.
