The Ministry of Propaganda

That is its actual name, in its own paperwork, since incorporation. The Guard has never seen anything to apologise for in the word.

It makes the educational material for member worlds, the morale material for the service, and the coverage of ceremonies, and then it puts all of it out.

The catch

It does not own the transmitters. See The relay network.

The interstellar relay network was built by religious organisations to carry sermons. When central government collapsed they defended those towers, hard, and they still own every one of them. So the most powerful information organ in the galaxy buys airtime, by the hour, from eleven separate proprietors, at rates that vary by proprietor and by what is in the broadcast.

Two of the eleven refuse whole categories of material outright, and the refusals are in the correspondence.

Airtime is the Ministry's single largest expense: 61,440,800 credits last year.

Miss Jaley

The woman at the front desk, sipping chai, who kept sweets in a drawer for whoever came through.

She worked the station, which on a fragment colony means she was the first face anybody saw and the last one to be counted as staff. She kept boiled candy from Shayron, four transfers and the better part of a month away, and gave it to the chief's boy when he turned up early to wait for his father.

She also had a bottle of pre-war Astrovin. She had been keeping it for years, for something worth keeping it for, in the way people do with a good bottle.

She opened it the night somebody else got good news.

Miss Liles

The Director's wife, and his secretary, which means she runs the diary, the correspondence and the door.

Twenty years ago she was his girlfriend, they were both barely out of college, and they took in a seven-year-old who had just lost everyone. She fed him, put a cake in front of him on his birthday, and was unfailingly kind to a boy who spent the next two decades quietly pulling away from her.

She is currently off sick with ulcers, and somebody else is covering her desk. A pilot, as it happens, who is very good at diaries and did not ask for the job.

Mister Flimmity Dimmity

A floom. He belongs, in the loosest possible sense, to Calsco Fritt.

His collar tag reads:

Mister Flimmity Dimmity. If lost, return to Calsco Fritt.

He gets lost. When he does, a seven-foot Katanzarian goes through the undergrowth singing Flimmity Dimmity, where are you, Flimmity Dimmity, I miss you, in a voice one witness described as belonging to somebody who had gargled gravel.

He is also a judge of character, which is what flooms are. They make up their minds about a person quickly and people on Maspin act on it. Flimmity's opinion of a stranger has changed at least one important decision that this archive knows about, and that stranger has no idea.

Modanick

Cold, close-built and comfortable. Brick, iron gates, chimneys, canals that freeze hard enough to skate by the second week. The kind of world that produces doctors and cheese and very little history.

Winter

Four months of it, and it is not violent. It is an inch a day, most days, for a third of the year. The canals go over and stay over, the skating leagues run, and the national game is played on them by people who learned it before they could read.

Nothing on this world is more than nine storeys, by municipal code, in every municipality, each of which passed the code separately.

Flowers

Spring here is a serious business. Botany is a national art rather than a hobby, the flower shows are old and formal, and the shortest route to being taken seriously in a Modanick town is to be good at growing something.

Why the doctors

Crowding plus long winters made this a plague world for six generations. Hospital foundation dates cluster tightly in that period, and so does the local expectation, still written into the school statutes, that a person be fully formed by twenty. The plagues stopped. The expectation did not.

The world now supplies more trained physicians to the member worlds than any other, and manufactures no weapons at all.

Defence

None. Modanick has never had a military. Its accession instrument settles the personnel obligation in cash, one of four such instruments in the register: it pays 3.9 per cent of member revenue and sends nobody.

A note on the weather

Guard tourism material issued between GC 4440 and GC 4455 describes Modanick as warm and bright the year round. Anybody who has actually wintered there describes something else entirely, at length, and with feeling.

Monver

Forest, rock and real mountains, some of which are ships. Colonial hulls came down here two thousand years ago and the country grew over them, and the largest is thirty-one kilometres long and carries mature trees.

The bargain

Monver's accession instrument is the most heavily qualified in the member register. It reserves local government, local statute on botanicals, and every local observance, each by name. In exchange it gives two years of everybody.

Most of that service is a trade school with a rifle in it. The certificates issued under it are good across the member worlds and a Monveri carpenter is a Monveri carpenter anywhere.

What it costs them

Monver holds about 0.9 per cent of the member population and supplies 4.1 per cent of member personnel, and has done every year since it joined. They are proud of this and say so.

The permissiveness

Redleaf is lawful here and taxed like anything else. The line, given to us more or less identically by nine people, is that men who fight hard should be allowed to relax hard, and that it helps with what fighting does to you. Mostly that is true.

The health there is, every year, a minority for whom it is not recreation any more. No local statute addresses them. No local politician has proposed one. It is the only subject on this world where a straight question gets a change of topic.

The Monver Refusal

The founding event of Monver. A colonial force refused an order to exterminate the population it had been sent to displace, and fought its own fleet.

Date

Approximately two thousand years before the present. No document survives from either party. The sending government has not existed for a comparable period and is not identified in any account we hold.

Account

Consistent across every Monveri source and not attested anywhere else. A colonial expedition established itself over decades, mingled with the native population, and received an order for their extermination. The expedition refused. The refusal became a guerrilla war against the fleet that had brought it, fought on the ground the expedition had settled, and won.

Inheritance

Every distinctive feature of Monveri political life is stated locally as descending from this event: the primacy of local government over distant authority, the refusal to impose on any other world's independence, and the fact that Monver has never founded a colony.

Note

Monver's accession instrument with the Guard provides two years of universal service in exchange for guarantees of non-interference in local government, statute and observance. Monveri sources describe the instrument as the same bargain their founders were given, drafted this time by the party that has to keep it.

Attributed to eleven informants across four settlements.

Moonball

The game they play on the ice. Modanick's national sport and the thing that world will actually raise its voice about.

Eleven a side, a stick, a weighted disc, and a frozen canal or a prepared rink. The season starts when the water goes over, which is the second week of winter most years, and everyone plays: children on the canals, works teams, a league with a published rulebook older than the war.

The Modanick championship is the best-attended thing that happens on that world all year, and it is not close. The canals fill with people who cannot get tickets and watch nothing in particular together.

Variants are played on forty-four worlds, and every mothership has a court in the rec room with a floor waxed to a shine and an argument in progress on it. Modanick's is the only code anyone has ever bothered to write down properly, and Modanick will tell you so.

The Mothership

The Guard's home. A single hull carrying operations, administration, medicine, courts, workshops and everybody's quarters, permanently on the move.

It runs a fixed circuit of the member worlds, published a year in advance, and takes rather more than a standard year to get all the way round. That circuit governs everyone's life aboard: when it is in a busy sector you deploy every couple of weeks, and when it is not, you have a month with nothing to do. People plan around it the way other people plan around seasons.

There are no separate branches. Pilots, infantry, engineers, doctors, clerks and the judge advocate share the same corridors, the same messes and the same seniority list. A commodore and a staff sergeant queue for the same food.

Somebody described it as being like college, in that you have free time and choose what to do with it, and the timetable is still pointed straight at you.

Mr Armstin

The neighbour who kept the air on.

He maintained the gravity spires on his fragment of the Wake colony: the towers that burn Corefuel to hold down an atmosphere and give a lump of rock something like gravity. Without them there is no colony, and he was the man who climbed them.

A tinkerer by temperament, always halfway through fixing something that was not strictly his problem, and the sort of person who ends up doing a job because he is the only one who understands it. He worked the station alongside the chief, he waved at the children, and he ran the decorations.

The spires were not the whole of it either. When something came in over the sky that should have been tracked and was not, his was the name shouted into the intercom, because the defences were his as well.

The part he needed

The regulator assembly is the piece that fails. Nobody can make one any more; they come out of salvage and pre-war stock, and a settlement of his class is entitled to them on request, every quarter.

He requested them. Correctly, on the right form, quarter after quarter, for nineteen consecutive quarters. His handwriting does not change across any of them. The last one is as neat as the first.

"The spires are down! I've been trying to get the fucking parts shipped for weeks! Just stay put"

His house was the first one hit.

Nardow

A cartel boss with a compound, a private army, and gold on his tusks.

Bloated and grey, moving on several limbs at once, in the manner of a thing that has not needed to hurry in a long time. He employs Vitula by the crew, on written terms, at rates that are honestly not bad.

The son

He has one, and the boy is nothing like him: a crustacean, wine-red shell, crab maw, green eyes with no iris in them, hair like seaweed.

He is also, at this stage of his life, not there. The young of some lineages in this classification pass through a long period, years and sometimes a decade, in which the body is awake and capable and responsive to stimulus and there is no one home behind it yet. It is not an illness and it is not a disability. It is a stage, and it ends.

His did not. He was killed in the compound before it did.

Every asset his father owned was held in trust in that boy's name. He was building an empire for an heir who never perceived him and was never going to.

The Nhath

There are two Nhath in the surviving record and they are not the same people.

The one in the invoices

1 gap

Guard contracting files, INTACT, complete in the way commercial files always are: scope, duration, rate, settlement. Eleven separate engagements across nineteen years. Paid in full and on the scheduled date, every time.

The fund that paid them is identified by an internal reference. We have not established what it denotes. [FILING INCOMPLETE]

Guard ministerial material describes the same people as raiders without political organisation.

The one in the grammar

Recovered language material, and it describes something else entirely. Verbs that conjugate by subject. Two levels of you, chosen by the status of the person you are addressing, where the wrong choice is not a rudeness. Numbers in base eight, named after the fingers, extending without limit. Colours that are all derived from things: red is blood-colour, white is clean-colour, silver is weapon-colour.

And a genealogy. Every Nhath carries a generation number, counted in eights, inherited and incremented. The recovered examples run into three figures.

A people with no political organisation does not keep an eighty-eight generation line. A people that keeps one is not described by an invoice.

How they say themselves

Their word for themselves is their word for we. Everyone else in the galaxy calls them by it, which means every world in this archive addresses them, without knowing it, as us.

There is one word for everybody outside: krayd. It serves for they, for other species, and for enemy. The language provides nothing neutral for a stranger.

Work

Armed contract, which is what the Guard bought and therefore what the record shows. Also haulage, salvage, and the sale of water rights. The survey notes an instructor of arithmetic at a settlement school, by name and generation number, and records his rate of pay.

The Nhath leader

The Nhath who signed the contracts. A lineage number in the hundreds, which means eighty and more generations of one family counted in eights and remembered.

He speaks flawless Galactic Standard, and enjoys the effect that has on people who were not expecting it. Told that his Standard is good, he corrects the compliment.

"Better than you."

The chip

He wears a Guard translator implant at the neck, bought with the credits from a job stealing Corefuel. He does not need it. He wears it partly because it covers a scar that was already there, put in that exact place by a woman who shot him.

Who paid

Eleven separate Guard engagements over nineteen years, paid in full, on time, every time, out of a fund identified in the paperwork only by an internal reference nobody has been able to resolve.

Reader's key

Seen in the manuscript at Ch. 9.

Nhath names

Three parts, in a fixed order, and every one of them is a compound.

Kakavai-Shtuv Aroniela-Kipo Deva Strongskull Moonchild, eighty-seventh generation

The given name is your body

A physical trait welded onto the body part it is true about. Kakavai is strong, shtuv is skull, and the man is Strongskull. It belongs to you alone and it passes to nobody.

The family name is what you believe

A spiritual element welded onto a family role. Aroniela is the moon, which is the sacred one, the one raids are timed to. Kipo is child. Moonchild. It goes to the children unchanged and it is the same sound in the four hundredth mouth as the first.

Note what that means side by side. A Nhath's private name describes their skull, and their inherited name describes their relationship to a moon. The flesh is the personal part and the faith is the shared one.

The number is the generation

Base eight, named after the fingers, because a Nhath hand has four: ka, da, ga, ra, ma, ba, va, sa, and then a block prefix for every eight after that. It goes up by one each generation and it never restarts. Higher numbers command more respect, and the recovered examples run past a hundred.

A new clan may be founded at any time and starts at one. Nobody is impressed by a one.

Succession, in full

Kakavai-Shtuv Aroniela-Kipo Deva · Strongskull Moonchild 87 Peus-Maika Aroniela-Kipo Desa · Bighands Moonchild 88

The father's skull and the son's hands. The moon stays where it is, and the number moves one.

How it is actually said

Almost never in full. The formal short form fuses the given name into one word, Kashtuv, and among family and friends it clips again to Kash. A Nhath goes his whole life as two syllables to the people who love him and eleven to anybody taking a statement.

And to strangers

Nhathian has two words for you, marlo and lo, chosen by the standing of the person addressed, and choosing wrong is not a rudeness. But there is no form at all for someone outside the people, because an outsider has no line and no number for the grammar to measure. They are krayd, which serves for they, for other species, and for enemy. It is not an insult. There is no other slot.

[Compiler's note: the Guard's contracts identify these same individuals by a single job code. An eighty-eight generation line and an invoice, for one man, filed in the same cabinet.]

Nhathar

The Nhath homeworld. Hot, dry, volcanic, and almost everything anyone knows about it has been reconstructed from the language rather than from a visit.

What the language says about the place

Nhathian has two weather words, rain and wind, and no others, which is a vocabulary you get on a world with two things the sky does. It has a dedicated word for creatures regarded as food. Its numbers run in base eight because Nhath hands have four fingers, and that follows the whole way down: tools cut for a four-finger grip, eight-sided rooms, days divided into eight-hour blocks, and fighting formations of eight.

Their word for the sun is short and hard. Their word for the moon is long and flowing. Sun means exposure. The moon is sacred, and raids are timed to it.

Black rock and lava

Outside accounts of the surface are few and consistent: volcanic country, dark stone, heat coming off the ground, and settlements built low.

The Guard's contracts with Nhath parties identify them by job code. They do not record where they came from.

Reader's key

Seen in the manuscript at Ch. 9.

Nhathian

The Nhath language, pieced together from a partial survey, two word lists, and people who remembered some of it. No native text has ever been recovered.

We print it at length because it is the only substantial evidence about this people that was not produced by somebody who was paying them.

How it sounds

Dry and deliberate, one syllable placed after another, with the strangeness carried in the vowels rather than in clusters. Consonants bite, vowels run long.

Us and everyone else

Their word for themselves is their word for we. Every other people in the galaxy calls them by it, which means the entire galaxy addresses them, without noticing, as us.

For everybody outside there is one word, krayd. It does duty for they, for other species, and for enemy. There is nothing neutral in the language for a stranger.

Counting

Base eight, named after the fingers, because a Nhath hand has four. It goes all the way down: tools cut for that grip, eight-sided rooms, eight-hour periods, formations of eight.

Colour

There are no abstract colour words at all. Every one is built off a thing. Red is blood-colour, white is clean-colour, black is night-colour, silver is weapon-colour. Two of them have no equivalent anywhere else: one means the colouring of a healthy prey animal, and one means the colour enemies bleed, which changes depending on who you are fighting.

Opposites are the same word backwards

This is the part that matters.

meaning word and its opposite
truth / lie ver rev
trust / suspicion falo olaf
respect / contempt keen neek
memory / forgetting kan naka
honour / shame kargo kaffe

A lie is not the absence of truth in this language. It is truth pronounced backwards. Hearing both in one sentence is a joke no translation can carry.

Names

Three parts. A given name describing something physical about you, compounded with a body part, not inherited. A family name, inherited unchanged. And a generation number, counted in eights, going up each time.

Higher numbers command more respect. Recovered examples run into three figures.

A name is said in full almost never. The formal short form fuses the given name into one word and the intimate form clips it again. See Nhath names.

One word with an origin

Bezoo, weapon, is the sound a plasma discharge makes. Every Nhath grows up hearing it, and it sits in the basic vocabulary next to the words for water and food.

[Compiler's note: the contracts call these people raiders with no political organisation. We have set the contracts and the grammar side by side. We are not going to say the rest of it.]

Nova Squadron

A fighter squadron off the mothership, and one of the better places in the Guard to spend four years.

They fly the morning patrols: a few laps of the hull, a slow pass over the thrusters to eyeball the plating, and back in. Routine to the point of boredom, which is exactly what a squadron wants and exactly what the youngest pilot on it complains about every single time.

On the net they are Nova, and the lead is Nova 01 Actual

When the squadron speaks with one voice, it is the oldest man aboard doing the speaking.

The cheer, which nobody can trace and which they do standing up, with shots in hand:

Nova, Nova, burn so bright. Nova Squad owns the night. Through the void, we lead the way. Nova Squad wins the day.

Then everybody drinks it and pulls a face, because rockroot mead is not for enjoying.

What they actually are

Four or five people who share a locker room and a morning, who know which one of them is hungover and cover for it, who tape their sunglasses back together, and who stick a decal from home on somebody else's helmet as a way of saying something they have no other way to say.

The helmets are the record. Every engraving on them is a mission that went well and a place somebody has been.

The old Maspin veteran

An old Maspin, met in passing, who fought in the war and has been thinking about it ever since.

"These kids have it easy nowadays." "Maybe not easy. Maybe I'm just bitter. I grew up during the war." "Some days, it feels like nothing's changed. I thought fighting would fix our problems, but here we are. Other times, it feels like everything's changed, and I'm just a fish out of water."

That is the whole conversation. It is also, as far as this archive can tell, the most complete account anybody has given us of what the war did to the generation that came through it.

The Palace of Riflo

The big stone building at the heart of Riflo, holding the Council chamber and the temple attached to it.

Vines have been growing into the stonework for a very long time and were never cleared, so the building and the jungle have arrived at an arrangement. Visitors consistently describe it as older than the settlement around it. No foundation date exists and no local authority claims to have one.

The temple is kept by a caretaker staff, some of whom are working off an indenture, which on Maspin is lawful and is administered by the Council that sits upstairs.

The palace staff

The people who keep the Palace of Riflo running, and who open its doors by hand because the doors have always been opened by hand.

The red-robed pair

Two figures at the great oak doors, and the thing you notice first is that they are made of smoke rather than wrapped in it. The robe is the outer edge of the person, not a garment over one. They take a leaf each and pull, and the weight of the oak is real enough that it takes a moment.

The attendant

An alien in flowing robes who bows without speaking, receives the instruction, and leaves to fetch appetisers. The bow is not deference exactly. It is the practised economy of somebody who has decided that talking is the slower way to do this.

Pashmirské

the mark is written by some people and not by others, in the same office, in the same year

Fought over for a hundred and fifty years by two powers that did not want it, and quiet now.

Before any of it

Pashmirské is volcanic, and the settlement of it is the story the world still tells about itself. Taming the vents took centuries. Learning to draw power off them took longer, and out of that work came the containment and discharge of plasma, which is to say that the weapon the galaxy has spent a hundred years being unable to replace was worked out here first.

For a long period the world was an economic centre on the strength of it. It armed a great deal of the settled galaxy and fielded soldiers with a reputation that outlasted them. Whether it ever held territory beyond its own system is asserted locally and is not attested in anything held here.

None of it survived. The decline is not attributed to any single event and appears in the record as a long shallow slope. By the time the civil war began, the world was manufacturing very little and selling ore.

The war was already here

That is the part outsiders get wrong. Nobody arrived and started it. There were factions on this world with grievances of their own, generations deep, and what the two powers did was notice them and pay.

The division was not ethnic, religious or regional. Every account, including those given by people who fought on opposite sides, describes the argument in the same terms: what should be permitted, and by whom, and how much disorder a population is obliged to tolerate. There was one people on this world before the fighting and there is one people on it now.

Neither sponsor ever fought here under its own colours. They wrote cheques, shipped crates, and let the argument that was already running do the work.

What was used on it

Rifles and ordnance. Men walking onto ground and taking it a street at a time, and then losing it, and then taking it again. Nothing on this world was ever worth a strategic weapon, and both sponsors understood that perfectly well, which is why the damage here is not a crater. It is a hundred and fifty years of small holes in everything.

Why it went on so long

Because neither sponsor needed to win it. A war on Pashmirské cost one of them very little and cost the other a great deal, and the accounting worked out the same in both directions, so both kept paying. On the sponsors' books this world appears as a line item that performed well.

How it stopped

Not with a victory, a treaty or a surrender.

The two powers paying for it destroyed each other. The money stopped. And in a galaxy that cannot manufacture, the resupply stopping is not an inconvenience: it is the end. There is a bottom to a war fought with weapons nobody can make another of, and after sixty more years of grinding toward it, they reached it.

The fighting did not conclude. It ran out.

And somebody was still standing

Whoever holds a capital on the day a war finally exhausts itself holds the world, and what followed was not a campaign. It was a consolidation, conducted mostly on paper, against factions that had no ammunition and no patron and nothing left to be promised.

Now

Quiet, orderly, poor and fed. There is one authority and it does not pretend to be anything else.

The ore

The world holds magnetic mineral of the grade used in plasma weapon manufacture, and it is still worked. There is nowhere to send it. Nobody has built a plasma weapon anywhere since the Wipe, including here, on the world where the process was devised. The material is stockpiled and sold in small quantities against a demand that does not presently exist.

Biodium

The second export and the one that actually pays. It is a combustible extracted from the residue of a rainforest that dried out on this world long before anybody arrived on it, and it runs domestic and light industrial plant. It flies nothing. It is catalogued separately.

Scrap

A century and a half of ordnance and vehicles is in the ground here, and in an age that cannot manufacture, that is stock rather than wreckage. INFERRED

The day

Pashmirské turns in about thirty hours, and everything on the world is cut to that: the shift, the school session, the broadcast schedule and the festival calendar.

Weather

Three seasons and none of them severe. A warm spring, a wet autumn, a winter with snow in it. For a world with this much volcanic geology under it the climate is unremarkable, and residents say so with some feeling.

What the administration provides

A food quota, sufficient and dull, issued to everybody. Healthcare that is free and limited, in that order. Maternity leave by statute. No paternity leave, and no record of it having been proposed.

What people do

Attendance at the festival calendar is compulsory and the ordinary entertainment is not, and the ordinary entertainment is largely the same material.

Every town stages plays, and the towns are expected to turn out for them. The repertoire is the old canon of the world, performed continuously for long enough that the audience knows the text, which is most of the pleasure. Outdoor screens run a catalogue of films that everybody has seen and everybody watches together anyway.

There is very little on this world that a person does alone, and very little of it is new.

Money

Pashmirské holds no Guard membership, no ledger standing and no network coverage, and prices its exports in Guard credits regardless, because that is what the buyers use. Fuel is sold through intermediary companies and from a small number of stations and orbital depots held offworld, which sell to whoever arrives.

The arrangement requires no agreement with the Guard and confers no obligation on it. It also means that the revenue holding the administration together is denominated in an instrument the administration does not control and cannot audit.

The Guard

There has been no approach in either direction. No application, no refusal, no incident, no complaint. The two parties have arrived at an arrangement that neither has written down and both observe, which is that they do not have anything to do with one another.

The mark on the name

Some filings carry it. Some do not. The same office does it both ways inside a single year and nobody local treats this as a matter to be settled.

[Compiler's note: we hold a great deal about this world, and every page of it was produced by somebody who was paying for the fighting. Requisitions, sortie returns, insurance schedules, casualty estimates prepared for a sponsor. What we hold about the sixty years since is four pages. The war is documented because outsiders were doing the accounting. The peace is not, because the man running it does not file.]

The Path of Blood

The hunt. You are put out into predator country and you feed yourself off what you can kill.

Marfeld's big animals are big enough that a walled settlement cannot hold ground against them all year. A boy on his own with a sharpened stick is not expected to take one of those. What he is expected to do instead is something nobody outside will explain, and everyone inside already knows.

Of the three paths this is the one outsiders assume is hardest. On Marfeld opinion is divided, and the division is usually along the lines of which one the person you are asking walked.

The Path of Root

The forage. You feed yourself off the ground.

On a world with no reliable growing season and two killing extremes, this is the path that needs the most knowledge and the least equipment. You have to already know what comes up where, in which month, and what will put you on your back. Nobody teaches it formally. You learned it or you did not.

Visitors call it the easy one. Nobody on Marfeld does.

The Path of Sky

The climb. Straight up.

The country for this is a formation of pillar mountains, near-vertical columns standing alone off the plain, and you go up them. You eat by taking eggs and honey out of nests and hives on the faces, while the things that built them object at close range. Some of those things are large and most of them can fly.

It is the only one of the three with a view at the end, which is exactly why a boy would pick it, and exactly why a boy is not allowed to pick.

Pavlock Jattern

Castle Team's engineer, and the reason the room is bearable after a bad day.

A dark brown beard, trimmed to the jaw with real care and kept that way in the field, where nobody else bothers. It frames a grin he uses constantly. Teal visor.

Put him in royal robes and the costume comes with eyewear best described as a pair of glasses that lost their lenses and turned to face the wrong way. Not ornamental. Just regal enough.

Marfeld

He is from a world where the big predators never died out and the seasons swing from killing heat to killing cold in a matter of weeks. At seventeen he was put out into that country with his clothes and nothing else, which is what Marfeld does to its boys. Three paths: Blood, Root, Sky. He walked all three.

He drew summer. Heat, insects that never let up, and blisters. The first thing he made out there was a knife barely worth the word, a sharpened stick jammed into split wood, and he kept his pockets full of dry kindling like it was money.

That is where he decided to be an engineer. Building the thing you need out of whatever is lying near you turns out to be a career.

Which is not the job he has

He is a combat engineer, which is that skill with a deadline and people shooting. What he wants is astral engineering, on the civilian side, where the thing you build is meant to last and nobody is timing you. He can describe it in detail. He has never filed anything about it.

No man who finishes the trial may speak about it. He never has.

The beard

It grew on him out there, and on Marfeld they say hair remembers. You may shape it, trim it, dye it. You do not shave, and shaving means renouncing your family. He spent fourteen months fighting Guard paperwork for the exemption rather than pick up a razor.

The rest of him

Business-minded in a way that surprises people. Face-blind. Hopeless with directions. Warmer toward non-humans than anyone else on his team, without making a thing of it.

His grandfather's question was never what job do you want. It was what kind of person do you want to be, and Pav is the one who says it out loud when somebody needs to hear it.

Maspin children bounce with excitement when he walks past. He straightens his back and enjoys it enormously.

He also carries something he has never said aloud, about the man he follows and the man he wishes were standing there instead, and he hates himself for thinking it, and he cannot make it not be true.

The personnel series

Why this volume can tell you the colour of a soldier's visor.

A Guard records depot was closed down and its paper duplicates were released for disposal as superseded administrative material. The Restoration collected them. It was lawful and it was almost certainly not intended.

The Guard files its people in extraordinary detail: colouring, height, old injuries, what kit they were issued, which faith they wrote on the form at seventeen, who gets the money if they die. Most of what this volume knows about anyone currently serving comes out of that one shipment.

It runs to a single date, which is the day the depot last bundled its paper, and stops.

A fungus that grows on the inner bark of certain jungle trees, cut out, pickled, and drunk.

Planetary Defence Forces

Twenty-two member worlds keep their own soldiers, and the Guard does not command a single one of them.

The right is written into the accession terms in every case, and in every case it is limited to defending the ground you are standing on. Which suits both sides: the world keeps its army and its pride, and the Guard keeps the bill.

What they actually are

Local. A Planetary Defence Force is people from the world defending the world, often the same families across generations, with their own colours, their own songs, and their own wars behind them. On some worlds it is the most respected institution there is.

And then a world accedes

When a Defence Force is absorbed, the paperwork records a transfer of persons, never of the formation. Everybody comes across as an individual, at an assessed rank, into the Guard's own seniority list. The formation does not come with them. Not the name, not the colours, not the battle honours.

That is why no unit in the Guard establishment is older than the Guard itself. It is not a coincidence and it is not an accident of record-keeping. It is the design.

What it costs a man

Service before accession does not appear in his Guard file, including service in a war he fought and won. The record begins at contract. A soldier who spent years defending his own forests, on the side that came out on top, joins the Guard as a private with no history, and everything he did before is a thing he can talk about and never prove.

Plasma knives

A blade that is not a blade, carried by everybody who cannot afford to run out of options.

It lives in the forearm gauntlet. A press of the panel and it snaps into being with a hard hiss: a dense, crackling wedge of blue-teal light, throwing its glow across the wearer's armour and the face of whoever is about to have a bad few seconds.

It does not last

A few moments, and then it is gone and the gauntlet needs to cool. That is the whole design constraint, and everything about how it is used follows from it. You do not fence with a plasma knife. You solve one problem with it and then you do not have it any more.

It goes through flesh like the flesh has agreed to it, and it will grind to a stop against bone. It cuts a clean glowing hole through a locked drawer. It cauterises as it goes, which is either mercy or the opposite depending on where it lands.

The bayonet variant mounts under a rifle barrel and burns longer, at the cost of being attached to something two feet long.

The shield variant is the same principle turned flat: a small teal plane of energy that does not block so much as burn. Pressed against something, it does not stop it. It cooks it.

Plasma rifles

The standard weapon of the age, and nobody can make another one.

The process was worked out on Pashmirské, off the volcanic vents of that world, and for a long period Pashmirské armed most of the settled galaxy. Every plasma rifle now in existence was built before the Wipe. The factories that made them and the charge assemblies they run on were among the first things both sides burned, because that was the whole strategy of the war: not taking ground, taking the ability to build.

So the total number only goes down. Armourers keep them alive by cannibalising the dead ones, and a serviceable rifle appreciates in value against almost everything else. Out on the rim, weapons work as currency. A rifle holds its worth better than money does.

Which makes the Guard's arsenal not just power but a fortune, sitting in racks.

Automatic plasma weapons are legal under planetary statute on nineteen member worlds and illegal under Galactic Standard everywhere. Both are true at once, and which one gets enforced depends on who is asking.

Polaris

the star. On several outer settlements an older common word for the sun remains in use

Primary of the agricultural system that supplies the greater part of the member worlds' staple grain, protein, and salt.

Type and survey data

filed complete in the navigational schedules, re-surveyed GC 4431.

Name

The star's name is older than its use. A family took the name from the star. Approximately a millennium later that family became royal, and the name is now borne by a Royal house, by the star, by the system, and by the shared calendar of ten inhabited bodies.

Consequently no resident of the system can name the star that grows their food without naming the house that holds the licence on it. Certain outer settlements retain a prior common word for the sun in daily speech. It appears in no filing, no contract, and no ledger, and the Restoration has been told by three separate informants that it is not used in front of buyers.

Polaris scrip

The money in the breadbasket. Excellent money, and only in the breadbasket.

Wages, rent, shopping, licences and local tax are all in scrip. Wages are good and savings are substantial, well above the member-world average, because the system pays properly and there is not much to spend it on.

You can change it for Guard credits at the exchange in Kelton City, at a rate set daily, up to an annual limit per person. Roughly four people in a thousand ever reach that limit.

Nobody is stopped from leaving Polaris. What you cannot do is take twenty years of it with you.

The Polaris System

also known as: the breadbasket

Ten inhabited bodies running one machine with the parts on separate worlds. Most of what the member worlds eat comes out of here.

How it fits together

Weton grows the grain. Dorrow mills it. Sheel raises the meat and, out of the same yards, renders the bone and blood the Weton soil runs on. Corr ships the water. Schriggé ships the salt. Tspa grows the protein. Tall holds the seed. Baline holds the cold. Kelton holds the paperwork.

Break any one of those and the system stops. Most people in it can name three.

What you get

A house, a guaranteed price for your crop, a wage floor, a rest day, and a repair entitlement that means when the combine breaks it gets fixed. We have compared these terms against forty-one other agricultural worlds. Nothing comes close. Farmers move here on purpose, and apply, and wait.

Clause 11

Leaving the system requires an approved leave filing that states a date of return. It sits at clause eleven of the standard residence instrument and the port authority on Kelton enforces it. Filings are approved 96.8 per cent of the time.

The scrip

Wages are paid in Polaris scrip, which is excellent money and is not money anywhere else. Conversion to Guard credits happens at the Kelton exchange, subject to an annual per-person limit that 0.4 per cent of holders reach.

You can leave. You cannot take it with you.

The libraries

Funded from the harvest levy and unusually good: a mean of 41,000 volumes a settlement against a member-world mean of 9,200. A great deal of it is about economics, which is to say about yield, supply, and the dignity of feeding people.

[Compiler's note: nothing is banned here. We checked. There is simply no line in the acquisitions schedule for it.]

Portaboards

One of the last mass-produced Levitation Matrix devices, and nobody alive knows how to make another.

It floats. That is the short answer and the one most people give. It carries a rider or a load a few feet off the ground, glides over broken country and standing water, and wobbles when the field has to adjust to uneven terrain, which is often.

The long answer is that the Levitation Matrix was a whole class of anti-gravity engineering that came out of the pre-war world and did not survive it. What is left in circulation is what was already built. They are traded, hoarded, stolen, and repaired by people who do not understand the thing they are repairing.

Why an engineer will trade everything he owns for one

Not to ride it. To open it. Take one apart, work out what the matrix is actually doing, and a great deal of what the galaxy currently cannot do becomes possible again.

Several people have tried. So far the boards have survived the attempts better than the reputations of the people making them.

Pre-human inhabitants of Wake

Something was on Wake before us, and it is buried in the mantle.

That is legend, and we would not print it at all except for one thing: it is told, in recognisable form, by at least six populations that had no contact with each other before the war. Traditions that share nothing else share this.

Where the versions agree

That they were very old. That they reached a point where they no longer died. That this turned out not to be what they wanted. That they had a hand in making humans afterwards. And that something of theirs is still in us, described in every version as a fault rather than a gift.

Where they disagree

Everything else, including whether any of them is left.

There is no artefact, no structure, no remains and no document. Ruins built by somebody nobody can identify do exist, on Katanzaria and elsewhere, which proves there were predecessors somewhere and proves nothing at all about these.

Reader's key

Seen in the manuscript at Ch. 33.

Pre-war language families

Before the war, several large human cultures held territory across multiple worlds, each with its own language. Some had done so for a thousand years or more. They fought one another periodically without any of them being destroyed.

They ended between roughly four hundred and one hundred years ago. The cause in each case was the collapse of movement: supply chains stopped, trade stopped, and worlds ceased to be able to reach one another. No multi-world human polity survived the war. What survived were planets, some of which acceded to the Guard and some of which did not.

The languages continued to be spoken locally. They ceased to be spoken between worlds.

Evidence

No literature, speech recordings or grammars are held here. The families are reconstructed from suffixes on proper names, which appear in shipping and licensing registers across worlds that have no relationship to one another.

Kanta

The language of the human homeworld and the oldest human tongue attested here. It marked descent. A name ending in -zin, -zon, -jin or -in denoted the son of a named person.

The ending is still functional in some lines. Ninzin, Jayzin and Iradin are inherited family names. In other cases it has become a given name with no patronymic force. Jimzon is a given name meaning the son of Jim. His father's given name was Korjin, meaning the son of Kor.

Kanta has the widest distribution of the three families named here. Its home planet was destroyed in GC 4394 and it has no remaining first-language speakers.

Myatugo

Marked a holding: ground registered to a named party. The suffix is -ton or -tom.

It appears on Kelton, Weton and Kinton. Kelton and Weton are the two planets of the Polaris system. Kinton is four systems distant with no recorded connection to either. All three are agricultural worlds.

Saolai

The clerical and administrative language, used in law, accounting, scholarship and court ceremonial. The suffix is a final -o, -a or -ia.

It appears on Maldo, Creta, Katanzaria, Kitalia, Saigo, Korno and Riflo. Maldo is the Royal administrative capital. Creta is the principal banking world. Katanzaria maintains a civil registry running eleven centuries. Saigo is the chartered university world.

Other families

At least four further suffix groups are attested and some had wider distribution than the three above. They appear as -ar, -or and -vor; as -eld; as -ow; and on two worlds whose registered names carry a diacritic that Galactic Standard does not use and that roughly half of all filings omit.

These families are not named here. Identification would require material produced in the languages themselves, and no such material has been recovered.

Convergence of two suffixes

Myatugo -ton and Kanta -zon are unrelated in origin and have converged in form. Penston, Armstin and Krostin are consistent with either derivation and cannot be assigned. The homeworld's older name, Waketin, is consistent with both simultaneously.

Irregularities

Penston is a personal name carrying a Myatugo suffix. Astrovin is a commodity carrying a Kanta suffix. Cross-borrowing of this kind is normal between languages in contact and is not treated here as evidence against the reconstruction.

Prodar

A name, and nothing attached to it.

He is spoken of once, by a man who trusted him, in a sentence that came out faster than the man intended and stopped him cold halfway through. He was not asked about and he was not explained. The name simply arrives, carrying the weight of somebody with the authority to be certain about, and then it goes.

No rank. No world. No service. No description of a face, a voice, or a room he has ever been in.

Whoever he is, at least one soldier of the Royal Shayron Defence Force believes Prodar knows exactly where he is and approves of it.

Profanity

Four words do almost all of the work, they are the same four words on every world in this volume, and they are older than anything else still in general use.

What is actually said

Two of them carry the load. One is a verb doing duty as a verb, a noun, an adjective, an intensifier and a piece of punctuation, and in the recorded material it appears in that last role more often than in all the others together. The second is a noun for waste that has quietly become the word for any situation. After those, a distant third for the underworld and a distant fourth for damnation, both of which survive in mouths that have never held the belief either one came from.

Everything else is regional, weak, and disappearing.

The thing worth noticing

Nobody teaches this. It is not in the centrally produced material, has never been printed in a primer, and no foundation anywhere has ever taught it under contract.

It is also, of everything in Galactic Standard, the part that varies least. A Guardsman off Modanick and a dock hand on a world that has never had a garrison reach for the same word, in the same position in the sentence, at the same provocation.

Nobody transmitted it deliberately. It moved anyway, on ships, in messes, between strangers with nothing else in common, and it arrived intact.

Where it is not allowed

Two of the eleven tower proprietors refuse it outright, which is why there are worlds where a broadcast drama sounds like nobody has ever been annoyed.

A separate class entirely

The words this volume catalogues as Crag and Scarg are not profanity and are not treated as profanity by anybody. They are ordinary vocabulary that happens to do harm. Nobody lowers their voice for either, no proprietor refuses either, and no notice anywhere discourages the second one at all.

Which is the whole distinction. The words people apologise for are the ones that mean nothing.

[Compiler's note: our holdings are eighty per cent commercial and administrative paperwork, in which nobody swears at all. Everything in this entry comes from the four thousand two hundred and six testimonies, where they do, constantly, and where nobody once stopped to explain what they meant.]

Proxy marriage

There is a form. Of course there is a form.

Why it exists

The Guard runs a rotation that can put a person six months from anywhere, and it does not adjust that rotation for weddings. So the galaxy long ago accepted that one half of a marriage may not be in the room, and built the machinery to handle it.

How the absent party appears

As a projection, where the relay will hold, which it frequently will not. As a stand-in, usually a sibling or a squadmate, who says the words and is then teased about it for the rest of their life. Or not at all: an empty frame set where a person should be standing, and everybody proceeds around it.

The empty frame is the older custom and the one people find harder to watch.

The paperwork

Countersigned, witnessed at both ends, filed against a service number. It is entirely routine. There is a queue for it. The clerk who processes them has processed thousands and can do one in under four minutes.

And the version nobody puts on a poster

Some worlds permit a marriage to be registered after one party has died, on application, with authorisation from an office high enough that the applications are counted in single figures per year. The reasons given are pensions, legitimacy and inheritance. The reasons given are not the reasons.

Quantum-thread armour

The good armour. Pre-war, unmakeable, and getting rarer every year in the most literal way possible.

Nobody knows how to spin the thread any more. Damaged suits are patched from suits that are past saving, which means every repair anywhere reduces the total amount of it in existence. The Guard tracks its remaining serviceable area as a single number, and that number goes down annually.

Ship hulls are armoured with the same material out of the same pool. Every year a committee decides how much goes on hulls and how much goes on people.

Who gets a whole suit is a priority list. Everybody else gets a patched one, a partial one, or the current-manufacture substitute, which is heavier, worse, and available in quantity.

The quarantine authority

Biosecurity authority of the Polaris system. Seated in Kelton City. Regulates movement of organic material between the ten inhabited bodies.

Basis

The system grows single crops at planetary scale. A blight established on Weton would not be contained on Weton. The authority exists to prevent that and has, on the record, prevented it: no system-wide crop failure appears in any return this archive holds.

Powers

Inspection, seizure, destruction, and the closure of movement between bodies. Closure requires no external approval and is not appealable. Movement of persons is subject to the same instrument as movement of material.

Use

Filed. Closures ordered GC 4442 to GC 4461: 61. Mean duration 9 days. Longest, 214 days, Dorrow to Kelton, in a year in which the Dorrow milling wage was in dispute.

The authority's closure notice gives the biological grounds, in plain language, every time. The Restoration has verified the grounds in every case it could check and could check 44 of the 61.

The Queen's Anniversary

The biggest day in the Royal calendar, held in the Capital District on Shayron, on a fixed date.

A procession the length of the processional way, an address from the High Castle, food put out for everybody, and rites in the evening in the quarters still keeping them. Nobody is ticketed. The way and the three great squares hold two hundred and fourteen thousand people, and in recent years the city has stopped pretending the crowd is that small.

It is a religious day and a civic one at the same time, because the Queen is not merely reigning by Tracine's favour. She is held to be Tracine present on Shayron. It is not her birthday and nobody treats it as one.

She has not been there for four years

No announcement, no explanation, no death declared. The day has been held in full each of those years, with the King giving the address.

Nothing in Royal law covers the absence of a sovereign who is identified with a goddess. There is no office with the standing to say she is gone.

Quinn Domnall

An accountant. Not a soldier, and about to be sent somewhere that will not care about the difference.

Deep lines cut into his face and heavy bags under his eyes, and neither of them arrived in a hurry. He looks tired in a way that has stopped being a state and become a feature.

The record, in his own words

Basic at Fort Actom. 704B, Accountant. Advanced training on Maldo. Officer school at Wedear. Led supply routes out to Fawn. He can recite it in about eight seconds and does, whenever somebody implies he has never been anywhere.

He works in the accounting division on the Mothership, under fluorescent light that hums, retyping twenty years of financial records by hand because the war killed every computer and Guardnet is barely walking. It is enormous, pointless, and never finished.

Years ago he started putting small deliberate errors into the ledgers. A private rebellion, one number at a time. Nobody has ever noticed, because what the division wanted from twenty years of retyping was the twenty years and not the numbers.

Older than the men he is about to be standing next to. Precise. Not brave and not a coward. A man who worked out a long time ago that his work does not matter and kept doing it correctly anyway.

His contract is nearly up.

And then a file lands on his desk

A transfer, to a security posting on a frozen moon called Sonaff. He is being sent to guard a hangar.

Ranzi

An officer Pavlock served under, and the reason he does not talk about that deployment.

What survives of him is one image, and it is Pavlock's: Ranzi pinned behind the shattered trunk of a tree, one of the tall pale ones that grow like palms, the trunk blown open and no longer thick enough to hide a man. Pulse rounds coming in with that high whine they make. Comms jammed. No line of retreat and nowhere on the flank that was not already somebody else's.

He was shouting, and the whole of it is on the record:

"PAVLOCK! GET THAT BIRD IN THE AIR OR WE'RE FUCKING DEAD!"

He got out

A last volley, a run alongside a private, and into the rear hull of a ship that should not have started. Whatever it is that Pavlock cannot put down about that day, it is not this man's death.

The rec room

A cavern of a room with a ceiling high enough to lose a ball in, and the loudest place on the ship that is not an engine.

The floor is waxed until it shines like liquid silver, and the walls are cheap warm wood, which fools nobody and works anyway. It sounds like a symphony badly conducted: laughter, the flat pock of moonballs on hardwood, the squeak of shoes, and the clang of dropped weights.

One half is for sweating

A moonball court, a weights area, and the grunting of men who have decided that today is the day.

The other half is for not

Booths and tables, vending machines dispensing snacks from six worlds, and screens running holo-movies nobody is really watching. Somebody usually has a bowl of luminescent starfruit out, which glows faintly like a handful of small nebulae and is mostly there to look at.

The Zero-G Cue table, tucked in a corner, is billiards adapted for low gravity, which means the balls travel forever and a badly judged shot is still travelling when your turn ends. It draws a small, obsessive crowd.

And the cards

Mead cards in partners, played for chips that mean nothing, at tables that stay occupied for eleven hours at a stretch.

It is the only room aboard where rank quietly stops mattering, which is not in any standing order and is enforced more strictly than most things that are.

Redleaf

The Monveri crop. A cultivated leaf with a psychoactive resin, legal there by name in their accession terms and legal on twenty-two other worlds by local statute.

Monver taxes it like anything else and enforces nothing, and the line you will hear if you ask, more or less word for word from anyone: soldiers who fight hard should relax hard, and it helps with what fighting does to you.

That is mostly true.

The health there is, every year, a minority for whom it stopped being recreation a long time ago. Nobody has proposed a statute. It is the one subject on that world where a direct question gets a change of topic.

The Refugee Displacement

The largest movement of people that has ever happened, and the thinnest file in this archive.

Somewhere between four and nine billion, by our own estimate, from housing stock, ration issues and port arrivals on forty-one worlds. Other figures in circulation run from two billion to eleven.

Why it broke everything

The receiving worlds could not manufacture. Housing, water, medicine and food could be moved and could not be made. A world of four hundred million taking in a billion people was not facing a policy question. It was facing arithmetic.

What worlds did, from the port records
  • Took everyone, 9 worlds
  • Took them and camped them, 22 worlds
  • Took some, chosen against stated criteria, 31 worlds
  • Refused, 19 worlds
  • Refused, and fired on the ships, 6 worlds

Each of those is a category of surviving document, because port authorities file their orders and the orders lasted.

What it did to the map

People moved along survival lines, not along which side they were on. So almost every world came out of it holding a population from the other side of the war, and the fighting inside borders started before anybody declared anything.

And what everyone learned

That where you were standing decided whether you lived. Which is why, when the Guard offered free movement between member worlds, that is the clause the accession debates argue about.

Still unfinished

Whether the descendants of those arrivals are citizens is a live question in the statute of forty-four worlds in this volume. In twelve of them it is unresolved in the third generation.

[Compiler's note: this is the largest thing that ever happened to ordinary people in this galaxy, and it is four pages.]

The relay network

Every word that crosses between stars crosses a tower, and the towers belong to churches.

How that happened

They built them to carry sermons. That was the entire purpose and nobody objected, because at the time there was a government, and infrastructure a faith paid for itself was infrastructure the government did not have to fund.

Then the government stopped existing. And in the years while everything else was being looted, burned or simply abandoned, eleven religious organisations defended their transmitters with everything they had, because to them the towers were not assets. They kept them. They still have them.

What that means now

There is no such thing as broadcasting in this galaxy. There is only buying airtime, by the hour, from one of eleven proprietors, at rates that vary by proprietor and by what is in the broadcast.

Music, news, sport, drama, education, weather, and the Guard's own morale material all compete for the same hours on the same towers, and the schedule is set by somebody whose actual job is theological.

Two of the eleven refuse whole categories of material outright

The refusals are in the correspondence and are not negotiable and have not moved in decades. Which means there are worlds where certain genres have simply never been heard, not because anybody banned them, but because the tower that reaches those worlds will not carry them.

Nobody voted for this and nobody can undo it

The towers are private property, lawfully held, defended at cost, and there is no authority in existence with the standing to take them.

The most powerful information organ in the galaxy is a customer.

The Renewal

Married on a two-year term, and then you both decide again.

The mechanism

The marriage runs for a fixed period. At the end of it, either party renews or does not. Declining is not a divorce, carries no penalty, and requires no reason. You simply do not sign, and it is over, cleanly, that day.

Inside a term it is strict

Physical infidelity during a term is a criminal matter and is actually prosecuted, which sounds severe until you notice the logic: you had a door, it was clearly marked, and you chose not to use it.

The stated intent is that trust should be active rather than assumed. You are not married to somebody who has not left. You are married to somebody who chose this again, recently, with a clean exit available, and that is a materially different thing to be told.

And that is exactly what makes it brutal

There is always a door. Both of you know precisely when it opens next.

People count months. Everybody on that world counts months, and everybody pretends not to, and the last few weeks of a term are the loudest silence in any household there.

The fertility clause, where it survives, allows either party to decline without any social cost at all if a couple has wanted children and not managed them within a stated period. It is cold, it is practical, and it is almost certainly a post-war demographic measure that nobody has got round to repealing.

The Rescue

Somebody's partner has been taken. Somebody is going to have to go and get them.

The rite

One of the couple is captured by the families, either one, and sometimes both at once. The other has to come and retrieve them, and between here and there is a gauntlet assembled entirely by people who have known them since they were small.

Swim the length of a pool while your relatives throw eggs at you. Climb something. Stand there and answer for a specific thing you did when you were nineteen. Be mocked, at length, by everyone who raised you, in front of the person you are marrying.

What it is not

It is not save them from us. Nobody is pretending. The framing is: your partner is in trouble, and everybody here would like to see exactly how far you will actually go.

What it is for

Two things at once. Every relative gets to discharge every frustration they have ever had about this match without doing the smallest amount of real harm. And everybody gets to watch somebody persevere, visibly, for the person they love, which is the thing the whole institution is supposed to be about and is otherwise almost never demonstrable.

It is done before the wedding rather than as part of it. It is open, it is enjoyed, and it is photographed relentlessly.

Resmole

Dust, a river, a clock tower and a fuel depot. Occupied because of where it is and for no other reason anybody has written down.

The town sits along the water between two mountain ranges, low buildings the colour of the ground, and it is held because it has enough flat land for airstrips and sits between two places that matter. That is the entire strategic case and nobody has ever pretended otherwise.

The rhythm of it

In daylight the streets are empty and the heat comes off the stone. At night the local militias come out and take shots from the dark, and the shots almost never land. A round cracks into a potted plant on a third-storey roof and brings the whole thing down into the street in a spray of soil, and nobody on the gate so much as looks up.

That is the thing about Resmole. The gunfire becomes furniture. Boys sit on munitions crates scraping dried mud off their boots and sharing a greyleaf cigarette while the town shoots at them, and after a few weeks they stop flinching, and after a few months they stop noticing.

Which is exactly how it kills you

Nothing about Resmole is a battle. There is no line, no objective, and nothing to take. There is only a long stretch of not much happening, and then one round out of thousands finds somebody, usually because they went somewhere they did not need to go.

The garrison

Casualties run eleven to nineteen a year and are filed by name. Some of those names belong to sixteen-year-olds. The local dead are not filed at all.

The civil reconstruction programme was chartered on occupation, funded for four years, and filed its final report. Every appropriation after that is nil.

The Restoration

Us. The people who put this volume together.

A civilian society with no charter, no powers, and no authority to make anybody do anything. Founded in GC 4443 by nineteen people who thought somebody ought to be collecting what was left.

Four hundred and eleven registered volunteers, of whom perhaps sixty to eighty do anything in a given year. Eleven paid staff. Funded by subscriptions and two endowments.

What we have

1,411,206 catalogued pages. 88,400 more transcribed off damaged media. 4,206 recorded testimonies. Three rooms.

What we do not have

Access. Between GC 4443 and now we have made 219 written applications to institutions holding material. We have had 61 replies. Nine of those granted access to anything.

We are not historians and we do not issue findings. We print what we have, we mark how we came by it, and we say plainly when we are guessing.

Riflo

The main settlement of the settled belt, and as close as Maspin gets to a city.

It sits where the jungle allows it: low buildings, stone and grown timber, walkways that go around trees rather than through them, and the Palace at the middle of it with the Council inside. Everything on this world that involves a decision happens here.

The port is the other half of the place. Almost every ship that touches Maspin is a Trailblazer hull or chartered by one, which is a small number of arrivals for a whole world and a very large number for this one. Crews come through, drink the local wine, and leave.

It is the only place on Maspin where a visitor is unremarkable, and the only place most Maspin will ever see an outsider.

Rockroot

A tuber that grows in thin soil, in rock cracks, in heat and in frost, and keeps for two years in a sack without anyone doing anything to it.

It is the food of last resort on a dozen marginal worlds and the food of the Path of Root on Marfeld, where a seventeen-year-old with no tools and no supplies is expected to find enough of it to live on.

It tastes appalling. No world in this volume exports it and eleven import it, which tells you everything about who is eating it and why.

The Royal Houses

They started as metalworkers.

A guild with trade secrets got rich, and then powerful, and then crowned. There is no divine right anywhere in the story and no conquest either. The progression is in the commercial record at every step: articles, apprentice indentures, oaths of secrecy about process, schedules of charges. You can watch a trade body turn into a landed interest turn into a monarchy by reading its invoices.

The court still speaks foundry. Titles, ensigns, the ceremonial of investiture, all of it is forge language, and a good deal of it is applied to objects and acts that have nothing to do with metal any more.

Two capitals

Maldo works. Shayron is where the crown lives and where the ceremonies happen. Parliament, ministries, embassies and the High Council are all on Maldo, on purpose, so the beautiful one never has to host the galaxy.

Names

Given name, then Vot, then house and line. Royal blood is spread very thin across a very large number of houses, and it comes with a seat and a small maintenance and not much else. Half the galaxy can claim some.

The war

They stayed out of it. Their account is prudence, the neighbours use other words, and neither is a document. What is certain is that the Royal fleet and the Royal archive both came through intact, which is why this volume knows more about a Royal childhood than about most worlds.

Money

Taxes from their own systems, dues from protectorates, and royalties from arrangements with third parties. The largest of those is Astonia, and it pays them by the head.

Seen in the manuscript at Ch. 24.

Royal scrip

The crown's own money. Struck and issued from Maldo, accepted in the Royal systems and in the protectorates, and it is the instrument in which every tax, due and royalty the houses collect is assessed.

What it is worth

What the houses say. There is no metal behind it, no grain, no reserve of anything, and no schedule anywhere setting out what would have to happen for that to change. It is worth something because the Royal treasury will take it back, and the Royal treasury will take it back because it issued it.

The name

Scrip is not the word the ministries use. The ministries say the Royal credit, in every instrument, without exception. Everybody else on every dock in the galaxy says scrip, and has since before anybody now living was working, and the two words have never once appeared in the same document.

Which is the entire political situation in one noun. Polaris pays its farmers in a currency that is excellent and only good in Polaris, and every person in that system knows exactly what that arrangement is. The crown does the same thing across two systems and a string of protectorates, and the difference is that on Maldo it is not sayable.

Against the credit

Not published. There is a rate, it moves, and it is quoted between banks and by nobody in public. The treasury has never printed one and has never been asked in a form it would have to answer.

The Restoration has looked for a stated conversion in nineteen years of ministerial filing and has not found one. What we have found, repeatedly, is contracts written in both units on the same page with no bridge between them, which is what people do when the answer is understood and nobody wants it in writing.

What comes in

Taxes from the Royal systems. Dues from the protectorates. Royalties from arrangements with third parties, of which by far the largest is Astonia, which pays by the head.

And the problem with that

The Astonian accounting is performed by the Guard. The treasury receives a figure and a payment in its own money, and does not receive the returns underneath, and has not, on the record, asked for them.

So the crown's single largest revenue line is a number somebody else worked out, converted at a rate nobody publishes, into a currency the crown values itself.

What it will not buy

Nothing scheduled. Nothing unreplaceable. Maldo steel is worked out and no quantity of Royal scrip will produce another tonne of it, which the maintenance books on every Royal building record in the plainest possible way, one repair at a time.

[Compiler's note: the treasury on Maldo has never failed to honour this money and we should say so. It has also never been asked to honour very much of it at once.]

Royal Shayron Defence Force

The Crown's own soldiers, and the other army in the room whenever the Guard is in it.

Shayron keeps a real military. Not the ivory line on the approach to the castle, which is ceremony, but formations with ranks, postings, transports and a rank structure that runs its own way: first and second sergeants, a whole ladder of them, arranged to a logic that predates the Guard and has never been brought into line with it.

How close they are to the Guard

Close. They train together, exercise together, and lend each other people, in the ordinary manner of two militaries that have never fought each other and both benefit from the arrangement. A Royal officer on a Guard transport is unusual enough to be worth a second look and not unusual enough to be reported.

The oath is recited rather than sworn, and every soldier in the force has it by heart:

"I serve the people of Shayron and uphold the dignity of the"

Names

A Royal soldier working outside Shayron very often is not using the one on his file. This is normal, it is authorised, and everybody on both sides of the arrangement knows it, which does not stop it being awkward whenever somebody says it out loud.

Saigo

Warm, coastal, and organised entirely around a university. It is the place trying to rebuild the machines that stopped in GC 4401, and it is losing, slowly, in public.

The programme

Every drone, remote and unmanned system in the galaxy died at once and none of them came back. The reconstruction was chartered here in GC 4412 and has been funded ever since. Output to date: 2,411 registered patents and eleven classes of working device.

What people think of that

The member consultations are consistent and they contradict themselves. Asked whether autonomous systems should be rebuilt, respondents say no by a wide margin. Asked separately what they miss most about the world before, they say those systems.

Both answers are in the same returns, from the same people, in the same year.

Character

There is no industry here that is not attached to the university and no politics that is not conducted inside it. The beaches are good and the students use them.

A religious note

What this volume catalogues as Simulationism is concentrated here and is professed disproportionately among senior faculty and the donors who fund them. Saigo does not treat this as a religious matter and files no observance for it.

Sakasin

A world Castle Team deployed to, remembered by exactly one of them for exactly one reason.

What happened there

A round went through Berji Kegeron's shoulder. He lived, the wound closed, and by every measure that the Guard records it was an unremarkable engagement on an unremarkable rotation.

Why it is in this archive at all

Because he has never stopped taking it apart. Not the pain of it. The geometry.

A few inches higher and the round takes his head instead. He has traced every choice he made that morning, every habit, every unconscious shift of weight, and every choice the man on the other end made across his entire life, and concluded that the two paths were always going to intersect at that exact point in the air.

Whether that is insight or damage is not a question the record can settle. But the shoulder healed, and the thought did not.

Sansvor

said quickly by anyone from there, the name comes out in about a syllable and a half

A rich world that stopped being maintained. Almost nothing here was destroyed. Almost nothing here has been repaired either, and the difference between those two sentences is the whole of the place.

What they built

The century before the war was an inventive one here and they spent it: airship terminals, rail, cut stone, cathedrals, civic halls, libraries with reading rooms sixty metres long. Then the paint ran out, and nobody made more paint, and a wall came down and there were no stonecutters left.

The characteristic building on Sansvor is structurally sound and open to the sky.

Why that is survivable

The weather is mild. A classroom missing a wall and half a ceiling is still a classroom here, and is used as one. Desks, board, books, and you keep your coat on. Birds come in. Nobody stops the lesson.

Nothing in the country is dangerous. Prey animals, and a raptor that takes them.

Who is still here

The universities did not close. Their endowments failed, the faculties went unpaid, and a good number of them kept teaching anyway. Literacy returns, where a local authority still bothers to produce one, are among the highest in this archive. The museums are intact and uncatalogued. Dragon's blood trees have come up through the roof of the north rail terminal and are now part of the roof.

Politics

1 gap

Between nineteen and thirty organised associations of any weight, the range being a disagreement about what counts. Read their literature and you find the argument is about what the world used to be and who gets to say what it becomes next. It is not about food. Nobody here is short of food.

The blockade, and the reason this entry is filed as contested.

Guard material, and most people in the port towns, hold that a belligerent closed the world's shipping during the war and the Guard broke it open in GC 4409, and that the Guard is therefore remembered here as the people who came.

A smaller number, mostly inland, hold that the closing continued after the war ended, and continued deliberately, until the world could be relied on to ask.

Port manifests would settle it. The port record for GC 4402 to 4409 is not in this archive. [FILING INCOMPLETE]

Scarg

Rubbish. Refuse. What you throw out.

An ordinary word, in ordinary use, on every world that speaks Standard. It carries no charge and nobody flinches at it.

Except

In a galaxy where nothing can be built any more, the line between rubbish and stock is a matter of who is looking. A dealer in pre-war components and a man carrying a sack to the tip are handling the same objects and using different words for them.

So the word does quiet work. Something is scarg until somebody who knows better sees it, and then it is not, and then it never was.

There are people who make a living entirely in that gap.
