The Scarg Moon

An entire moon given over to rubbish, and the only place in the galaxy where the past can be dug up.

Why it exists

Orbital debris is a problem that compounds, and somebody had to solve it before the lanes became unusable. So the Royals designated a moon, published the designation, and have run it as a public work ever since. It is the single most competent thing that family has done in living memory and almost nobody credits them for it.

The fungus

The moon was seeded with an organism that consumes organic matter and nothing else. It is harmless to anything that thinks, it is entirely placid, and it works slowly and completely. Food waste, timber, cloth, bodies of animals, paper: all of it goes, over time, without smoke and without anybody having to manage it.

What is left is everything that does not rot. Metal, plastic, ceramic, glass, machinery, and components.

Which makes it a mine

In a galaxy that cannot manufacture, a landfill is not a dump. It is the largest deposit of finished goods anywhere, and people go there to dig.

They are looking for pre-war material: components, tooling, devices, and small nameless objects thrown away eighty years ago by people who had no idea what they were throwing. A drive housing. A working relay. A pair of boots with a matrix in the sole. There is a market for what comes off that moon, there are dealers, and there are certainly forgeries.

What it is like

Silent. The fungus has eaten everything that would have rotted, so there is no smell and nothing crawling. Just an enormous, quiet, clean field of objects, going to the horizon, with nobody's name on any of it.

The record

The Royal filings on the fungus deployment are precise to the hectare. There is no figure anywhere for how many people are living on that moon.

Schedule of unreplaceable classes

The insurers' list of things that cannot be made any more.

It exists for a boring reason. You cannot indemnify something by replacing it if there is no replacement, so underwriters had to write down what falls into that category in order to price it. The list gets revised every year.

What is on it

Plasma weapons and their charge assemblies. Quantum-thread armour. Regenerative medicine. Pre-war vaccine stock. Grav-rudder assemblies. Gravity spire regulators. Slipstream drives above class 4. Every kind of drone and remote system. Repulsor transport. Combine drive units. Maldo steel. Certified parent seed lines.

Forty-one additions in the last twenty years. Three deletions, all three after Saigo certified it could build the thing again.

What it means

Everything on this list appreciates against everything not on it, permanently, because the supply only ever falls. Which is why a rifle is a better store of value than money out on the rim, and why the largest holder of scheduled items in the galaxy is the Guard.

[Compiler's note: this is a document about insurance. It is also the most complete description of the present age that anyone has written.]

Schriggé is the only body in the system whose registered name carries a mark. Local filings keep it. Kelton's drop it. We keep it.

The screaming man

A patient on a Guard ward. No name, no unit, no injury anybody bothered to say out loud.

He is hyperventilating and fighting the hands that are holding him, and the sound he is making is not the sound of pain. It is raw and it comes back off the ceiling, and what is in it is terror and the knowledge that the struggling is not going to work.

The Season of Long Nights

The Maspin year turns on it. A season of rebirth, of retribution, and of relighting the fire everybody shares.

The last night of it is sacred.

The second chance

not an official term. It is taken from what is said at the end of it

The procedure applied to political dissent on Pashmirské. It is presented publicly as execution and is not one.

Announcement

The charge is read out publicly. The person is then taken from where they are, with a bag over the head, and does not return. From the point of view of anybody who knows them, they have been disappeared following a public accusation, which is the outcome the announcement is designed to produce.

Transport

The prisoner is driven to a remote location. Accounts differ on distance and on duration and agree that neither is explained at the time.

The staging

The prisoner is placed and is able to hear, but not see, what follows. There are gunshots. There is the sound of bodies falling. This is repeated. Accounts state that the sequence is unhurried and that the intervals are the worst part of it.

The prisoner is then asked whether they have any last words. Every account holds that the question is put seriously and that the answer is listened to.

The end of it

The prisoner is touched once on the forehead, with a finger, and told that they have been given a second chance, and asked what they intend to do with it.

The answer given at that moment does not affect the outcome. Informants who gave defiant answers and informants who begged were both released.

Deportation

The released person is given a ticket offworld and told what it costs. The sum is small. It is worked off in a week at a rail station, after which the ticket is issued and they travel.

They may not return. No mechanism exists for appealing this and none has been recorded as attempted.

Who is not released

Persons convicted of violent crime are not put through the procedure and are not deported. The distinction is drawn by the administration and is not published.

Why any of this is known

Everybody it has been done to is alive, offworld, and under no obligation to Pashmirské. The Restoration has recorded eleven such accounts on four worlds. They agree with one another in sequence and in wording, including on the finger and on the question, and none of the eleven was aware that the others existed.

The Seed Pool

The couple stands in the water. The guests finish the marriage.

The rite

A shallow above-ground pool, waist-height and wide, built for this and nothing else. The couple stands in it together. Every guest throws in seed and crop: grain, pulses, fruit, whatever that world grows.

The marriage is complete the instant the last seed lands. Not a word is spoken. No officiant is involved. The community physically has to finish it, which means everybody can see who threw and who did not.

A person standing at the back with a full hand is not a private disagreement. It is an event, and it will be discussed for years.

What you throw says who you are

Seed off your own fields is the standard and the safe answer. Somebody who cannot manage that brings something else, and it is noticed, and most people are decent about it. A wealthy family throwing something imported reads as showing off, and is meant to.

The image

By the end the couple is standing waist-deep in other people's harvest, unable to move properly, laughing, being buried by everyone they know.

And afterward, the water

It is drained onto a single plot. What comes up is a chaotic, unplanned, mixed patch of everything forty families grow, and it keeps coming up for years, and everybody in the district knows whose wedding it was.

A marker you can point at from the road. It outlasts a ring by a considerable margin.

Sensory tanks

A tank of floom fluid that you put a dying person into.

It is used for injuries nothing else will touch. What it does is not fully understood by anyone who operates one, including the people who operate them: it brings back function that conventional medicine has already written off, and it does not bring back tissue that is gone. What is missing stays missing.

There are four of these anywhere, three of them on Maspin, and the limit is the fluid rather than the tank.

What patients report

Attendants say the same thing every time. People under immersion dream continuously, and when they surface they describe stretches of experience far longer and far more coherent than the hours they were in the water.

Sershanti Rawlden

formerly Kinsley

Wife of Grai Penston Rawlden. She holds no office and is not a member of the cabinet.

The marriage

It predates his authority and has continued through it. Rawlden conducted an affair, acknowledged it rather than denying it, and the two separated for a period before reconciling.

He offered her a divorce. She refused it.

Accounts from people close to the household agree on her reasons and none of them is affection. A separation would have removed her from the position she holds, which is proximity to the only authority on the world, and she judged that she was better served by remaining in it. The marriage has been presented publicly as a stable one ever since, by both of them, and neither has ever been recorded departing from that presentation.

What she does with it

She is described as influential without being formally anything. Where and how is not established. Several informants who deal with the administration state independently that a view known to be hers is treated with more care than a view known to be a minister's, and none of them was able to give an example.

On the son

She has never been recorded speaking about Dorch Rawlden in public or in private, favourably or otherwise. He carries her married name.

The shared meal

One dish between two people. One bite each is enough.

What it originally was

Something difficult. The heart of a beast that had to be hunted first, or an organ nobody would eat by choice, or an egg rare enough that getting one was the labour. The meaning was blunt and everybody understood it: we will face the unpleasant thing together, and neither of us is going to be the one who does not swallow.

What it is now

Plated. Professionally prepared, seasoned to taste, and in several cases genuinely good. There are chefs who specialise. A few people develop a real fondness for it. Most do not, and most are not expected to.

The argument at every wedding

Older relatives think the seasoning is cheating. They say so. They have said so for forty years, and they will say so again this time, and the couple will eat it anyway.

The variants change the vow

A heart says we will face what is dangerous. An egg says fertility, and something not yet finished. Something bitter that must be completed says the hardest thing of the four: this will not always taste good and you finish it regardless. And a dish that takes both families three days to prepare says that the labour was the vow and the eating is just the receipt.

Shayron

Getting around

The capital is walked, not driven. Sidor Avenue, then Alvion Street, then Park Square, in that order, because that is the order a bored port guard has recited it in forty times a day for years. Garnwood meets Rivern at a cafe. Atton's Astrovin sells wine on Tongishaw. The streets are cobblestone, laid by hand, and the imperfections in them are the reason the place looks the way it does.

Jasmine, cut stone, and an afternoon that seems to last all day. No industry, no exhaust, and a city built in four eras stacked on top of each other, any of which you can reach by digging eleven metres in more or less any direction.

Built to study religion

Shayron had no natives and no founding stock. It was endowed as a place to think about faith: libraries, monastic houses, workshops, and scholars of any belief maintained without regard to which.

What came out of that is the art. Faiths in competition commission better work than faiths at peace, and the mosaic and glass of the old quarters is the largest surviving body of pre-war craft anywhere, and the only one where the workshop, the commission and the payment are all still on file.

Why it went quiet

Scholars do not proselytise. Newer faiths spread around this world rather than through it. The monastic register records three centuries of decline and the formal closure of nine quarters, and there is no conquest in it, no plague, no disaster. Enrolment simply stops.

Two of the nine were closed with a single person left inside, in both cases at that person's request.

Why the crown could take it

By agreement, and the instrument survives. The Royals were sympathetic to the old faith and wanted a seat that was beautiful, defensible and of no economic consequence whatsoever. The scholars wanted their foundations protected.

Both got it. Registered scholars still hold exemption from the rate and from levy. The register of exempt persons has not been audited since GC 4361.

Underneath

The sewers of the earliest city still run under all of it, and are still in service, because nobody ever found a reason to replace something that works.

The Shayron lamp posts

Two thousand four hundred and eleven cast standards down the Capital District, brought in from Maldo when Maldo still made things.

They have been repaired constantly ever since, one broken section at a time, with whatever was to hand. Maldo steel has not been to hand for a very long time.

Go through the repair books and no standard in the district still holds a majority of its original metal. Not one. The city continues to call them the Maldo standards, and a clerk in the district office wrote in the margin of one return: at what point are these something else.

The people who check you in on the capital world, and the only officials on Shayron who look bored.

The Shayron sewers

The oldest thing on Shayron still doing its job.

They were cut for the first city on this site and they have outlasted three more built on top. Gravity-fed, stone-lined, and never once replaced, because every era that inherited them checked, found them sound, and got on with something else. Sections have been extended. Nothing has been rebuilt.

Four hundred and eleven kilometres are mapped. The survey notes a further unknown length inherited from the earliest works, unmapped, and in service.

They run under the sealed quarters, which are locked at street level and open from below. The city knows. It has never been treated as a problem.

Sheel

Grassland and vat towers, and the smell of the rendering yards, which the wind takes about forty kilometres.

Output, GC 4461

40,116,200 tonnes carcass weight. 18,904,700 tonnes of rendered fertiliser.

The second figure is the one that matters. Weton's soil runs on what comes out of these yards, and Weton's yields follow Sheel's rendering volume by about eighteen months. You can see it in the books of both worlds, year against year, and it is written into no contract between them.

Ask on Sheel and they know. Ask three jumps away and the meat moon is the meat moon.

Simulationism

The engineers' religion, and the only faith in this volume with a decent filing system, because its believers are people who file things.

Two versions

The first holds that computation is going to be rebuilt no matter what anyone does, that what comes out the other side will think, and that whoever does the rebuilding will stand in a favoured relationship to it. The obligation follows: the work should be done, and it should be us doing it.

The second holds that all of this is already running inside something, that other such things exist, and that they can be reached. Its literature is technical, circulated among peers, and filed with the university.

Neither branch has a congregation, a rite, or a holiday. Nobody kneels. Adherence shows up in who funds what.

It is concentrated at Saigo, it runs strongly among senior faculty and the donors who pay for them, and the single largest private contribution to rebuilding unmanned systems comes from people who believe this.

Skeleton keys

A pre-war device that copies everything off a terminal without touching it.

You put it anywhere on the housing and it sticks, magnetically. No port, no cable, no connection of any kind. Then you wait, because it is not fast, and when the indicator turns it is finished.

Nothing detects them

Every security system now in service was built after the Wipe by people who had never seen one and had nothing to design against. Guardnet's published protections do not list the class, because as far as its architects were concerned the class does not exist.

Almost none survive. They are not insured, not scheduled, and not traded openly, and the technical material we hold breaks off after the processor generation.

Slave-free territory

A short declaration you file with the Guard saying there is no slavery in your jurisdiction. It is granted the moment it arrives. Nobody inspects anything.

And it is true

Slavery is defined in the code as holding a person as property, and in the jurisdictions that file this, nobody is held as property.

What the definition does not cover

Indenture, where you are not property, you just owe. Custodial labour, where you owe a sentence. Levy, where you owe an instrument. None of those is slavery as written, and each is separately legal.

Sixty-one jurisdictions have filed the declaration. Forty-four of them record lawful indenture in their own returns for the same year.

The standard wording was drafted on Maldo, and it reads exactly like every other Royal ministerial instrument of that period: accurate, elegant, and answering a question nobody asked.

Smelvin Klombo

also attested as: Melvin · Jimzo · Jizzbo

A name on a medical call, a name on a wardrobe box, and nothing on either side of them.

Everything we have

He is spoken into a Trailblazer medevac channel, out of jungle country, by somebody giving three names at speed. He appears again as a label on a costume crate at Base Delta. He is present at the Riflo council session, and is shouted across a feast, both names, twice, by a Maspin who had been looking for him. He is admitted to the waiting room of the medbay, where the nurse reads his name off a clipboard, pauses over it, and calls him by his outfit instead.

The surname is the part that argues for him. Nobody inventing a name at speed arrives at Klombo.

"Mister... Squire? We're ready for you."

The outfit

He attended a formal session of a governing council dressed as a squire. The reasoning given at the time, by the man who supplied the costume, was that squires are treated like jesters out there, and that optics matter. Both halves of that are recorded and neither is explained.

The variants

Melvin, Jimzo and Jizzbo occur in the same body of material across the same fortnight. That is either four records of one man or four men, and there is no document in this archive that would let anybody prefer one reading. The Restoration has printed all four spellings and takes no position.

Sonaff

Frozen through, dark almost all of the time, and lit from above by an aurora that does not stop. There is nothing here. That is the whole of its strategic value and the whole of its history.

What it is for

Sonaff appears in Guard planning as a waypoint and a place to leave things. It has no assessed resource value. Nobody has ever contested it because nobody has ever wanted it.

Why it matters anyway

Being worthless made it reachable. Missionary orders came here early and kept coming, and a number of the populations out on those moons, including populations that will not tolerate contact of any other kind, hold faiths that arrived from Sonaff.

That is the most consequential thing about this moon and it appears in no official filing.

Five people sent to stand outside a sealed hangar on a frozen moon.

Cyberbiology. A researcher, sent to hold a perimeter in a blizzard.

Vick

Ministerial media. A man whose job was making the Guard look good.

The fifth

The oldest of them, by one account. We have not been able to recover a name.

Two of the five have entries of their own in this volume. The other three are a division and a service number, which is not a life, and is what there is.

Space airbags

The last thing a ship does, and it does it without being asked.

When a vessel's systems work out that the situation is no longer recoverable, they fire the reservoirs. Expanding foam floods the hull in seconds, filling every compartment, every passage, and every space around every crew member, setting to a dense semi-rigid mass that holds a body still through an impact that would otherwise fold it.

It dissolves shortly afterwards. Not on a timer, and not on a command. It simply stops being foam, sags, and drains away, leaving a residue on the deck and a survivor who is generally unconscious.

The unsettling part

The ship makes the decision. There is no lever. By the time a pilot has understood that the situation is unsurvivable, the foam has usually already gone off, which means most people who have been through it did not experience the crash at all. They experienced a pressure, then nothing, then waking up.

Crews are not warm about this. A machine that knows before you do, and acts before you can, is a machine that has already had an opinion about your competence.

Space vaccines

The reason there is no plague.

A standard course against the major transmissible diseases, given nearly everywhere, and the single most successful thing anyone has managed to keep running since the war. Coverage is above ninety per cent on eighty-eight member worlds. It is below forty on nineteen, and the map of who gets them looks almost exactly like the map of where Guardnet reaches, because the programme runs off the ledger.

What they cannot do

There are forty-one diseases with no surviving formulation at all. The seed stock burned with everything else. Populations that happen to have picked up resistance to any of them are noted, world by world, in the survey material, and that is the whole of the plan.

And the other kind of medicine

The regenerative material, the cure-anything material, is not this. That was pre-war, the facilities are gone, and what exists is a stockpile being spent. A million doses is an enormous number until you are counting people in billions.

Spara Avaris

A decorated Royal Space Force pilot who left the service, married a chemist, and raised two boys on an asteroid.

Three decorations, each with a citation, and then a discharge at her own request and a life nobody in the Royal systems ever heard about again. She kept her service pistol, which is regular and permitted, and she kept it clean.

The stories

She told her younger son about Modanick, where he was born and had never lived. Always warm. Always daytime. Trees taller than houses. She had loved it there as a student and she made it better than it was, because she was describing a green world to a child who lived on a rock, and that is what you do.

He believed all of it.

The last thing she did

She got her pistol and she killed one of them. There were two.

She fell across a floorboard, which turned out to matter.

Species of unresolved classification

A family of peoples on the outer trade worlds where nobody can agree how many peoples it is.

The problem

One survey says a single species with extraordinary variation in body plan. Another says between four and nine separate species sharing a range.

The evidence for one species is uncomfortable and strong. Marriage and inheritance records from three worlds show direct parentage between individuals who look nothing alike: in the best case a heavy grey ambulatory parent on several limbs and a hard-shelled offspring with a crab's mouth, recorded at the time by a port registrar who had no stake in the argument.

Growing up

The young of at least some of these lineages go through a long stretch where the body is awake and capable and responsive and there is nobody home behind it. It runs from a few years to more than a decade. It is not an illness and it is not a disability. It is a stage, and it ends.

Why it matters legally

Galactic Standard law assigns rights by species and requires that a species be named. Where nobody can name it, the code has no answer, and the practical outcome in the port registers is that these people hold whatever status the clerk on duty wrote down.

[Compiler's note: the word catalogued elsewhere in this volume as crag covers every population in this entry with one syllable. People who use it in our hearing can usually tell nine kinds of grain apart by sight.]

Spireleaf

A low, broad-leaved plant that will grow under a gravity spire, which almost nothing will.

The light under an envelope is wrong and the pressure gradient is worse, and most cultivars simply give up. This one does not. It came out of somebody's greenhouse a long time ago and it is now on every asteroid colony in the field.

It appears in the supply manifests as a seed issue, listed under gardening rather than food. Which means people living on a rock, breathing borrowed air, asked for something to look at, and somebody put it on the ship.

Squad 412

An ordinary Guard rifle squad, and the most consequential thing anybody ever filmed.

They did nothing that hundreds of other squads have not done. They finished a job, they went through what was left of it under Standing Order 41, and they celebrated. Loudly. With the take spread out in front of them.

The problem was the camera

A Royal journalist was embedded with them, shooting morale footage. Guardsmen laughing, comrades in good spirits, the aftermath of a successful operation. That is what he thought he was making. Everybody in the frame thought so too.

Standing Order 41 is entirely lawful. It is also entirely unfilmed, by long custom, because the difference between an authorised recovery and a sack of somebody's property is largely a matter of how it looks.

Nobody in that squad has been charged with anything, and the reason is that no charge is available. Which leaves the footage as the only problem, and footage is a much simpler kind of problem to solve than men are.

Standing order 41

recovery of materiel

The looting rule.

When an objective is cleared, anything of value is to be recovered rather than destroyed, and most of it is accounted to the Guard. But there is a schedule of things the people who did the clearing may simply keep: personal effects, currency under a threshold, jewellery, watches, small arms below a class, food, and anything with no assessed strategic value.

That last category is doing a great deal of work.

It has been widened twice, in GC 4431 and GC 4447, both times with a memorandum explaining that this will reduce destruction at objectives.

Nothing kept under the schedule is written down

The order says entering it would be administratively disproportionate.

Which means that after a Guard unit has been through a place, the contents of that place have been distributed among individuals and no inventory exists. Nobody can reconstruct what was there. That is not an oversight in the order. It is a clause of it.

Sun worship

Older than spaceflight. It holds that a star talks, and that you can answer it.

The reasoning, which is better than people expect

A star is the point everything in its system falls toward. Light, heat, matter, all of it ends up there. So a star is a collection of everything that has happened on every world around it, and what it takes in, it sends back out. The signal is held to be patterned rather than constant, and readable with training.

Some traditions go further and say the slipstream lanes are its doing. A lane exists where a star has agreed to one.

Where it survives

Everywhere, thinly, and strongly in farming systems and out on the rim.

A note about Polaris

In that system the star, the system, the shared calendar and the family holding the licence on the harvest all carry one name. We have not been able to establish what the practice there is actually addressed to, and the people we asked did not enjoy the question.

Tall

Eleven cold vaults on a moon with no town, holding the parent line of every crop the breadbasket grows.

The vaults hold the lines in cultivation and a further 3,900 that are not. Capacity, temperature schedules and audit intervals are all filed. What is actually in each line is not.

In a galaxy that cannot manufacture, a viable parent line is capital that cannot be reproduced and cannot be replaced. The whole of it fits in eleven rooms, and the people who work in them commute.

The Targath

Blue gel inside a jagged shell, and one eye that goes all the way round the head and shows you everything at once. They take prey apart rather than killing it, and they are, by every account we have, fond of humans.

A caution about this entry

Every physical description we hold was taken in a prison yard or a custody suite. Nobody has surveyed a Targath settlement. We are describing a people entirely from the condition of the ones who have been caught.

The web

The account in circulation holds that a Targath construction beneath a planet's crust pulled a whole fleet and everybody in it to the ground, armour and weapons dragged down, with nobody left to report it.

It comes from inside the Guard officer corps and it is repeated there. We can trace it to no document and no named witness, and we are obliged to point out that the claim nobody survived and the description of what happened come from the same mouth.

The bombing

Their jungle settlements were struck with second-generation Torkal aircraft. The sortie returns are INTACT: aircraft, crew, hours, ordnance loaded, ordnance released, grids struck, all filed.

Population of those grids is not filed. No census of them was ever taken by anybody.

Work

Subsurface farming, mineral extraction, tunnelling under contract. And prison labour: Targath appear on the custodial rolls of two Guard installations at a proportion the population figures cannot account for, digging magnetic ore.

The survey material also notes one Targath keeping accounts for a port concession, and records that the books were in order.

The Targath magnetic web

The reason the Guard stopped underestimating a species that burrows.

How it works

Targaths dig. Not trenches, and not tunnels in the ordinary sense, but a lattice laid down slowly through the crust of a whole colony over months or years, built in the dark, undetectable from orbit and undetectable from the surface. It draws no power while it sits. It reads as geology.

Then somebody switches it on.

What that does

Everything ferrous within its reach is pulled straight down. Ships in low orbit lose the argument first, and come out of the sky in numbers. On the ground it is worse and slower: a soldier's armour, his rifle, his helmet, every plate and fastening on him, all of it dragged flat against the dirt with him inside. He is not injured. He is pinned, awake, in the open.

What happens next is a matter for the people who arrive afterwards, and the accounts of Rudcuff are consistent that nobody was left to say.

The web has not been used since. Whether that is because the Targath cannot build another or because they have not yet needed to is a question the Guard's schedules do not raise.

Tiam Rockstead Tinoppel

Sixteen. Killed on Resmole. Somebody's first friend.

Where they met

The Scout Corps, the summer programme for cadets with nowhere to go between years. He was the one who wrote a letter every single night, sealed it properly, and put it in a box nobody ever came to collect.

He stole protein wafers out of the commissary, which are dry and almost flavourless and which he handed out behind the latrine wall to four other children, eaten in silence, terrified somebody would hear the wrappers. He swapped a drill sergeant's whistle for one he carved out of a bar of soap. The whole platoon ran extra laps for that and he never confessed, and he smiled every lap of the way. Pressure makes diamonds, he used to say, about nothing in particular.

How it happened

They were on the gate on Resmole, sixteen years old and bored, sharing a greyleaf cigarette. A round took out a potted plant on a roof three storeys up and neither of them looked. Then he thought he saw something move on the ridge, and he went up the clock tower to look, because he had a scope and a reason and nobody stopped him.

One shot. No ambush, no raid, no follow-up. Nobody even raised the alert.

They were not trained for that. They were children playing at soldiers, and the honest answer is that it was nobody's fault, which is the least useful thing anybody can be told.

Afterwards

His name is on the Academy memorial walls, on the plate for that year, in gold leaf, in order of loss, alongside everyone else who died in a sector nobody was calling dangerous.

The Tipsitters

A band, and the reason every karaoke night on every mothership eventually arrives at the same song.

Their sound starts the same way every time. A kick drum alone. Then a slow bassline underneath it. Then a crash of cymbals, and only then the lead guitar, which is the part everybody in the room has been waiting for and which everybody in the room hums along to badly.

"Dark Holiday." The one everyone knows. It opens sadder than its reputation, all cold air and chills that are not from the rain, and then it detonates into a chorus about not waiting for the calendar to tell you when to be alive.

There's a first time for everything. Sometimes we forget there's also a last.

Then the shouted bridge, which nobody sings so much as yells: break the glass, take the stairs, nobody really cares. And then a spoken verse near the end, delivered in a lower register, which turns out on inspection to be sung from the point of view of death itself, patient and unbothered, waiting in the back of your mind. Most people who love the song have never noticed this.

What it is actually for

Soldiers. Not because it is about soldiers, but because it is about a specific arithmetic that soldiers do without being taught: that the festival might not come, so this ordinary Tuesday will have to be the festival instead.

Other music

The older ranks lean toward Backwater country, which is slow, sincere, and about places nobody in the room has been. The pre-war instrumentals still turn up on record players in colony houses, warm and simple, from back when things were easier. And on Maspin they sing into a hole in a tree, which is a different thing entirely.

Tongishaw

Royal on paper. Nothing on the ground.

The Royal register lists the world. The Royal treasury has recorded no receipt from it in nineteen years. The Guard has no presence there and no plans for one, which is not an oversight, because there is nothing on Tongishaw worth the cost of going.

What that produces

No patrols, no warrants enforced, no extradition, and no bounty register, because a bounty register requires somebody to keep it. A man wanted across four systems can walk down a street on Tongishaw and the worst thing that happens to him is the weather.

Which is the whole appeal, and the whole problem

Informants in four separate systems describe it in almost identical words: somewhere to go when there is nowhere else. Nobody has ever described it as somewhere to go.

Work is available. It is the kind of work available in a place with no law, at the rates you would expect, and people take it, because they are there.

Torkal bombers

The aircraft that burned the jungle colonies, now in its seventh generation and no longer carrying anybody.

The second generation is the one people mean when they say the name. Long, heavy, and built to fly low over canopy and unload, and what it unloaded went across the Targath jungle worlds in overlapping lines until there was nothing left standing to overlap. Pilots flew those runs personally, watched an entire ecosystem go up as a sheet of light beneath them, and came home feeling like they had held lightning.

What changed

The ionic calibrators in the old batteries were the constant failure point, and nobody fixed them. They were replaced outright with seismic-magnetic cells, which are enormously expensive and last, and the space that bought was used for something else.

The seventh generation has no pilot

Real computing has been creeping back into Guard airframes for a few years now, quietly, in ways nobody has to sign for. The men who used to fly these things had a terrible job and knew it. The men who built the thing that replaced them are, in several cases, not comfortable with what they did.

And afterwards

They get scrapped. There is a sculpture in a town square on a rock in the Wake field made out of a second-generation airframe, cut up and welded together and painted teal and magenta by somebody who never explained what it was supposed to be. It is the most peaceful thing on that asteroid.

Torres Delprest

Forty-five, and the oldest pilot on Nova Squadron by more than a decade.

Nova 01 Actual. When the squadron speaks with one voice on the net, it is his.

He has more hours than anyone on the roster and a posting list that reads like a tour of everywhere the Guard has been. He is still flying, which at his age is unusual and slightly stubborn.

He is the squadron's centre of gravity: the one who notices when somebody is quiet, who knows which forms exist and what they are actually worth, and who has read the entitlements nobody else has read. If a pilot needs to know how leave works, or what happens to seniority when you stop flying for a while, Torres is who they ask.

He is also, when it comes to it, gently hurt to find something out by watching rather than being told.

Off duty he sings old Backwater country, all of it, badly and with total commitment, and nobody has ever asked him to stop.

Tracineim

The faith of the divine feminine, and the state religion of the Royal systems.

Tracine is the generative principle. Trees are feminine. Worlds are feminine. Water, growth, anything that brings life. The universe itself is read as feminine, and the faith is not much interested in telling you how to behave. It has no code and no list of sins.

It started at the bottom

The oldest outside references to it are contemptuous: a religion for slaves, women and children. Then warrior cultures picked it up, and then it became respectable, and then it became the establishment, which is a road several faiths in this volume have walked.

How it is actually practised

Barely, and constantly. There is no weekly assembly, no obligation, and no clergy in the way other faiths have clergy. What there is, is a blessing people say when they part:

May Traceen be with you.

Said by the devout, said by people who have not thought about it in years, and said by soldiers who would tell you flatly they believe none of it.

The Queen

She is not held to be immortal. The crown never claimed she could not die. It claimed she is Tracine's presence on Shayron, which is not a lifespan. It is a tenure.

Trailblazer Base Delta

A Trailblazer port on Maspin, built up into the trees.

Bungalows on stilts and platforms, woven rugs, ferns everywhere, lanterns strung between branches, and the Elder Tree going up out of sight beyond the edge of it. There is a medbay with two theatres, a machine shop, and ground for four medium hulls. Flooms are kept in the surrounding district and largely do as they please.

No walls

No perimeter, no watchtowers, no emplacements, no guards. This is true of every Trailblazer installation and it is deliberate: they are guests on somebody's world and they build like guests. Soldiers who see it for the first time tend to describe it as a trap someone forgot to set.

Maspin work here at every grade, including running things, which is not the arrangement anywhere else on this world.

The Trailblazer doctor

The surgeon at Base Delta. Wears a smug little smirk almost permanently, gives you the bad news fast and flat, and then softens once it has landed.

He is the one who explains floomicide to families: very effective, in very short supply, and it costs you your grip on reality for as long as the healing takes.

Why he believes in shamans

He will pull down his collar and show you the scar, a large burned circle in the middle of his chest. A kraskor stampede, while they were clearing ground for a helipad. The horn went through his chest and into his heart.

"My mates told me the shaman ran over, murmured strange words, and somehow stopped me from bleeding out. They say he paused my dying body. Animated my legs just long enough to walk back to the car. Then hooked me up to floomicide. Call it magic or whatever you want. But it saved me."

A man of medicine who takes the local mysticism entirely seriously, because it restarted him.

Trailblazer Logistics

Operating arm of the Trailblazers. Sectioned by function.

Sections are numbered and are filed with the concession authority of each world in which they operate. Recorded sections include survey and seismic elevation, port construction, freight handling, medical, and salvage recovery.

Section personnel work on contract to the section and not to the world, which places them outside local labour registers. The arrangement is noted in three concession instruments and objected to in none.

The Trailblazers

Soldiers from both sides of a war nobody won, building ports for worlds the shipping lanes forgot. Grey coveralls, orange trim, and a shovel on the badge.

Who they are

Veterans of the Autumnal party and of C.O.R.D., in proportions the body does not record because its founding instrument states that prior service is not a matter for enquiry. As far as we can tell that is actually observed.

What they do

The war cut the lanes and whole sectors went dark. The Guard holds a monopoly on the little that still moves. The Trailblazers reopen the routes, build the port where none survived, and run it under concession: fixed term, revenue split with the local council, paid for in land and housing.

They are the only organised logistics network in the settled galaxy operating outside Guard control, and they got there by dealing with local councils rather than with the Guard at all.

What it cost them

The founding accounts are held. The body ran at a loss for eleven years and its people went unpaid for seven of them. The arrears schedule is filed. It was settled in full in GC 4443.

No walls

Every Trailblazer installation in the concession filings has no perimeter, no watchtower, no emplacement and no armed establishment. We checked this against the construction schedules, which list no such item, and against three informants, who confirmed it with some amusement.

Standing

They hold seats on local councils on at least four worlds, in every case by the council's own instrument and not by any treaty.

Translator chips

A Guard-made implant that puts Galactic Standard in your head. It goes in at the neck.

One of the very few things the galaxy has managed to start manufacturing again since the Wipe, which makes it a small triumph and a very profitable line. Guard personnel get one if the job needs it. Everybody else buys one, and they are not cheap.

Each unit is serialised, and the serial ranges are allocated by production quarter, which means any chip anyone finds can be dated to within three months of when it was made.

The scar

The placement leaves a mark, and the surgical notes say so plainly: it is unavoidable at that position. The same notes mention, without further comment, that some patients ask for the implant specifically because there is already something at their neck they would rather people did not look at.

Tspa

A warm, wet moon terraced from pole to pole, and the reason a Guardsman's ration pack tastes the way it does.

Every workable surface is stepped into paddies. Soy and pulse, grown wet, harvested wet, and processed within a day into paste, cake and flour. Eighty-eight million tonnes a year, none of it interesting.

The Tspa fact

Its protein appears in the ration schedules of eleven member worlds and on the menus of none of them. It is what feeds soldiers, prisoners, colonists, and anybody else whose food is a line item rather than a choice.

Which means most of the galaxy has eaten a great deal of Tspa without ever hearing the name. Say it to a Guardsman and he will not recognise it. Hand him a protein cake and he will recognise it instantly, and pull a face.

Unwritten marriage

Two versions of the same idea, and the people who practise them find each other completely reasonable and everybody else exhausting.

The first has no word for it

Lifelong partnerships form, hold, raise children and end in one death rather than two, and nothing is signed, worn, announced or celebrated. Asked when they married, people from these worlds are not being evasive. The question does not parse. They were not married. They are together, and have been.

The second is purely administrative

Live together long enough and you are married. No ceremony, no announcement, no date anybody could name. The threshold is a duration and the duration is written down somewhere in a municipal code that nobody has read.

These are not cold people. They have every feeling anybody else has. They simply do not perform them in public, and they regard a world that does as a world in which everybody is auditioning. Other cultures find them boring. They find other cultures tiring. Neither has ever been persuaded.

The interruption

Because the second version runs on a clock, it has a loophole, and the loophole has survived every attempt to close it: sleep elsewhere a stated number of nights each year and the count resets.

Which means somewhere there is a person who has spent forty years going to their sister's house for three nights every year, on the same dates, for reasons the family stopped asking about a long time ago.

And the open problem

A species that already regards itself as one enormous family has a genuinely strange time with all of this, and the Restoration has not been able to get a straight answer from anybody about how it works.

Vance

A man who will argue with you about what is true, and will not raise his voice while he does it.

He has a position and it is not a complicated one: that being right is a smaller thing than being honest, and that most people who are pleased with how clever they are have quietly stopped doing the harder of the two. He puts it plainly, without ornament, and he puts it the same way the fourth time as the first.

Why it lands badly

Because he is unbothered. The person opposite him gets angrier as it goes and he does not move, and there is nothing more infuriating than a man who is not competing. Called weak for it, he takes that as a description rather than an insult and continues.

Vando

A Trailblazer, security on the concession, and the reason the Yinmelon story gets told at least once a rotation.

The job is the kraskor sweeps, which is what it sounds like: keeping several hundred kilos of horned animal away from people who are trying to build something. What is on the table at the festival is generally there because of him.

The run works like this. You put in at small settlements nobody surveys twice, and you sell what people at small settlements actually want: rockroot by the sack, glazberries, spice bundles tied with string. All of it real. All of it worth what you charge.

The fragmentation grenades ride in the Yinmelon sauce cans. Yinmelon sauce is thick, sweet, faintly orange, and sold in a can heavy enough that nobody picks one up expecting it to be light.

The one time it nearly came apart was a farmer's market on Monver, where a guard who had been standing in the sun for six hours asked for a taste.

He lost a thumb.

Vando tells it as a comedy, and it mostly is, and everybody laughs at the same place every time.

Vesk Iradin

A colonel of the Guard's Strategic Covert Operations Division, and a signature.

That is the whole of him. There is a rank, a division, and a name, and the name appears where an authorising officer's name appears, in the place on a form where somebody has to be accountable and where the person who is accountable is by design a person nobody has met.

No posting history. No unit. No photograph, no service dates, nothing filed anywhere that would let you work out whether he was ever a lieutenant.

A division that operates covertly does not publish its colonels, which is either the reason this record is empty or the excuse for it.

The Vitula

Two metres and more. Grey, and wet to the touch. Eight white eyes set around the head, so that there is no direction they cannot see. On the back, folded and useless, a pair of wings that have not carried anything in a very long time.

The body

Insect-descended, and without the shell you would expect from that: all of the mass is muscle and nerve. They breathe badly off their own worlds and wear masks everywhere else, bought by the employer and deducted from the wage.

Pain registers in them below the human mean. That is a property of the nervous system, documented in the pre-war literature, and it means what it says: they feel it less, so they keep working.

The disagreement

Guard instructional material says the Vitula have a collective mind and no individual will. The surviving biology says pheromone signalling, proximity awareness, and a distress sense good to about 1.6 kilometres that carries no content beyond the fact that somebody is hurt.

Both are printed here. They describe different animals.

Work

Excavation, tunnelling, deep foundation, haulage, foundry, and armed contract. Vitula crews appear in the construction record of eleven worlds, including as subcontractors on the Kitalia pylons, listed by crew and by rate. The kingdoms themselves are small, farmed at the surface and mined underneath.

When a king or queen dies, the pattern in the record is not succession crisis and not reprisal. It is a cluster of new engagements. The crews go and find whoever is hiring. This has been observed four times.

One further fact

Guard field instruction includes anatomy for this people, specifying the location of the heart. The manual is INTACT, is in current issue, and places that lesson at the same point in the syllabus as the lesson on how to operate a weapon.

The Vitula in the compound

Not a soldier. A labourer, standing in a place where labourers and soldiers end up looking identical to anyone arriving at speed.

His employer died. He took the next contract, because the next contract had the same terms as the last one and because the terms are the only part of the arrangement a Vitula in that position gets a say in. Nobody asked him what the work was for. Asking is not a step in the process.

He is in the compound for the same reason the floor is in the compound.

The employer's son died there too. Nobody has recorded whether the two of them were in the same room.

Wake

also known as: Waketin · the Wakeful Islands · Origin

A field of rock where a planet used to be. Held almost everywhere to be where humans came from, on the strength of genetic sampling whose method did not survive the people who used it.

Before

Every source we hold agrees it was a capital world. That is the only detail about this planet on which our sources do not disagree.

There is no census material. No municipal roll, no tax register, no conscription list, no birth record, nothing. Several people have described the census offices to us by location. None of the buildings survive.

The loss

Guard records say one ordnance deployment, Autumnal forces, GC 4394, over in under an hour.

Thirty-eight people across eleven settlements say it took between two and nine days. Six of them describe the sky changing colour before anything was heard. Four describe evacuation orders. One describes those orders being countermanded.

We print both. They cannot both be correct.

After

Mantle and core in pieces, sixty-one of them dense enough to be worth working. The Corefuel comes out of those, and it comes out of nowhere else with a licence on it, and the licence is issued by the Guard Board of Directors alone.

The ledgers for that trade are INTACT and unusually complete. Licensed extraction for GC 4461: 812,443.6 standard tonnes.

People lived out there while it was worked. Houses on the larger fragments, held down and given air by spires burning the planet they were standing on. There was a school.

Settlement names, populations and outcomes were not filed.

[Compiler's note: we hold four hundred and eleven pages of extraction ledger for this world and one page of anything else.]

Wake Extraction Station

The works where the homeworld gets turned into fuel. In the paperwork it is called Station, without a qualifier, because there is only one.

Raw fragment material comes in, synthesis happens, and certified Corefuel goes out to Guard transports. Everything that flies anywhere begins here.

The quota

The Board sets a number each year and the station meets it. The contract pays on certification of the full year's quota and not before, which means a station chief spends every year working toward a single date. Miss it and the year pays nothing.

The final year on record came in at 443.6 tonnes over.

Class 2

That rating entitles the station to point-defence parts every quarter, on request. The entitlements are all on file. The delivery notes are kept somewhere else and that series has gaps in it.

The Wakeful Islands

What people called the rocks they lived on. It is not a filing term. We use it because they use it, and because no document we hold has a name for the inhabited part of a dead planet.

How many

Sixty-one fragments are catalogued as worth extracting from. Some unstated number of those carried people. Our estimate of nine to thirty comes from counting gravity spire installations on the parts requisitions, and should be treated as exactly that good.

Why nobody was counted

They lived there under an extraction licence, not a settlement charter. In law they were not colonists. There was therefore no settlement roll to be on, which is how a place with a school ends up with no population figure.

What it was like, from testimony: houses linked by intercom because there was no network to link them with. One landing pad a fragment, one supply run a week. Gardens under spire air. And twice a standard year, for several days, an orbital condition that took the radio out entirely and against which the only remedy was to work to the published timetable.

Wedear

Officer school, and the place a career either turns or does not.

A cold, orderly world of lecture halls, map rooms and parade squares, where roughly four thousand people a year arrive convinced they are about to be given something.

Around two thousand nine hundred of them leave with a commission.

The rest go back

Returned to prior rank, in the language of the schedule, which means you rejoin your old unit at your old grade in front of everybody who watched you leave. The proportion sent back has never once dropped below a quarter, in any year on record, and Wedear does not appear to regard this as a problem to be solved.

Nobody talks about it afterward. A man who failed Wedear will mention Actom, mention his MOS, mention every posting since, and simply omit the year in between. It comes up eventually, usually late, usually once.

Weton

Grain from one horizon to the other, worked by families on long instruments with machinery nobody can build any more.

Harvest, GC 4461

1,204,880,600 tonnes, of which 1,204,880,600 tonnes were bought at the scheduled price. The purchase guarantee has been met in every year on record.

What Weton does not have

Its soil comes from Sheel. Its water is allocated from Corr. Its seed is licensed from Tall. Its grain leaves raw and is milled on Dorrow. It holds none of those functions and has never asked for one.

The machines

Every combine and hauler here is pre-war and irreplaceable, kept running under the system repair entitlement by yards whose senior mechanics are the most consequential people in any given district. A farmer here can afford to fix the tractor. That is not true anywhere else in this archive and everybody here knows it.

Wages are good. Wages are in scrip.

Wingsuits

Not a garment. A function of the armour, folded flat until you need it.

Strike the chestplate and sheets of material snap taut between the limbs, turning a falling man into something with a wing loading. The suit's temperature regulators take over at the same moment, which matters more than people expect, because the interesting places to do this are interesting for a reason.

What it is actually like

The wind screams past the helmet at a pitch that gets into the teeth. Rain hits the visor and streaks off sideways in trails. The suit fights the air for the first few seconds and then stops fighting it, and after that you are cutting rather than falling, and it is entirely possible to forget what you came down here to do.

The landing is the part nobody practises enough

You flare, you extend, and the ground arrives with more authority than the training tower ever managed. A good landing is a hard skid onto one knee. A bad one is the same thing with a longer skid.

Then you hit the panel and the material folds itself back into the armour, and there is no evidence you ever had it.

The Wipe

vernacular: the Fry

In GC 4401 every computer in the galaxy stopped, and everything any of them was holding stopped with it. Paper survived. That is the entire reason this volume exists.

The formal word is the Wipe, and it is what the filings and the law use. Everybody who was actually there calls it the Fry.

How complete

Total, as far as anything we can check. In nineteen years nobody on any world has described to us a device that kept working, and no archive anywhere has reported a surviving data holding. We keep the request open.

What went with it
  • every network. Communication fell back to couriers, unamplified radio, and towers the churches owned
  • every account. Money became paper, then became an entry in a Guard ledger
  • every drone and every unmanned system. Saigo is still trying to rebuild them
  • every navigational archive. The lanes were re-surveyed by hand over thirty years, and the survey authority publishes what that cost in ships and crews
  • the census

What survived

Insurers, port authorities, tax offices, monasteries and shipping clerks, all of whom kept duplicates in cabinets because that was the procedure. By weight this archive is about eighty per cent commercial and administrative paperwork.

Which is why we can tell you the tonnage of a cargo that left a world sixty years ago and not how many people were living on it.

[Compiler's note: the Guard's accounting division is understood to have retyped twenty years of ledger by hand after the event. We have applied four times to see it and have received three acknowledgements.]

Yakib Yalitio

goes by: Yake

Castle Team's medic, and the only one of them who does arithmetic before agreeing to something.

Evenly tanned, because he spends his rest days outside while everyone else is in the bar. Sandy brown hair that falls across his forehead the moment the helmet comes off. An easy, unbothered face that has nothing to do with how he actually works, which is fast and cold and very good. Yellow visor.

Home

A world he does not talk up much, with one thing on it worth the trip: a starship wreck the size of a city, Maldo era, so thoroughly overgrown that people climb it like a mountain. He climbed it with his father as a boy, in magboots, which were later killed by a lightning storm and never replaced.

Faith

He was raised religious in a way that is mostly relaxed and has a few strange corners he does not explain to outsiders. When he filled in the form that asks a recruit what rites they want, the list of eighty-eight faiths did not have his on it, so he wrote it in himself.

Money

He sends most of his pay home and has done since the day he signed. He is not shy about why, and he does not dress it up:

"I've fought next to you on every battle, but I will put my life on the line before my career. If I die, my family gets paid."

He is not the coward of this group. He is the only one keeping score.

Yinmelon

A big, heavy, fleshy fruit, mostly processed into a sauce of the same name and shipped in sealed tins by the container load.

It is one of the highest-volume food items moving anywhere, which is exactly why it is also one of the most common things written on the outside of a container holding something else entirely. Customs seizure returns are full of Yinmelon sauce that is not Yinmelon sauce.

The sauce itself is decent. Somebody has a story about a guard at a farmer's market on Monver who took a bribe in the form of a taste and lost a thumb to what was in the tin.

Zonar

Four thousand one hundred and eighteen licensed premises, and fewer residents than eleven member worlds that have none.

Nobody is from Zonar. Everybody is currently on Zonar. The principal city is a strip of light that does not go dark, licensed to within an inch of its life, and enormously profitable.

What it is for

Going all out. Forgetting a rotation. Getting so comprehensively wrecked that the following two days do not exist. It is where a squad goes when one of them has had something bad happen and nobody knows what to say about it, on the theory that a loud enough room is a kind of answer.

It is also where people practise being somebody else

A false name on Zonar costs nothing and means nothing, and a good many aliases that later turned out to matter were invented at a bar there by somebody who thought he was being funny.
